bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.name: Bone health: what helps keep bones strong
bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.summary: NHS pages link bone health to weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D, not smoking and keeping alcohol low.
keyPoints: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for bone strength.
Calcium is important for bone health, and vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
Being inactive, having a low body weight, smoking and heavy drinking are listed as risk factors for weaker bones.
The NHS advises adults aged 65 and over to include strength and balance activities on at least two days a week.

body.heading: What helps keep bones strong?
body.body: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for improving bone density. Running, skipping, dancing, aerobics and jumping are named as higher-impact examples that strengthen muscles, ligaments and joints. Swimming and cycling support general fitness but are not weight-bearing, so they do less for the bones. Lack of physical activity is listed as a risk factor for osteoporosis.

body.heading: What do calcium and vitamin D do?
body.body: The NHS says most adults should be able to get the calcium they need from their daily diet. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and the NHS says it can be difficult to get enough vitamin D from food alone, so a daily supplement may be considered. Sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September helps the body make vitamin D, and the NHS suggests considering a daily vitamin D supplement.

body.heading: What raises the risk of weaker bones?
body.body: Osteopenia is the stage of bone loss before osteoporosis, and being underweight is listed among the risk factors for bone loss. Smoking and heavy drinking are also listed, and one source gives the low-risk alcohol guidance of less than 14 units a week. The Royal Osteoporosis Society says too much salt may increase the amount of calcium lost in urine.

body.heading: What changes after 65?
body.body: NHS guidance for people aged 65 and over advises activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. It also advises 150 minutes (2 and a half hours) of moderate-intensity activity a week, ideally spread across the days. NHS 111 Wales suggests that people diagnosed with osteoporosis talk to a GP or health specialist before starting a new exercise programme. A DEXA bone density scan is often used to help diagnose osteoporosis or to assess the risk of it.

references.title: NHS: Keep your bones strong over 65
NHS inform: Bone health and falls

bone-marrow-biopsy-what-happens-and-why.name: Bone marrow biopsy: what happens and why
bone-marrow-biopsy-what-happens-and-why.summary: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone, to find out why blood counts are abnormal or to look for abnormal cells.
keyPoints: A bone marrow biopsy takes a small sample of bone marrow, usually from the back of the hip bone.
It is done to find out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells in the marrow.
Local anaesthetic numbs the area, and sedation may be offered; aching or bruising for a few days afterwards is common.
Results can take from a few days up to about four weeks, depending on the hospital and the tests, and are usually discussed at a clinic appointment.

body.heading: What is a bone marrow biopsy?
body.body:
Bone marrow is the spongy tissue inside bones where blood cells are made. A bone marrow biopsy removes a small sample so that it can be examined in a laboratory.

Macmillan says the sample is taken from the back of the hip bone, which is part of the pelvis, or occasionally from the breastbone. The test usually has two parts. An aspirate draws out liquid marrow with a syringe, and a trephine biopsy takes a small core of marrow using a slightly larger needle.

body.heading: Why might I need one?
body.body:
The test is usually done to work out why blood counts are abnormal and to look for abnormal cells. NHS leaflets list a low or high number of red cells, white cells or platelets, and infection, among the reasons.

The results help the doctor diagnose the illness and make decisions about care and treatment.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body:
Local anaesthetic is used to numb the area, and gas and air may also be available. Medicine to help the person relax, called a sedative, may be offered.

It may feel uncomfortable for a few seconds while the liquid marrow is drawn into the syringe. A Macmillan booklet says the test takes about 20 to 30 minutes, though hospitals vary. One hospital leaflet says the whole appointment takes about an hour.

body.heading: What is it like afterwards?
body.body:
A dressing is placed over the area, and hospital leaflets say how long to keep it on and dry. After sedation, Macmillan advises not driving for 24 hours and having someone take the person home and stay with them overnight. Aching or a bruised feeling for a few days is common.

Hospital leaflets say patients are usually asked about blood-thinning medicines beforehand. Leaflets say to contact the hospital team about swelling or redness at the site; a GP or NHS 111 can also advise.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body:
Soreness and bruising at the site are common and usually last a few days. Serious complications are uncommon.

Bleeding at the site usually stops with pressure, sometimes leaving a small bruise. Infection and nerve injury are described as rare, and an allergic reaction to the numbing medicine is listed as a possible risk.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body: Timing varies by hospital. One trust says results can take up to two weeks, and another up to four weeks. Results are usually given at the next clinic appointment.

breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.name: Found a breast lump: what happens next
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.headline: Found a breast lump? Causes, the GP appointment and what the breast clinic does
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.summary: Most breast lumps are harmless, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any new lump so it can be checked. A GP examines the breast and refers to a breast clinic if the cause is unclear.
keyPoints: The NHS says most breast lumps are harmless, with fibroadenomas and cysts among the common causes.
NHS 111 Wales advises getting any new breast lump checked by a GP.
If the GP is unsure of the cause, they refer to a hospital breast clinic.
At a breast clinic you may have an examination, a scan and sometimes a biopsy.

body.heading: Are most breast lumps harmless?
body.body: The NHS says most breast lumps are not cancer. Common causes include fibroadenomas, which are solid benign lumps, and cysts, which are fluid-filled sacs. Sometimes a breast lump can be a sign of something more serious, such as breast cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises contacting a GP about any lump in the breast or armpit. The NHS also advises seeing a GP about other changes to the breast that are unusual for you. A new lump is worth getting checked even if it is painless. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP rather than trying to work out the cause of a lump yourself. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in the breast, chest or armpit, skin dimpling or redness, and a change in the size or shape of a breast among the symptoms to have checked. Nipple discharge, which may be bloody, and nipple changes such as inversion or a rash are also listed. Having one of these symptoms does not definitely mean breast cancer, but the NHS says it is important to have it checked by a GP.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales says the GP may ask about any breast screening you have had and whether anyone in your family has had breast cancer. The GP then examines the breasts. If the GP is not sure what is causing the lump, they refer the person to a breast clinic at a hospital.

body.heading: How is an urgent referral decided?
body.body: In England, NICE guidance on suspected cancer sets out who should be offered an urgent referral to a breast clinic. An urgent referral in England aims for an appointment at the breast clinic within two weeks. Referral guidance can differ between the UK nations.

body.heading: What does the breast clinic do?
body.body: Tests at a breast clinic usually include an examination of the breasts and an imaging scan, usually a mammogram or an ultrasound. Sometimes a biopsy is taken, in which a needle removes a small sample of cells from the lump. Some results may be available on the same day, while others, such as a biopsy, can take one to two weeks.

body.heading: How can breasts be checked at home?
body.body: The NHS has a page on how to check your breasts or chest, so that a person knows how they normally look and feel. Its guidance describes looking in a mirror with the arms at the sides and then raised, and feeling each breast along with the area up to the collarbone and under the armpit. The NHS says to contact a GP about any change, including a new lump.

breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.name: Breast screening: who is invited and what happens
breast-screening-mammogram-what-to-expec.summary: NHS breast screening uses mammograms to look for breast cancer in people without symptoms. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment, results and harms.
keyPoints: The NHS offers breast screening from age 50 up to the 71st birthday, with invitations every three years.
A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast, with each breast pressed between two plates.
Breast screening is offered to people without symptoms to look for breast cancer, and it does not prevent breast cancer.
Screening can miss a cancer and can raise false alarms, and some people are diagnosed with a cancer that would never have caused harm.

body.heading: Who is invited for breast screening?
body.body: The NHS says screening is offered from age 50 up to the 71st birthday. The first invitation usually comes between the ages of 50 and 53, and further invitations follow every three years until the 71st birthday. Anyone registered with a GP as female is invited automatically. People over 71 are not invited automatically but can ask for screening every three years. For trans and non-binary people, eligibility for breast screening depends on the sex registered with the GP and on any hormone treatment or surgery, so NHS guidance advises checking with the GP or local screening service.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: A mammogram takes two X-rays of each breast. Each breast is pressed between two plates, which some people find uncomfortable or painful, but any discomfort should not last long. NHS pages say the mammogram itself takes only a few minutes and the whole appointment should take no longer than 30 minutes.

body.heading: How and when are the results given?
body.body: Results usually come within two weeks of the appointment and are also sent to the GP. If the mammogram needs a closer look, the person is invited back to an assessment clinic for further tests. A Royal Marsden page says about 4 in 100 women are asked to come back, and about three in four of those have normal results after further tests.

body.heading: What are the benefits?
body.body: Breast screening is offered to people without symptoms, using mammograms to look for breast cancer. It does not prevent breast cancer.

body.heading: What are the harms and limits?
body.body: Screening does not always find a cancer that is there, so some people with breast cancer are missed. Some people are asked back for more tests and then found not to have cancer, and the follow-up tests can be invasive and time-consuming. Some people who are screened are diagnosed and treated for a breast cancer that would never have been found or caused them harm.

body.heading: How is it presented as a choice?
body.body: The NHS leaflet 'Helping you decide' describes breast screening as a personal choice and sets out its benefits and risks. It says screening does not prevent breast cancer from developing. Overdiagnosis means finding a cancer that would never have caused harm, and estimates of how often it happens vary between studies. A 2012 independent review estimated that among 10,000 UK women invited to screening from age 50 for 20 years, about 43 breast cancer deaths would be prevented and 129 cancers would be overdiagnosed, although other estimates differ.

body.heading: What if there is a lump between screens?
body.body: Cancer Research UK says anyone who notices changes to their nipples, chest area or armpits should not wait for screening and should tell their doctor.

burns-and-scalds-first-aid-and-when-to-g.name: Burns and scalds: first aid and when to get help
burns-and-scalds-first-aid-and-when-to-g.summary: Cooling a burn under running water for 20 minutes is the first step; the NHS says large, deep, facial, chemical or electrical burns need A&E or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS says a burn should be cooled with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible after the injury.
NHS advice is never to use ice, iced water, creams or greasy substances such as butter on a burn, and not to burst blisters.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a burn that is very large or deep, is on the face or genitals, or is caused by a chemical or electricity.
For children, the NHS says that, depending on how severe the burn or scald is, the choice is a GP, a minor injuries unit or A&E.
The NHS says small burns and scalds usually close in about two weeks, and that a wound not healed after two weeks needs urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111.

body.heading: What is the difference between a burn and a scald, and how are they sized?
body.body: Burns are skin damage from dry heat such as fire or a hot object, and scalds are skin damage from hot liquid or steam. NHS-linked guidance describes a minor burn as affecting the outer layers of skin, which look red or pale pink, slightly swollen and painful. Deeper burns that cause white or charred skin are described as needing emergency assessment. A burn the size of the person's hand or bigger is described by the Healthier Together service as an emergency. Blistering at the burn site is also listed as a reason to seek urgent help for a child.

body.heading: What first aid does the NHS describe?
body.body: The NHS describes cooling the burn with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible after the injury. Clothing or jewellery near the burn is described as taken off, but anything stuck to the burnt skin is left in place because removing it could cause more damage. After cooling, the NHS describes covering the burn with cling film laid in a layer over it, rather than wrapped around a limb. NHS 111 Wales adds that a clean, clear plastic bag can be used for a burn on the hand. For a child, the NHS describes keeping the child warm and avoiding ice or very cold water, which can make the wound worse.

body.heading: What should be avoided, and what helps with the pain?
body.body: The NHS says never to use ice, iced water, or any cream or greasy substance such as butter on a burn. Blisters will burst naturally, and the NHS advises against bursting them because this can cause infection. For pain, the NHS suggests paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the maker's instructions on the packet. It adds that children under 16 should not be given aspirin.

body.heading: Which burns need A&E or a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a burn that is very large or deep. The same applies to a burn on the face, genitals or bottom, and to a burn caused by an acid, a chemical or electricity. The NHS also says not to drive to hospital, and to ask someone else to drive or to call 999 for an ambulance. NHS treatment guidance also says to go to A&E if someone has been injured on purpose or if that is suspected. Healthier Together guidance adds burns on the neck, hands, feet or any joint to the list needing urgent assessment. Breathing in smoke can cause delayed symptoms such as coughing, a sore throat, difficulty breathing or singed nasal hair, and these still need A&E. Where a burn is smaller and less deep, the NHS says it can often be treated at home.

body.heading: What about chemical and electrical burns?
body.body: For a chemical burn, the NHS acid and chemical burns page lists calling 999 first. It then describes removing contaminated clothing, brushing off dry chemicals and flushing the area with cool or lukewarm running water for about an hour. The NHS says treatment for these burns happens in hospital, where painkillers, antibiotics and fluids into a vein may be given. A burn caused by electricity is also in the NHS list of burns needing 999 or A&E. Burn network guidance gives longer rinsing times for some chemical burns, so the duration is not the same in every source.

body.heading: What about children and babies?
body.body: For a child, the NHS describes putting the burn or scald under cool running water for 20 to 30 minutes straight away. It then says to see a GP, or go to a minor injuries unit or A&E, depending on how severe the burn or scald is. Where there is no running water, the NHS child page describes using cold water or another cool fluid such as milk.

body.heading: How does a burn heal, and what are the signs of infection?
body.body: The NHS says how long a burn takes to heal depends on how serious it is and how it is treated. Minor, superficial burns usually close in about two weeks, while deeper burns can take months or longer. The NHS advises urgent medical advice from a GP or NHS 111 if the wound has not healed after two weeks. The NHS Recovery page lists a wound that becomes painful or smelly, a high temperature, or a dressing soaked with fluid as other reasons for urgent advice. Hospital patient leaflets add spreading redness, swelling, warmth and discharge as possible signs of infection. The South West Burns Clinical Network says a burn not healed in this time can carry a risk of sepsis.

cardiovascular-service-framework-england.name: Heart disease and stroke framework for England
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.headline: Government and NHS England publish a 10-year framework on heart disease and stroke
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.summary: The government and NHS England have published a cardiovascular disease framework that aims to cut premature deaths from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England published a cardiovascular disease modern service framework on 7 July 2026.
It sets a 10-year aim of cutting premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England by a quarter.
The government describes 12 priorities for the first three years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: The government and NHS England say the framework is a 10-year strategic vision to reduce premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England. It sets out 12 priorities for the next three years. The government says the priorities include finding people at risk of cardiovascular disease, blood pressure and cholesterol treatment targets, stroke care and rehabilitation. It also includes a partnership with Diabetes UK to raise public awareness of the link between type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The government estimates that successful implementation could prevent between 1,600 and 2,400 premature deaths a year from heart disease and stroke in people under 75 in the first three years. It estimates this would rise to between 3,850 and 4,900 deaths a year after a decade. These are the government's projections, not results already achieved. The government describes the framework as part of a shift from reactive care towards prevention.

caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.name: Looking after someone with dementia
caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.headline: Looking after someone with dementia: what the NHS advises
caring-for-someone-with-dementia-nhs-adv.summary: The NHS suggests a daily routine, and says carers can ask the council for a free carer's assessment.
keyPoints: Guidance from dementia charities and NHS trusts suggests speaking slowly with simple words and keeping eye contact.
The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem.
A carer's assessment is free, and the NHS says anyone over 18 can ask for one.
A lasting power of attorney must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used.
The NHS route for sudden confusion is to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: How can I talk with someone who has dementia?
body.body:
Guidance from dementia charities and NHS trusts suggests speaking a little more slowly and using simple words. It also suggests keeping eye contact, which helps the person focus on the speaker. Asking fewer questions can help, and so can offering options or questions with a yes or no answer.

One guide advises that if the person does not understand even after a repeat, the speaker can try saying it in a slightly different way. When the person is distressed, the advice includes reassurance, for example by holding their hand if that feels appropriate.

body.heading: What helps with daily routines and safety at home?
body.body:
The NHS suggests having a daily routine, including daily walks. Another source notes that a familiar routine, with activities in the same order, can really help the person.

For people who walk about and may go missing, carers are advised to consider tracking technology, because a switched-on mobile phone may make it possible to trace someone. Alzheimer's Society material also describes movement monitors and pressure pads that send an alert to a carer when they are stepped on. These can be placed at the front door.

body.heading: Why might behaviour change, and what can help?
body.body:
The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem. It says it is very important to ask a doctor to rule out or treat any underlying cause, such as uncontrolled pain, untreated depression, infection (for example a urinary tract infection) or side effects of medicines.

Alzheimer's Society advises asking the doctor to review all the medicines the person takes, including any bought without a prescription. If the GP rules out health problems as the cause, they may refer the person to a mental health team. Alzheimer's Society says antipsychotic drugs should only be prescribed by a doctor as a last resort, when other treatments have been tried and did not work. It adds that they should only be used if the person's behaviour is persistently causing severe distress or putting them or others at risk of physical harm.

body.heading: What if confusion comes on suddenly?
body.body:
The NHS route for sudden confusion is to call 999 or go to A&E. NHS 111 Wales also advises going to A&E or calling 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused, and notes that it may be life threatening.

The NHS lists infection, such as a urinary tract infection (UTI), a stroke or TIA (mini-stroke), and low blood sugar in people with diabetes among the most common causes. Other causes include head injury, some prescription medicines, and alcohol or drug issues. NHS Inform Scotland says infections, including urinary and chest infections, can trigger delirium, which is more common in older people and those with dementia.

Dementia UK describes delirium as a state of sudden, intense confusion that can make people increasingly anxious, distressed and disorientated. It also says that for an emergency the route is 999 or A&E, and that NHS 111 is the contact for medical advice that is not an emergency.

body.heading: What support is there for the person doing the caring?
body.body:
A carer's assessment is free, and the NHS says anyone over 18 can ask for one. It is arranged through the local council's adult social services. A council worker asks how caring affects the carer's physical and mental health, work, free time and relationships. The NHS guide says the assessment is usually face to face, though some councils can do it over the phone or online.

Several councils say a carer does not need to live with the person they look after, or care full-time, to have an assessment. The assessment is separate from any needs assessment the person being cared for might have, but both can be done at the same time. If the carer qualifies for help, the carer and the council agree a care and support plan.

Admiral Nurses are specialist dementia nurses. Dementia UK runs a free Admiral Nurse Dementia Helpline that gives information, advice and support on any aspect of dementia. It is open Monday to Friday 9am to 9pm, and on weekends and bank holidays 9am to 5pm.

body.heading: How can a family plan ahead?
body.body:
There are two kinds of lasting power of attorney (LPA), one for health and welfare and one for property and financial affairs. An attorney can only make a decision on the donor's behalf where, even with support, the donor is not able to make that decision on their own. A health and welfare LPA can only be used if the donor does not have mental capacity. A property and financial affairs LPA can be used as soon as it is registered, if the donor chooses that.

The property and financial version covers things such as managing a bank or building society account, paying bills, collecting benefits or a pension, and selling a home. The health and welfare version covers daily routine, medical care, moving into a care home, and life-sustaining treatment.

An LPA must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian before it can be used. If an LPA can no longer be used, someone may have to apply to the Court of Protection to become the person's deputy. A deputy must send a report to the Office of the Public Guardian and pay a fee every year.

body.heading: Where can I get urgent help if things become too much?
body.body:
Caring can be hard on the carer. One source encourages carers to talk to a friend or family member, or to a professional such as a counsellor or dementia adviser.

NHS Every Mind Matters says that if there is an immediate danger to life or safety, the route is to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help that is not an emergency, the route is to dial NHS 111 and choose the mental health option. Callers are connected to someone trained to help people in an urgent mental health crisis, who can listen, assess what support is needed and help find the right service.

NHS trust pages say Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time.

cdc-2026-2027-respiratory-season-outlook.name: CDC outlook for the 2026-27 respiratory season
cdc-2026-2027-respiratory-season-outlook.summary: The US CDC's outlook dated 23 September 2026 expects the peak of combined COVID-19, flu and RSV hospital admissions to be similar to last season, with low to moderate confidence.
keyPoints: The CDC published its 2026-2027 Respiratory Disease Season Outlook on 23 September 2026.
It expects the combined peak hospitalisation rate for COVID-19, influenza and RSV to be within 20% of the 2025-2026 peak.
The CDC calls the outlook high-level information, not a forecast, and says it may change.
This outlook describes the US, not the UK.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a 2026-2027 Respiratory Disease Season Outlook dated 23 September 2026.

The CDC describes it as high-level information on how the season could unfold, and says it is not a forecast.

It expects the peak combined hospitalisation rate for COVID-19, influenza and RSV to be within 20% of the 2025-2026 peak, with low to moderate confidence.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
For influenza, the CDC says there is no evidence that a high-severity season is more likely this year.

For RSV, it notes that the 2025-2026 peak came later than in earlier seasons and that the cause of the late peak is unclear.

The CDC lists a higher peak as a risk, driven by viruses that evade existing immunity or by lower vaccine uptake or effectiveness.

This outlook describes the US season; UK figures and vaccination advice come from UKHSA and the NHS.

cervical-screening-what-to-expect.name: Cervical screening: what happens and results
cervical-screening-what-to-expect.summary: Cervical screening checks a sample from the cervix for high-risk HPV. This guide covers who is invited, the appointment and what each result means.
keyPoints: The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening.
The sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus that can lead to cell changes.
A negative HPV result means the person is offered screening again in five years.
Cancer Research UK says cervical screening is not a test for cancer; it looks for HPV and cell changes.

body.heading: Who is invited and how often?
body.body: The NHS in England invites people with a cervix aged 25 to 64 for cervical screening. Routine screening is every five years. From 1 July 2025 in England, people who test negative for HPV are offered screening again after five years rather than three; guidance says some people last invited before that date may still be on a three-year interval.

body.heading: What is cervical screening for?
body.body: The NHS describes cervical screening as a test of the health of the cervix that helps to prevent cervical cancer, rather than a test for cancer. The NHS says screening is still important for people who have had the HPV vaccine. Booking is usually through the GP surgery, online or in the NHS App, and some sexual health clinics also offer it.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: Cervical screening is usually done by a female nurse or doctor, and a person can ask for a female practitioner when booking. The clinician gently places a tool called a speculum in the vagina and uses a soft brush to collect cells from the cervix. One source says the test itself should take less than five minutes, and the whole appointment usually lasts 10 to 15 minutes. People can ask for a smaller speculum or ask to insert the speculum themselves. Light spotting for a few hours afterwards is normal.

body.heading: How can the appointment be made easier?
body.body: The NHS suggests wearing something that can stay on during the test, such as a skirt or long top, and bringing someone for support. The NHS says the person can ask to stop at any time and can ask for adjustments, such as a smaller speculum or a different position, to feel more comfortable.

body.heading: Why is the sample tested for HPV?
body.body: Current NHS practice tests the sample for high-risk HPV first. The NHS England guide says high-risk HPV can cause abnormal cell changes that may lead to cervical cancer. If HPV is found, the laboratory then looks more closely at the cells for changes.

body.heading: What do the results mean?
body.body: If HPV is not found, the person is offered screening again in five years. If HPV is found but the cells are normal, the person is usually retested in about 12 months. If HPV is found with abnormal cells, the person is referred for a colposcopy. If more tests are needed, the results letter says what to do next. Results are sent by letter or given by telephone, and the letter says what to do if more tests are needed.

body.heading: What is a colposcopy?
body.body: A colposcopy is the usual next step after an abnormal screening result. Cancer Research UK says cervical screening is not a test for cancer; it looks for HPV and cell changes. A biopsy is examined by a pathologist, who grades any cell changes as CIN1, CIN2 or CIN3.

body.heading: Bleeding or symptoms between screens
body.body: Cancer Research UK advises that bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, or unusual discharge, should be checked by a GP.

chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.name: Chest pain: causes and when to get help
chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.summary: Most chest pain does not come from the heart, but sudden pain that does not ease or spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E.

For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

body.heading: What causes chest pain?
body.body: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem. Common causes that do not involve the heart include heartburn or indigestion, a strained chest muscle, anxiety or panic, and chest infections such as pneumonia or pleurisy. Shingles can also cause chest pain, often with a skin rash. Angina, heart attack and pericarditis are heart conditions that can cause chest pain. Pericarditis is inflammation of the lining around the heart, and the NHS says it often follows a viral infection such as a cold or flu.

body.heading: How do angina and a heart attack differ?
body.body: Angina is chest pain that is a sign of a heart problem, and GTN can be used to ease an attack or before a known trigger such as exercise. Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes. The NHS says chest pain is the most common symptom of a heart attack, but symptoms vary from person to person. Other signs include pain spreading to the arms, jaw, neck or back, sweating, breathlessness and feeling or being sick, and some people have these without any chest pain. Unlike the pain of angina, the symptoms of a heart attack are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray. A heart attack can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Chest pain that comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness is in the same group. The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E. For someone already diagnosed with angina, the NHS treats pain that does not settle after rest or after their usual angina medicine as an emergency that needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When should chest pain be checked the same day?
body.body: For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111. Angina that feels worse than before, happens more often, lasts longer or happens at rest is a reason to contact a GP urgently.

body.heading: What happens at the GP or in hospital?
body.body: If a GP thinks someone may have angina, they can be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist). Tests to find out whether someone is having a heart attack include an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram. An ECG records the heart's electrical activity. An NHS emergency department leaflet says staff check for serious causes such as a heart attack, a blood clot in the lung and a collapsed lung. The Sussex hospital leaflet says staff may test for troponin, which shows whether the heart is involved, and for D-dimer, which looks for clots in the lungs. The Sussex hospital leaflet says a normal troponin result makes a heart problem less likely, but does not necessarily mean the pain is unrelated to the heart.

body.heading: How are angina and a heart attack treated?
body.body: Tests for a heart attack include an ECG and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram, which can show exactly where blood flow to the heart is blocked. A heart attack needs emergency treatment in hospital, and treatment can include medicine, coronary angioplasty (opening blocked arteries with a stent) and coronary artery bypass surgery. NHS treatment for angina aims to help stop attacks and reduce the risk of further problems such as a heart attack. Medicines for angina include GTN, beta blockers, which slow the heart, and calcium channel blockers, which relax the arteries, and surgery may be recommended if medicines are not controlling angina. A GP may ask about lifestyle, such as diet, smoking and drinking, and healthy lifestyle changes alongside treatment can help control angina.

childhood-rashes-chickenpox-measles-hand.name: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth
childhood-rashes-chickenpox-measles-hand.summary: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth all cause rashes in children, but their other signs and the advice on getting help differ.
keyPoints: Chickenpox causes red, itchy spots that turn into fluid-filled blisters and then scabs.
Measles starts with cold-like symptoms, and a rash appears a few days later.
Hand, foot and mouth disease usually clears up on its own in seven to ten days, and antibiotics will not help.
For measles, the NHS advises phoning the GP surgery before going in, because it can spread easily.
A rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: How can a parent tell these three rashes apart?
body.body:
All three illnesses can cause a rash, so the other symptoms and the pattern of the spots help to tell them apart. Chickenpox may start with mild flu-like symptoms, and these tend to be more common and worse in adults than in children. The rash is made of red, itchy spots that turn into fluid-filled blisters. The blisters then crust over to form scabs, which eventually drop off.

Measles begins with cold-like symptoms, such as a runny nose, a cough, red and watery eyes and a high temperature. A rash then appears a few days later. It usually starts on the head or neck and spreads over the body. The rash is made of small red-brown spots that may join into blotchy patches, and it is not usually itchy.

Hand, foot and mouth disease typically starts with a fever, a sore throat, a poor appetite and feeling unwell. Mouth ulcers and a rash of red spots on the hands and feet follow. The spots become blisters that are grey in the centre and can be painful.

body.heading: How do the infections spread?
body.body:
Chickenpox is infectious from one to two days before the rash starts. UK government guidance says children with chickenpox should stay away from nursery or school until five days after the rash first appears.

Measles virus is contained in tiny droplets that come out of the nose and mouth when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The NHS says people are infectious from when symptoms start until about four days after the rash first appears. Measles can spread easily to others, which is why the NHS advises calling the GP surgery before going in.

Hand, foot and mouth disease spreads through coughs, sneezes and poo. NHS guidance says people are infectious for a few days before symptoms begin and for the first five days after symptoms start.

body.heading: What is the usual course of each illness?
body.body:
There is no treatment for chickenpox itself. Pharmacy remedies include paracetamol for fever and calamine lotion or cooling gels for itching. After one to two weeks the crusted skin falls off naturally.

With measles, UK guidance is to keep a child away from nursery or school for at least four full days from when the rash first appears. The NHS says normal activities can restart after four days if the person feels well and no longer has a temperature.

Hand, foot and mouth disease usually clears up on its own in seven to ten days, and antibiotics will not help. NHS guidance says drinking fluids helps to prevent dehydration, and it advises avoiding acidic drinks such as fruit juice.

body.heading: When should a parent phone NHS 111 or the GP?
body.body:
For chickenpox, NHS guidance for parents says to contact the GP straight away if the blisters become infected. NHS guidance says to phone NHS 111 if the GP practice is closed.

For measles, the NHS says a child with the illness will need to see a GP. It advises phoning the surgery before going in, because measles can spread to other people easily.

For hand, foot and mouth disease, NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if symptoms do not improve after seven to ten days, if the fever is very high or if dehydration develops. Signs of dehydration include sunken eyes, drowsiness or no urine for 12 hours. Swollen lips or tongue with struggling to breathe is listed as an urgent warning sign, with advice to call NHS 111 or seek emergency care.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS says a rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and to call 999 straight away. The NHS adds that not everyone with meningitis gets a rash, so other signs matter too. These include a high temperature, a headache, vomiting, drowsiness, a stiff neck and sensitivity to light.

On darker skin the rash is harder to see, so NHS guidance suggests checking paler areas such as the palms, the soles of the feet, the roof of the mouth and the eyelids.

For measles, the NHS lists a seizure, severe breathing difficulty, being unable to stay awake, sudden confusion or a rash that does not fade under a glass as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E. NHS guidance for parents lists breathing difficulty, confusion, a seizure or a rash that does not fade under a glass as emergencies in chickenpox.

body.heading: What if someone is pregnant or has a weak immune system?
body.body:
People at higher risk from chickenpox include pregnant women, people with a weakened immune system and very young babies. UK guidance says these groups should contact the GP for advice if they have been exposed, even when there is no rash or other symptom. The NHS chickenpox page advises urgent help for anyone who has been near someone with chickenpox and is pregnant or has a weakened immune system.

Complications of measles are more likely in people with a weakened immune system, in babies under one year old and in pregnant women. Anyone who is pregnant and has been in close contact with measles is told to contact the GP urgently.

For hand, foot and mouth disease, NHS guidance says there is normally no risk to the pregnancy or baby. An infection shortly before birth can mean the baby is born with a mild version of it. NHS guidance advises contacting a GP or midwife if pregnant and infected or exposed.

body.heading: Can vaccination prevent these illnesses?
body.body:
Measles can be prevented with the MMR vaccine, which is given in two doses as part of the NHS childhood vaccination programme. The NHS says two doses of MMR give the best protection against measles, mumps and rubella.

UKHSA says the MMRV vaccine, which also protects against chickenpox, has been added to the routine childhood schedule from January 2026. GOV.UK guidance for healthcare professionals says children born on or after 1 January 2020 who need MMR catch-up should be offered MMRV. Children born on or after 1 January 2025 are due two doses of MMRV, at 12 months and 18 months.

choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.name: Choking in adults and children: what to do
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.headline: Choking in adults, children and babies: what first-aid guidance describes
choking-what-the-nhs-and-resus-council-d.summary: First-aid guidance describes back blows and abdominal thrusts for severe choking, 999 if the blockage stays, and a medical check after abdominal thrusts.
keyPoints: Mild choking is described as being able to speak, cough or breathe, and encouraging the person to keep coughing is the advice.
Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe, and the person may become unconscious without help.
For adults, first-aid sources describe up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts, repeated in turn.
Babies under one are described as having back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
Anyone treated with abdominal thrusts or chest thrusts is described as needing a check by a health professional afterwards.

body.heading: How can mild and severe choking be told apart?
body.body:
First-aid guidance describes mild choking as a person who can still speak, cough or breathe. Such a person can usually clear the blockage alone, and the advice is to encourage them to keep coughing. The Resuscitation Council UK advises against blind finger sweeps of the mouth, because they can push the object further back.

Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe. Without help, the person eventually becomes unconscious. First-aid guidance only moves to back blows when coughing is not possible or is not working.

body.heading: What do first-aid sources describe for a choking adult?
body.body:
NHS inform describes leaning the person well forward and giving up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand. If the blockage remains, it describes abdominal thrusts, with a clenched fist placed between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone, gripped with the other hand and pulled sharply inwards and upwards. This is repeated up to five times.

The British Red Cross gives the same order of steps for an adult: encourage coughing, then up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts. The Resuscitation Council UK 2025 guidance describes alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts until the choking is relieved or the person becomes unresponsive. For a pregnant person, the Resuscitation Council UK says abdominal thrusts are not performed, and the hands are placed higher, over the lower end of the breastbone.

body.heading: When is 999 called, and what if the person stops responding?
body.body:
NHS inform describes calling 999 if the blockage has not cleared, then repeating the back blows and abdominal thrusts while waiting for help. The Resuscitation Council UK describes calling 999 once choking has not been relieved after the first five abdominal thrusts. The British Red Cross says to call 999 if the person is still choking. St John Ambulance describes calling 999 or 112 for a baby or child if the blockage has not cleared. The wording on timing differs a little between sources, but each links the call to a blockage that has not cleared.

If the person becomes unresponsive, the Resuscitation Council UK describes starting CPR and making sure 999 has been called. NHS inform describes opening the airway, checking breathing, and starting CPR if the person is not breathing.

body.heading: How does choking in a baby under one differ?
body.body:
The NHS describes up to five sharp back blows, with the baby lying face down along the thigh or forearm and the head kept low. If the blockage stays, the NHS describes up to five chest thrusts, with the baby face up and two fingers placed in the middle of the chest, just below the nipple line. The NHS describes checking the mouth between each blow or thrust.

Abdominal thrusts are not used on babies under one year old. The NHS says to call 999 if the object does not come out, and to keep alternating back blows and chest thrusts until help arrives. If the baby becomes unconscious, it describes calling 999 and starting CPR. The Resuscitation Council UK likewise describes back blows and chest thrusts rather than abdominal thrusts for infants. The NHS also advises against finger sweeps, which can push the object further back.

body.heading: What changes for a child over one?
body.body:
The NHS pairs back blows with abdominal thrusts for children over one. It describes a clenched fist placed between the navel and the ribs, pulled sharply inwards and upwards, repeated up to five times, checking after each whether the object has come out. If the blockage does not clear after back blows and abdominal thrusts, the NHS describes calling 999 and continuing the cycle until help arrives.

The British Red Cross describes continuing cycles of back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object comes out, help arrives or the child becomes unresponsive. St John Ambulance describes starting child CPR if the child becomes unresponsive. For children, the Resuscitation Council UK paediatric guidance describes up to five back blows if coughing is not possible or is becoming ineffective, followed by thrusts.

body.heading: Is a medical check needed afterwards?
body.body:
The NHS says that even when the object comes out, medical help is advised, because part of the object may remain or the child may have been hurt by the procedure. The Resuscitation Council UK gives a similar reason for adults, saying that complications and injuries can occur after abdominal thrusts or chest compressions, so a healthcare professional should see anyone treated this way.

St John Ambulance says that every baby who has had chest thrusts, and every child who has had abdominal thrusts, should be seen in hospital, even if the blockage has cleared.

The Resuscitation Council UK published new first-aid guidelines in October 2025, so its current pages are the reference if details change.

cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.name: High cholesterol: diet, tests and medicines
cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS says cutting down on saturated fat can help lower cholesterol, and that medicines such as statins are considered when lifestyle changes are not enough.
keyPoints: High cholesterol means too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood, and it usually causes no symptoms.
The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially saturated fat, and swapping to unsaturated fats.
Soluble fibre from foods such as oats, barley, beans and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol.
A blood test measures cholesterol, and an NHS Health Check in England may offer it.

body.heading: What is cholesterol and why does it matter?
body.body: High cholesterol means having too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood. Too much cholesterol in the blood can build up in the artery walls and make them narrower over time. HDL is often called good cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from the blood, while LDL is often called bad cholesterol because it can build up in artery walls. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms, which is why a blood test is used to find it.

body.heading: Who is more likely to have it?
body.body: Causes and risk factors listed include eating a lot of food high in saturated fat and a family history of high cholesterol. It can also run in families, and the British Heart Foundation lists ethnicity, being male and having been through the menopause among the factors that raise risk.

body.heading: What does diet change?
body.body: The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially food containing saturated fat. The NHS suggests unsaturated fats instead, such as oily fish, nuts, seeds and olive or rapeseed oil, and lists meat pies, butter, cakes and coconut or palm oil among foods to limit. Soluble fibre from oats, barley, beans, pulses and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol. Plant sterols and stanols, added to some foods such as spreads, can also help lower cholesterol. The British Heart Foundation says cholesterol in food has a minimal impact on blood cholesterol levels, and that cutting down on saturated fat matters more.

body.heading: When are medicines considered?
body.body: The NHS says medicine may be needed if cholesterol has not gone down after changes to diet and lifestyle, or if a person is at high risk of a heart attack or stroke. Statins are the most common medicine for high cholesterol, and the NHS says people usually need to take them for life.

body.heading: How is cholesterol tested?
body.body: Testing is a blood test. In England it can be offered as part of an NHS Health Check for people aged 40 to 74 who do not already have cardiovascular disease. A GP may also suggest a test for someone with high blood pressure, diabetes, overweight, smoking or a family history of heart disease. Targets depend on factors such as age and other health conditions, so a clinician advises what applies to each person.

cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.name: Cholesterol test results explained
cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.summary: A cholesterol test reports total, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides, and doctors read them with other risk factors.
keyPoints: A standard cholesterol test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured with them.
Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL, and it covers all the harmful types together.
Doctors use cholesterol results with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Where treatment is needed, guidance recommends lifestyle support and often a statin, with the test repeated afterwards.

body.heading: What does a cholesterol blood test measure?
body.body: A lipid profile measures lipids in the blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides. The sample is taken from a vein in the arm, sometimes after fasting. A standard test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured alongside them. NHS laboratories usually calculate LDL cholesterol from total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides rather than measuring it directly. Total cholesterol is the combined figure, covering both good and bad cholesterol together. NICE guidance dropped routine fasting for a lipid profile, according to one NHS laboratory.

body.heading: What do HDL, non-HDL and triglycerides mean?
body.body: HDL is generally treated as the protective part of the total, and a low HDL counts as a risk marker. Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL. It captures the combined harmful types of cholesterol, and some NHS laboratories prefer it to LDL when samples are not fasting. Lab Tests Online UK notes that non-HDL does not need a fasting sample, which makes it practical. Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. Fasting is no longer routinely required, though some laboratories ask for a fasting repeat when a non-fasting triglyceride result is very high. The BHF gives healthy cholesterol targets and says the goal is lower after a heart attack or stroke. Sources differ slightly on where they place the line for triglycerides, and laboratories differ in their reference ranges. For that reason the laboratory report shows the range used for each result.

body.heading: How does a doctor use the result?
body.body: Doctors use the cholesterol result with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease. The QRISK tool estimates cardiovascular risk and helps decide whether treatment is needed. For people who already have cardiovascular disease, pathways move to secondary prevention, which does not use QRISK. People can ask their GP, or may be offered a test at a pharmacy or through an NHS Health Check in England.

body.heading: What helps lower raised cholesterol?
body.body: People at higher risk are offered support with lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, stopping smoking and managing weight. In primary prevention, lifestyle support is given for a few months before the level is reassessed. Pathways list atorvastatin as the usual first statin for primary prevention, with a higher starting dose for people who already have cardiovascular disease. Ezetimibe is a second-line option if the aim is not reached. Someone who has side effects on a high-intensity statin can be offered a lower dose or another statin. The test is repeated after treatment starts to see whether the level has fallen.

body.heading: Why does raised cholesterol matter?
body.body: The BHF explains that extra cholesterol can build up as fatty material in the arteries and narrow them. That gradual build-up raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Having more risk factors, such as smoking or high blood pressure, raises the overall risk further. Most people with high cholesterol have no symptoms.

body.heading: What is familial hypercholesterolaemia?
body.body: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is an inherited form of high cholesterol. In familial hypercholesterolaemia the high cholesterol is usually present from birth. The BHF says a heart attack or stroke at a younger age, or relatives with early heart disease, can point to it. The BHF lists lumps around the knuckles, knees or back of the ankle (Achilles tendon) and a pale white ring around the coloured part of the eye as possible signs of familial hypercholesterolaemia. The BHF says that if one parent has familial hypercholesterolaemia, a child has a 1 in 2 chance of also having it.

body.heading: What do statins do, and who is offered them?
body.body: NHS guidance says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They are also used in people who already have heart disease and in people with inherited high cholesterol. If statins are unsuitable, other cholesterol-lowering medicines can be offered. The NHS says statins should not be taken by people with liver disease or blood tests suggesting the liver may not be working properly, or by anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding. The NHS says statins may be offered if a QRISK health assessment shows an increased risk of cardiovascular disease in the next 10 years, or if you have a condition such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease or inherited high cholesterol. The BHF says most people have no side effects from statins.

choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.name: Which NHS service to use: 999, 111, GP, A&E
choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.headline: Choosing between 999, NHS 111, a GP, a pharmacy and urgent care
choose-the-right-nhs-service-999-111-gp-.summary: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies and NHS 111 for urgent problems or when unsure, with pharmacies, GPs and urgent treatment centres for others.
keyPoints: The NHS advises calling 999 for life-threatening emergencies, such as a suspected heart attack, a suspected stroke or severe bleeding.
NHS 111 can be used online, in the NHS App or by phone, at any time, when help is needed urgently but the situation is not life-threatening, or when it is unclear where to go.
The NHS says a pharmacist can help with a minor illness, and in England the Pharmacy First service covers seven common conditions without a referral.
Urgent treatment centres give urgent help when a problem is not life-threatening, for example for sprains and strains, suspected broken bones or skin infections.
If it is unclear where to go, the NHS suggests using NHS 111 first, which will advise where to go for treatment.

body.heading: How do the NHS urgent care services differ?
body.body: The NHS has several services for different levels of need. The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies. NHS 111 is for urgent problems that are not life-threatening, or for when a person is unsure where to go. Urgent treatment centres give urgent help when a problem is not a life-threatening emergency. For less urgent health needs, the NHS says to contact a GP or a pharmacist in the usual way. A pharmacist can help with a minor illness.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to call 999?
body.body: The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies. Examples in NHS guidance include loss of consciousness, an acute confused state, chest pain, breathing difficulties and cardiac arrest. Further examples include fits that are not stopping, a suspected stroke, severe bleeding, severe allergic reactions, severe burns or scalds, serious head injuries and major trauma. The NHS advises calling 999 for a heart attack or a stroke. Hospital emergency departments, often called A&E, are the place for serious emergencies.

body.heading: What does NHS 111 do?
body.body: NHS 111 is for medical help that is needed urgently when the problem is not life-threatening. It can be used online at 111.nhs.uk, in the NHS App, or by phone. It is available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and calls are free from landlines and mobile phones. The online service is for people aged 5 and over. The NHS says to call 111 instead for a child under 5, for complex problems caused by an existing medical condition, for people with a care plan from their doctor for the current problem, or for end-of-life care.

body.heading: What happens when someone calls NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says the call starts with basic questions, such as who is calling, where they are, and whether the problem affects the caller or someone else. The adviser then asks about the symptoms, including when they started and what has already been tried, as well as any medicines being taken and any existing medical conditions. These questions are there to rule out a life-threatening condition first. The NHS says the call does not give a diagnosis, but it does tell the person what help they need. The outcome may be an ambulance, a referral to urgent care, a GP or another service, or advice on looking after the problem at home. If a nurse is due to call back, the NHS says someone needs to be available to answer.

body.heading: What can a pharmacist help with?
body.body: The NHS lists seeing a pharmacist for help with a minor illness as an option for less urgent needs. In England, the Pharmacy First service lets people use seven pathways by contacting or visiting a pharmacy directly, without a referral. The seven conditions are sinusitis, sore throat, earache, infected insect bites, impetigo, shingles and uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Each has its own age range, so not everyone is eligible. NHS England says the pharmacist assesses the person privately, advises on self-care and, only if appropriate, supplies a limited set of prescription-only medicines. If the pharmacy cannot help, the person is directed to a GP surgery or A&E as appropriate.

body.heading: What do urgent treatment centres and GPs do?
body.body: The NHS says urgent treatment centres give urgent medical help when it is not a life-threatening emergency. They can help with problems such as sprains and strains, suspected broken bones, stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, skin infections and rashes, and a high temperature. Some centres also offer tests such as an ECG, blood tests or an X-ray. A GP registration is not needed to attend. NHS England sets a national standard of opening at least 12 hours a day, seven days a week, with both booked and walk-in patients seen. Appointments can be booked through NHS 111. For less urgent needs, the NHS says to contact a GP in the usual way.

body.heading: What if it is not clear where to go?
body.body: When it is unclear which service fits, the NHS suggests calling 111 first. The NHS says NHS 111 will assess the problem and may offer the chance to speak to a nurse, doctor or paramedic. The person is then advised where to go for treatment. What a local urgent treatment centre offers can vary, so tests and opening arrangements may differ between areas. If someone appears to be in a life-threatening situation, the NHS advises calling 999.

colic-in-babies-what-it-is-and-what-help.name: Colic in babies: what it is and what helps
colic-in-babies-what-it-is-and-what-help.summary: Colic is a baby crying a lot with no obvious cause; NHS guidance says it usually gets better by around 3 or 4 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says colic is a common problem in which a baby cries a lot for no obvious reason.
The NHS lists clenched fists, a red face and drawn-up legs among the signs, with crying often in the afternoon or evening.
NHS pages point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing.
NHS formulary guidance says there is not enough good-quality evidence that simeticone or lactase drops help colic, so they are not recommended.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried, and going to A&E or calling 999 for a weak or high-pitched cry.

body.heading: What is colic in babies?
body.body: The NHS says colic is when a baby cries a lot and there is no obvious cause. It describes colic as a common problem. A baby may be said to have colic if they cry for more than 3 hours a day, on 3 days a week, for at least a week, but are otherwise healthy. Colic usually begins a few weeks after birth. NHS pages describe crying that gets more frequent over the first weeks and tends to peak at about 6 to 8 weeks. After about 8 weeks, babies start to cry less each week. Crying is not always colic, because babies may also cry from hunger, a wet or dirty nappy, tiredness or illness.

body.heading: What are the signs of colic?
body.body: A baby with colic may clench their fists, go red in the face or draw their legs up. Arching the back is also listed as a sign. The NHS says crying often begins at about the same time each day, often in the afternoon or evening. The crying often winds down when the baby is exhausted, or after they have passed wind or a poo. Sources describe a baby with colic as otherwise healthy. Other signs that sources say need a check by a doctor include a weak or high-pitched cry, a floppy baby, poor feeding, green vomit, blood in the stool, a fever or a bulging soft spot on the head.

body.heading: What causes colic?
body.body: NHS guidance says the cause of colic is unclear. Food sensitivities such as cow's milk allergy are sometimes suspected. Other NHS pages suggest indigestion, trapped wind or a temporary gut sensitivity to breast and formula milk. One source says the cause is unknown but likely linked to intestinal discomfort such as bowel cramping. Colic may also be at the extreme end of normal crying in babies. It can affect babies whether they are breastfed or formula fed. These are possible explanations rather than proven causes.

body.heading: What may help a baby with colic?
body.body: NHS pages point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing. Burping during and after feeds is standard advice. The NHS suggests holding a baby upright during feeds so they swallow less air. For bottle feeding, the NHS says to sit the baby as upright as possible, which helps stop them swallowing too much air. It also says to hold the bottle just slightly tipped, so that milk fills the teat, there are no air pockets and the milk flows steadily. One NHS page suggests an anti-colic bottle may help. It adds that some parents use a fast-flow teat, which may help a baby swallow less air. A Midlands NHS trust gives a slower guide for how quickly milk should drip from the teat, so advice on teat flow differs between NHS sources.

body.heading: What is not proven to help?
body.body: NHS formulary guidance says there is not enough good-quality evidence that simeticone drops (such as Infacol) or lactase drops (such as Colief) help colic, so they are not recommended. A Frimley NHS pathway lists simeticone, probiotic supplements and herbal supplements among the products it does not recommend. Most of these sources instead point to soothing methods such as winding, rocking and bathing.

body.heading: When does colic get better, and when should parents seek advice?
body.body: The NHS says colic should get better by around 3 or 4 months of age. Another source says it usually stops by four to six months at the latest. The NHS advises calling NHS 111 or seeing a GP if a parent is worried. Poor weight gain, or colic-type symptoms that are still present after about 4 months, are also reasons for a baby to be checked. The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if a baby has a weak or high-pitched cry. NHS 111 Wales adds that a cry that does not sound like the baby's normal cry also means A&E or 999. For concerns outside normal hours, one NHS source says NHS 111 can give advice.

body.heading: Where can parents get support?
body.body: Local NHS programmes say infant crying is normal and comforting methods can help. Several NHS sources say that if a parent feels overwhelmed, it is fine to put the baby in a safe place and walk away for a few minutes to calm down. A Berkshire NHS page says a crying baby will not be harmed by being left alone in a safe place for a few minutes. These sources also say never to shake a baby, because shaking moves the head violently and can cause brain damage. Shaking will not stop the crying and can cause severe injury or even death. If a parent feels they might harm their baby because of the constant crying, one source says to get help immediately. Cry-sis is a charity for parents of unsettled babies, and NHS Best Start and a Kent NHS page list its free helpline as 0800 448 0737, open 9am to 10pm every day. Older NHS pages list a different number, so cry-sis.org.uk can be checked. A GP, health visitor or midwife can also be asked for help.

colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.name: Colonoscopy: preparation and what happens
colonoscopy-preparation-and-what-happens.summary: A colonoscopy uses a thin camera to look inside the large bowel. This guide covers bowel preparation, sedation, risks and when results arrive.
keyPoints: A colonoscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the bowel to look for the cause of symptoms, to screen for bowel cancer, or to follow up earlier problems.
The bowel must be empty for a clear view, so a bowel preparation, which can include laxatives, is taken beforehand.
Polyps, which are growths on the bowel lining, can be removed during the test and examined under a microscope.
Perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, is the main serious risk and is uncommon, with higher risk when polyps are removed.

body.heading: Why is a colonoscopy done?
body.body: A colonoscopy is often done to look for the cause of bowel symptoms, such as abdominal pain or a change in bowel habit. Colonoscopy is also used to follow up after earlier polyps or bowel cancer, according to MedlinePlus, a US source. People who have had polyps removed before are routinely advised to have repeat colonoscopies.

body.heading: How is the bowel prepared?
body.body: For a clear view, the bowel needs to be empty. Preparation can include laxatives to empty the bowel. Preparation can include clear liquids the day before and laxatives, according to MedlinePlus, a US source. A review of bowel preparation lists vomiting, colicky stomach ache and dizziness among the most common problems. Preparation depends on which type the doctor recommends, and it can differ between hospitals.

body.heading: What happens during the procedure?
body.body: A nurse sees the person first to discuss their medical history, carry out simple checks and explain what will happen. A thin, flexible tube with a camera is passed through the anus and around the large bowel. Air is pumped in to open the bowel, which can cause bloating or cramps. The NHS says a colonoscopy can be uncomfortable but should not be painful. NHS England says a colonoscopy should take 30 to 45 minutes, and a person may be at the hospital for around two hours in total. A leaflet says some people have sedation, some breathe a pain-relieving gas called Entonox, and some have no pain relief. Sedation is given through a thin tube called a cannula in the hand or arm.

body.heading: What are polyps and biopsies?
body.body: Polyps are growths on the bowel lining, and they are usually not cancer. Doctors usually cannot tell the type of polyp just by looking, so suspicious polyps are usually removed and examined under a microscope. Staff can also take small tissue samples, called biopsies, which people typically do not feel. Some findings may be shared once the sedation has worn off, according to MedlinePlus, a US source.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets describe colonoscopy as very safe, with serious complications rare. The main risks are a tear in the bowel wall, called perforation, and bleeding. Trust leaflets give perforation figures that differ, and one says about 1 in 1,000 procedures. The risk rises when polyps are removed, especially large or complex ones. A perforation is treated in hospital, and surgery is sometimes needed, according to NHS trust leaflets. It is common to pass a small amount of blood from the anus after a biopsy or polyp removal. Trust leaflets say a colonoscopy can occasionally miss a problem, including, rarely, a cancer. The NHS says to call NHS 111 or the hospital where the test was done for some symptoms after a colonoscopy, and to call 999 or go to A&E for more serious ones; its page lists which symptoms apply.

body.heading: When do the results come?
body.body: Some NHS trusts say a letter or call with the results comes about two to three weeks after a colonoscopy, though waits can differ. The result will say whether anything abnormal was found and whether further treatment is needed, according to NHS trust pages. If a biopsy was taken, trust leaflets give differing waits for the biopsy results, from several days to several weeks.
