heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.name: Heavy periods: causes, tests and treatment
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.headline: Heavy periods: what can cause them, which checks a GP offers and how they are treated
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.summary: Heavy periods are common and often have no clear cause, but fibroids, endometriosis and other conditions can be behind them. The NHS advises a GP visit when they affect daily life.
keyPoints: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, and the NHS says help is available when they affect daily life.
Often there is no underlying medical reason, though fibroids, endometriosis and some other conditions can cause heavy periods.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect life, have lasted some time, come with severe pain, or if there is bleeding between periods or after sex.
Treatment choices include some contraceptives, medicines to reduce bleeding and surgery, and heavy periods do not always need treatment.

body.heading: What counts as a heavy period?
body.body: The NHS describes heavy periods in practical terms, such as needing to change pads or tampons every one to two hours. Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, but the NHS says that when periods are so heavy that they affect life, help is available. Feeling tired or short of breath, or avoiding daily activities because of periods, are other signs that bleeding may be a problem.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body: Heavy periods often have no underlying cause. Fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, are one of the identifiable causes. Other conditions that can cause heavy periods include endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease. Some medicines, such as anticoagulants and some chemotherapy medicines, can also be responsible. Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect your life, have lasted for some time, or come with severe pain. Bleeding between periods or after sex is also a reason to see a GP. For severe period or pelvic pain that is worse than usual and not helped by painkillers, the NHS advises getting urgent advice, from NHS 111 if needed.

body.heading: Which tests might a GP arrange?
body.body: A GP can investigate why bleeding is heavy, which may include a physical examination, blood tests or scans. A blood test to look for iron deficiency anaemia is usually offered to people with heavy periods. A pregnancy test, an ultrasound scan and, less often, a hysteroscopy (a look inside the womb with a small camera) may follow.

body.heading: How are heavy periods treated?
body.body: Heavy periods do not always need to be treated. If they affect daily life, options include a hormone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) or the combined contraceptive pill. Medicines to reduce the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as mefenamic acid or naproxen are also used. Surgical options also exist for heavy periods.

high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.name: High blood pressure: what happens next
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.headline: High blood pressure: how it is found, what causes it and what treatment involves
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.summary: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is found by measuring it; treatment starts with lifestyle changes and may include medicine.
keyPoints: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the only way to know is to have it measured.
In most people no single cause is found; age, family history, ethnicity and lifestyle all play a part.
Readings taken at home or by a 24-hour monitor can be used alongside clinic readings to confirm the diagnosis.
Lifestyle changes are the first step, and a GP may prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high or stays high.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure reading mean?
body.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. A reading gives two numbers: the pressure when the heart beats and the pressure between beats. The site's page on blood pressure measurement explains how they are taken.

Doctors use different thresholds for readings taken in a clinic and for readings taken at home when deciding whether blood pressure is high.

body.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
body.body:
Usually not. The NHS says high blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, and the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely it can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain.

Over time, the NHS says, untreated high blood pressure raises the chance of problems such as stroke and heart disease.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body:
For most people there is no obvious cause, which is called essential hypertension, and it can run in families. In a small number of people there is an underlying cause, such as a kidney or adrenal gland condition.

The NHS says risk rises with age, with Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity, and with a family history. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active are also linked.

The NHS advises calling NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, chest pain that comes and goes, or other symptoms thought to come from high blood pressure.

body.heading: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
body.body:
A single clinic reading is usually followed by other checks. NICE advises confirming raised clinic readings with home monitoring or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor, which takes readings through the day.

Some people have higher readings in a clinic than at home, sometimes called the white coat effect, which is one reason these extra checks are used. A GP may also arrange blood and urine tests and an ECG, which checks the heart rhythm.

A reading taken in a clinic is less accurate than home or ambulatory readings and is not enough on its own to diagnose high blood pressure.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes come first for many people. The NHS lists cutting down on salt and alcohol, being more physically active, losing weight where needed, and stopping smoking.

A GP will usually prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high, if the person has a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, or if it stays high after lifestyle changes. Several types are used, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and the choice depends on things such as age and ethnicity.

Some people need to take blood pressure medicine long term, though if blood pressure stays under control for several years it may be possible to cut back or stop treatment.

Most blood pressure medicines are taken as tablets.

Making lifestyle changes early on may mean some people can avoid needing medicine.

Water tablets (diuretics) work by increasing the amount of salt the kidneys remove.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

NHS guidance for pharmacy staff says a very high clinic reading together with symptoms such as headache, palpitations, new confusion or chest pain should be referred to A&E, using 999 where necessary.

high-crp-what-it-means.name: High CRP: what it means and what happens next
high-crp-what-it-means.summary: A high CRP means there is inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but not where or why, so doctors read it with symptoms and other tests.
keyPoints: A high CRP shows that inflammation or infection is likely, but it does not show where it is or what is causing it.
CRP is a protein made by the liver whose level rises when there is inflammation in the body.
Doctors read the result with the wider clinical picture, and the test is often repeated to see whether treatment has worked.
Some raised results are linked to things other than illness, such as obesity or taking the combined contraceptive pill.
Laboratories and sources do not all use the same cut-offs, so a CRP result is read against the range on its own report.

body.heading: What does a CRP test measure?
body.body:
CRP stands for C-reactive protein, a protein that the liver makes. Its level in the blood rises when there is inflammation somewhere in the body. Infection and several other causes of inflammation can push the level up.

Doctors usually request the test when they suspect an infection or inflammation, for example after surgery. It is also used to help assess long-term inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Lab Tests Online UK says no special preparation is needed for the test.

body.heading: What does a high CRP mean?
body.body:
A high or rising CRP suggests that there is an acute infection or inflammation. It does not show where the inflammation is or which condition is causing it. For that reason the test is not diagnostic on its own. Berkshire and Surrey pathology services say a raised CRP is linked with infection, particularly but not only bacterial, and with inflammation.

A small rise is hard to interpret by itself, so doctors consider it alongside the whole clinical picture. In long-term inflammatory conditions the test is often repeated to see whether treatment is working. The cause of a high CRP cannot always be found.

body.heading: Which conditions can raise CRP?
body.body: MedlinePlus lists cancer, heart attack, infection, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and related diseases, and rheumatic fever among the conditions that can raise CRP. Not every cause is an illness. A Danish blood donor study found low-grade inflammation was more common in women using the combined contraceptive pill. Obesity is linked with low-grade inflammation and with higher CRP levels. StatPearls describes smoking, diabetes and other long-term conditions as associated with low-grade inflammation that can raise CRP.

body.heading: What happens after a high CRP result?
body.body:
Lab Tests Online UK says CRP is used to assess how severe inflammation is and how well treatment is working. The doctor may then arrange further tests or treatment.

The test is often repeated to see whether treatment has been effective. NHS laboratories often report CRP results within about a day, though timing depends on where the test is requested. A CRP result does not show urgency; the NHS says chest tightness or pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw needs a 999 call straight away. StatPearls notes that small CRP rises can occur without obvious widespread inflammation.

body.heading: Is hs-CRP the same test?
body.body: High-sensitivity CRP, or hs-CRP, is a separate and more sensitive version of the test. It has been used to estimate the risk of heart disease in people who seem healthy. Lab Tests Online UK notes that current UK guidelines on cardiovascular risk assessment do not recommend hs-CRP testing. A Sheffield NHS laboratory leaflet says hs-CRP should not replace assessment of the usual cardiovascular risk factors. The same leaflet says people with active infection, inflammation or trauma should not have hs-CRP testing until these have resolved.

body.heading: Can medicines or other factors change the result?
body.body: StatPearls states that some medicines, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and statins, can lower CRP. Long-term conditions linked with low-grade inflammation can lift it.

body.heading: Where else is CRP used?
body.body: Regional NHS guidance on suspected giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels, asks for a CRP before steroids are started. A Devon formulary page says polymyalgia rheumatica is possible but very rare when inflammatory markers are normal. Scottish referral guidance for suspected rheumatoid arthritis refers to CRP and ESR results alongside anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor tests. It advises referral for persistent symptoms even when CRP is normal and antibodies are negative. A Scottish NHS guideline on giant cell arteritis says it is rare to see the condition with normal inflammatory markers, and that CRP, plasma viscosity or both should be raised.

high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.name: High white blood cell count: what it means
high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.summary: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
keyPoints: A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.

body.heading: What does the full blood count measure?
body.body: A full blood count measures the number and type of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets. The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types. Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.

body.heading: What does a high white cell count mean?
body.body: A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause. A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders. Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause. Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.

body.heading: What else can raise it?
body.body: Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies. Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it. Physical or emotional stress can affect the white cell count. Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count. Corticosteroids raise the white cell count by releasing neutrophils from the bone marrow into the circulation. A review says the white cell count can double within hours after stressors such as surgery, exercise, trauma or emotional stress, because of large neutrophil stores in the bone marrow and blood vessels.

body.heading: What does the differential add?
body.body: A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body. A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease are among the conditions that can cause a high white cell count. Smoking commonly causes a mild rise in neutrophils, lymphocytes or both.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking. The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology. Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film. Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used. The NHS says severe breathing difficulty, or someone who has passed out and is not responding normally, needs a 999 call. MedlinePlus says some medicines, such as corticosteroids, can raise the white cell count, while others can lower it.

body.heading: When might a blood disorder be considered?
body.body: A GP may arrange a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high white cell count could be a sign of it. In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist. UK sources list tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections among leukaemia symptoms. Cancer Research UK says leukaemia symptoms can be vague, and that minor conditions are common while leukaemia is rare. For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear.

how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.name: How long antidepressants take to work
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks before the full benefit and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. For citalopram, the NHS advises against stopping after only 1 or 2 weeks just because it seems not to be helping, since the full benefit takes longer to appear.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include tiredness, feeling nervous, dry mouth and sweating. The NHS says common side effects like these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS lists sexual problems, such as a lower sex drive, among the common side effects of citalopram. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. It also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

If side effects last beyond 1 or 2 weeks, the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor about them.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says a GP may recommend trying a different antidepressant if the first one is not helping. People respond differently to different antidepressants, so a change of medicine can sometimes help. Anyone worried about their progress can raise it with a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says stopping is usually done by reducing the dose gradually.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects, and that the taper is agreed with the person's healthcare professional. NICE guidance for adults with depression also says people who want to stop should talk to the person who prescribed the medicine. Tapering is typically needed, and most people manage to stop successfully. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline, the NHS says most doctors recommend treatment for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. The decision to stop or continue depends on symptoms and how well the medicine is working, and is made with the prescriber.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, adults aged 18 or over can refer themselves directly to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral. These services are for anxiety and depression and are not for urgent crisis help.

how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.name: How to read food labels: traffic lights
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.headline: How to read food labels: traffic light colours, per 100g figures and salt
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.summary: Red, amber and green traffic light labels show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt, and per 100g figures allow comparison.
keyPoints: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt.
Red means high, amber medium and green low; energy is not colour-coded.
The colours are mainly based on 100g or 100ml, which makes comparing similar products easier than portion figures do.
When a label lists sodium, multiplying by 2.5 gives the salt content, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What do the traffic light colours mean?
body.body: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt. Red means a high level of that nutrient, amber means medium and green means low. Guidance suggests choosing products with more green and amber and fewer red. Energy, shown in kilojoules and kilocalories, is not colour-coded.

body.heading: Should products be compared per 100g or per portion?
body.body: The colours are mainly based on the amount in 100g or 100ml of the food. Using the per 100g column makes it easier to compare the nutrient content of similar foods. Portion sizes are chosen by manufacturers and can differ, so per portion figures may not be comparable between products. A serving can be as small as one biscuit, so eating two means doubling the figures.

body.heading: What are reference intakes?
body.body: The percentages on front-of-pack labels are based on guidelines for how much of each nutrient and how much energy an average adult needs in a day. They show how much of that daily amount one portion supplies. Where a label has no colour coding, comparing the percentage of the reference intake in a portion is another way to compare foods.

body.heading: How is salt shown on a label?
body.body: Some labels give sodium rather than salt, and the NHS says multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. The NHS describes a food as high in salt when it has more than 1.5g of salt per 100g, and low when it has 0.3g or less per 100g. The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day.

body.heading: Are these labels compulsory?
body.body: Government guidance describes front-of-pack nutrition labelling in the UK as voluntary. The nutrition table on the back of the pack is mandatory. Labels therefore differ between products, and the per 100g figures are the common point of comparison.

ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.name: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together: NHS view
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.headline: Can you take ibuprofen and paracetamol together? What the NHS says
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.summary: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, but children should not be given them at the same time.
keyPoints: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, and NHS inform says the two can be taken together if required.
For children, the NHS says paracetamol and ibuprofen should not be given at the same time but one at a time.
The NHS lists groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check first, including people with repeated stomach ulcers or bleeding, asthma, or severe kidney failure.
Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen, so using several products can make it easy to take more than the recommended amount.
The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction, and to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor for other serious effects such as stomach bleeding or kidney problems.

body.heading: What is each medicine used for?
body.body: Ibuprofen belongs to a group of painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS describes ibuprofen as a painkiller that also treats inflammation. It describes paracetamol as a painkiller for pain and high temperature. For a dental abscess, NHS inform says ibuprofen is the preferred painkiller, and paracetamol can be taken instead if ibuprofen cannot be taken for medical reasons. The NHS also says that if you need pain relief while taking warfarin, paracetamol is the one to take instead of ibuprofen.

body.heading: Can adults take both at the same time?
body.body: For adults, the NHS says paracetamol can be taken at the same time as ibuprofen if needed. It also says paracetamol can be taken with other painkillers that do not contain paracetamol, such as ibuprofen, aspirin or codeine. NHS inform, the NHS information service for Scotland, also says the two can be taken together if required. For a dental abscess, it says that if one painkiller does not work, taking both paracetamol and ibuprofen may help. The advice is different for children. For them, the NHS says paracetamol can be given alongside ibuprofen but not at the same time, and the two should be given one at a time.

body.heading: Who is told to check with a pharmacist or doctor first?
body.body: The NHS lists several groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check with a professional before using it. These include people who have had an allergic reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs, with signs such as wheezing, a runny nose or skin reactions. They also include people who have had a hole in the stomach, bleeding in the stomach or a stomach ulcer more than once, and people with severe heart, kidney or liver failure. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are also on the NHS list. The NHS also says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor when breastfeeding. People over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen, according to the NHS. Other medicines can interact with ibuprofen. The NHS interactions page lists warfarin and other anticoagulants, medicines for high blood pressure, steroids such as prednisolone, certain antibiotics and some antidepressants. It advises against taking ginkgo biloba with ibuprofen because it can increase the chance of bleeding. For other herbal products, it says there is not enough information to say whether they can be taken with ibuprofen. NHS inform advises anyone already taking other medication to check with a pharmacist first.

body.heading: Why do other products containing the same ingredients matter?
body.body: Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen. NHS inform says this makes it easy to take more than the recommended dose. The NHS says to avoid taking other medicines that contain paracetamol at the same time as paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies, because too much can be dangerous. It adds that taking two different medicines that contain paracetamol carries a risk of overdose, and that too much paracetamol can sometimes damage the liver. For ibuprofen, the NHS says to check the label of cold and cough remedies for aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Taking ibuprofen with other NSAIDs such as aspirin or naproxen is not advised without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor, because side effects such as stomach ache become more likely.

body.heading: What side effects do the NHS pages describe?
body.body: The NHS lists common side effects of ibuprofen as indigestion, stomach aches, feeling sick, being sick and headaches. Serious ones include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, and allergic reactions. The NHS also lists kidney problems, such as swollen ankles or blood in the urine, as a reason to get urgent advice. For paracetamol, the NHS says there may be no obvious symptoms at first after taking too much, so feeling well does not rule out harm.

body.heading: When should someone get help, and from whom?
body.body: For signs of a serious allergic reaction to ibuprofen, such as swollen lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing or a tight throat, the NHS says to call 999. The NHS also says to call 999 for severe chest or stomach pain, which can signal a hole in the stomach or gut, and for difficulty breathing or worsening asthma symptoms. Vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo can be signs of bleeding in the stomach, and the NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor. Swollen ankles or blood in the urine can point to a kidney problem, and the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a doctor. If too much paracetamol has been taken, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice, even when the person feels well. For questions that are not urgent, NHS inform says to speak to a pharmacist if unsure.

inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.name: INR blood test and warfarin explained
inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.summary: The INR blood test shows how long blood takes to clot, and it is how the effect of warfarin is monitored so the dose can be adjusted.
keyPoints: The INR measures how long the blood takes to clot, and it is the main way warfarin treatment is monitored.
Warfarin has no fixed dose, so the dose is adjusted from INR results by an anticoagulation clinic.
New medicines, alcohol and diet can change the INR.
The main side effect of warfarin is bleeding; NHS leaflets advise a GP or NHS 111 for minor bleeding and 999 if it will not stop.

body.heading: What does the INR measure?
body.body: INR stands for international normalised ratio. It is a standard blood test that measures how long the blood takes to clot. One NHS trust explains that it compares the clotting time of a person taking warfarin with that of someone who is not.

body.heading: Why is the INR checked on warfarin?
body.body: Warfarin does not have a fixed dose. The dose needed depends on how much the medicine slows the clotting of the blood, and the INR test measures that effect. The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding. One NHS trust leaflet explains that a typical target INR means the blood takes just over twice as long as normal to clot.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: At the start, testing is frequent. Once the result is stable, the gaps between tests lengthen. Some people need tests more regularly than others. The INR results go to the warfarin clinic, which advises on the ongoing dose and the date of the next test. One NHS trust leaflet says that once the dose has stabilised, blood tests become less frequent, and your anticoagulant clinic decides how often you need one.

body.heading: What can change the INR?
body.body: New medicines can change the effect of warfarin, so one NHS service asks for an INR test soon after any new medicine is started or stopped. Alcohol, diet and other medicines can also move the result. Sources name cranberry and grapefruit juice as drinks to avoid on warfarin, and binge drinking as able to raise the INR. They also name ibuprofen and similar painkillers as able to increase the risk of bleeding. The NHS advises telling your doctor about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements, checking before starting any new medicine, and avoiding St John's wort. Guidance warns that binge drinking while taking warfarin is dangerous because it can raise the INR and the risk of bleeding.

body.heading: What should people know about bleeding?
body.body: Signs of bleeding include bleeding gums, blood in vomit, blood in urine or stool, and prolonged bleeding from small cuts. For women, heavier periods can be a sign. NHS trust leaflets say to contact the GP or NHS 111 about minor bruising or bleeding. NHS leaflets say to call 999 if bleeding cannot be stopped. NHS trust leaflets list vomiting or coughing up blood as a reason to seek care at A&E. NHS guidance says a significant blow to the head is a reason to call 999.

body.heading: What else do people on warfarin carry or watch?
body.body: People on warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card to carry. The card lets medical staff identify that someone takes warfarin if there is an accident. Foods high in vitamin K, such as leafy green vegetables, can affect how warfarin works. Dietary advice from an NHS trust stresses eating a steady amount of such foods, because the clinic adjusts the dose to match. The NHS says the food and drink restrictions do not usually apply to the newer anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran. The NHS says to carry the anticoagulant alert card at all times and show it to your doctor or dentist before any medical or dental procedure. NHS dietary leaflets say that a big increase or decrease in foods containing vitamin K from week to week can affect the INR, so it is best to keep intake steady and talk to your anticoagulant clinic before major diet changes.

jet-lag-what-it-is-and-what-helps.name: What is jet lag and what helps?
jet-lag-what-it-is-and-what-helps.headline: Jet lag: what it is, why it happens and what the NHS says helps
jet-lag-what-it-is-and-what-helps.summary: Jet lag is a temporary sleep disturbance after long flights across time zones; the NHS says it usually improves within a few days.
keyPoints: Jet lag is a temporary disturbance to the sleep pattern that can follow a long flight across time zones.
The body clock is set partly by cues such as sunrise and sunset, so it takes a few days to catch up with a new time zone.
Symptoms include trouble sleeping at night, waking early, daytime tiredness and poor concentration or memory.
The NHS suggests plenty of rest before travel, drinking water on the flight, and avoiding daytime sleep and sleeping at night after arrival.
The NHS jet lag page says melatonin is not recommended on the NHS because evidence is lacking, while the NHS melatonin page says it can be taken short term by adults.
NHS inform advises contacting a GP practice when better sleep habits have not helped or poor sleep affects daily life.

body.heading: What is jet lag?
body.body:
Jet lag is a disturbance to the normal sleep pattern that can follow a long flight across time zones. The NHS says it usually improves within a few days as the body clock adjusts, and that medicines are usually not needed.

nidirect, the Northern Ireland health information service, describes it in the same way.

body.heading: Why does jet lag happen?
body.body:
MedlinePlus, a US health information service, notes that the body clock is set partly by cues from the environment, such as sunrise and sunset. After a long flight these cues no longer match the clock, so it takes time to adjust.

US CDC travel guidance says jet lag is typically worse after flying east than west. It explains that eastward travel needs the body clock to move earlier, which is harder than moving it later.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of jet lag?
body.body:
The NHS lists trouble sleeping at night, waking early, tiredness during the day, and poor concentration or memory.

These symptoms are the body clock and the local time being out of step. The NHS describes them as temporary.

body.heading: What helps before and during a flight?
body.body:
The NHS suggests getting plenty of rest before travelling and gradually moving bedtime and waking time towards the destination's schedule. MedlinePlus gives the same idea, going to bed earlier before an eastward trip and later before a westward one.

For a short trip of two to three days, the NHS says it can be easier to eat and sleep at the times used at home.

On the flight, the NHS advises drinking water, moving around the cabin and trying to sleep if it is night at the destination. It mentions an eye mask or earplugs if these help. nidirect says too much caffeine or alcohol can make jet lag worse.

body.heading: What helps after arriving?
body.body:
The NHS advises avoiding sleep during the day and sleeping at night. MedlinePlus recommends spending time in sunlight to help reset the body clock.

CDC travel guidance says the best timing of light depends on the direction of travel and the number of time zones crossed. Light in the morning tends to move the body clock earlier, while light in the evening tends to move it later.

On meals, the CDC says most dietary changes have not been found to reduce jet lag. In one study, flight crews who ate at more regular times on days off reported a small improvement in their overall jet lag rating.

body.heading: Do melatonin or sleeping tablets help?
body.body:
The NHS jet lag page says melatonin tablets are not recommended on the NHS for jet lag, because there is not enough evidence that they work.

The NHS melatonin page takes a different tone. It says melatonin can be taken as a short-term treatment for jet lag in adults, and that it may not be available on an NHS prescription. The two NHS pages therefore differ in emphasis.

On sleeping tablets, NHS pages say they may help if jet lag causes insomnia, but they can be addictive. They say these should be used only for a short time and only if symptoms are severe.

body.heading: When should someone get medical advice?
body.body:
The NHS says jet lag usually improves within a few days. NHS inform, in its general guidance on insomnia, advises contacting a GP practice if better sleep habits have not helped or if poor sleep is affecting daily life.

This guidance is about sleep problems in general rather than jet lag in particular.

joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.name: Joint pain: causes and when to see a GP
joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.summary: Joint pain has many causes, including osteoarthritis, injury and gout, and the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint with a fever.
keyPoints: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers.
The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly.

body.heading: What causes joint pain?
body.body: Gout is a form of arthritis in which small crystals form inside and around the joints. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system targets the joints, with stiffness that is often worse in the morning or after a period of inactivity. The NHS says rheumatoid arthritis is usually first felt in the small joints of the hands and feet. The NHS arthritis overview says gout often affects the big toe joint, which can become painful, swollen and hot. Psoriatic arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness and swelling, and is linked with the skin condition psoriasis, which causes a red, scaly rash.

body.heading: What can ease joint pain at home?
body.body: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers. NHS 111 Wales says being overweight often makes osteoarthritis worse, because it puts extra strain on some joints. NHS 111 Wales describes exercise as one of the most important treatments for osteoarthritis, and says hot or cold packs can relieve symptoms in some people. NHS 111 Wales says osteoarthritis has no cure but does not necessarily get worse over time.

body.heading: When is a GP appointment sensible?
body.body: The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home. It also lists joints that stay stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking. For gout, the NHS advises seeing a GP for a first episode, or when the usual treatments are not helping.

body.heading: Which joint pain needs urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly. A warm, swollen joint that is hard to move, with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery, may mean a joint infection called septic arthritis.

body.heading: How is the cause found?
body.body: A GP examines the joints for swelling, checks how easily they move and asks about symptoms. Blood tests such as ESR, CRP and a full blood count may be used, and X-rays or MRI scans may show inflammation and damage. No blood test can definitively prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, although several tests can show signs of it. If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP usually refers the person to a rheumatologist. A rheumatologist is a doctor who specialises in conditions of the joints and immune system.

kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.name: Kidney stones: symptoms and treatment
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.headline: Kidney stones: symptoms, how they are diagnosed and how they are treated
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.summary: Kidney stones form when chemicals in urine build up; small ones may cause no symptoms, while larger ones can cause severe pain, and some may need a procedure.
keyPoints: Kidney stones form when chemicals from urine build up in the kidneys, and small stones may cause no symptoms.
Larger stones can cause severe pain that comes and goes, sometimes with nausea or blood in the urine.
A GP can often diagnose kidney stones from symptoms and history, with urine and blood tests and sometimes a scan.
Most stones can be treated at home with medicines and plenty of fluids; larger stones may need to be broken up or removed.
Severe pain, a high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What are kidney stones?
body.body:
Kidney stones are hard lumps that form in the kidneys. The NHS says they are caused by chemicals from urine building up in the kidneys.

Small stones often cause no symptoms and may pass unnoticed.

body.heading: What symptoms can they cause?
body.body:
Larger stones can cause severe pain. It can come and go in waves.

Other symptoms can include nausea or vomiting, blood in the urine, sweating, a high temperature and a urine infection.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body:
The NHS says kidney stones can be caused by dehydration, by some medicines, and by some medical conditions. Not drinking enough water raises the chance of getting one.

Other things that raise the risk include a diet high in protein and low in fibre, being inactive or bed-bound, repeated kidney or urine infections, and a close family member who has had stones.

body.heading: How are kidney stones diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP can usually diagnose kidney stones from the symptoms and medical history. Urine and blood tests may be used.

If the pain is severe, the NHS says the person may be referred to hospital for a scan. If a scan is needed, the NHS says adults have a CT scan, while pregnant women and children under 16 have an ultrasound scan.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
Most kidney stones can be treated at home. The NHS says this usually means painkillers, anti-sickness medicine, medicines that help a stone pass, and drinking plenty of water.

Larger stones may need to be broken up or removed. One option is shockwave lithotripsy, where shock waves are aimed at the stone to break it up. Other procedures use a thin scope to reach the stone.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for anyone with kidney stone symptoms who is in severe pain, or has a high temperature, or feels hot, cold or shivery.

A high temperature can be a sign of infection, so it needs prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111. Hospital leaflets advise A&E for anyone who cannot pass urine, and 999 in an emergency.

Hospital leaflets also advise A&E when pain is not controlled by painkillers.

Signs of infection with a stone can include a high temperature, burning when passing urine, and feeling tired or unwell.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Shockwave lithotripsy can be uncomfortable, so painkillers are usually given first, and more than one session may be needed. In ureteroscopy, a thin telescope is passed through the urethra and bladder into the ureter, and it is done under general anaesthetic.

knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.name: Knee pain: causes and when to get help
knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.summary: Knee pain can often be treated at home, and NHS 111 is the route for a badly swollen knee or a hot, red knee with a high temperature.
keyPoints: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease.
The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

body.heading: What causes knee pain?
body.body: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease. The NHS knee pain page links sprains and strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting the knee, often during exercise. An NHS trust leaflet lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling as symptoms of osteoarthritis. NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history. An NHS trust page says changes seen on an X-ray do not necessarily match how bad the symptoms are. NHS inform says strengthening the muscles around the knee helps manage osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What can ease it at home?
body.body: The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.

body.heading: When should knee pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks. The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP. An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee. An NHS trust leaflet on hip and knee osteoarthritis describes regular exercise, over-the-counter pain relief and losing a small amount of body fat.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.name: Levothyroxine: timing and other medicines
levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.headline: Levothyroxine: why timing and other medicines matter, as the NHS describes
levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.summary: The NHS says levothyroxine replaces a missing thyroid hormone and is taken at the same time each day on an empty stomach.
keyPoints: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid that replaces a hormone the body is not making enough of.
The NHS says it is taken at the same time each day, on an empty stomach, before the first meal, any caffeinated drink or other medicines.
MedlinePlus, a US source, says calcium, iron, multivitamins and some antacids are best spaced apart from thyroid medicine.
The NHS says regular blood tests continue until the right amount is reached, then usually once a year.
The NHS says treatment is usually lifelong, and both the NHS and MedlinePlus say not to stop without medical advice.

body.heading: What does levothyroxine replace?
body.body: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid, also called hypothyroidism. The NHS says an underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. It explains that the tablets simply replace a hormone that is missing, which is why they do not usually cause side effects. The NHS also says that in the UK, combining levothyroxine with a second thyroid hormone, T3, is not routinely used because there is not enough evidence that it works better than levothyroxine alone.

body.heading: Why does the NHS say to take it at a consistent time?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine is usually taken once a day, at the same time each day. It also says the tablet is taken on an empty stomach, before the first meal of the day, any drink with caffeine such as tea or coffee, or any other medicine, and swallowed with water. NHS inform Scotland says the morning is usually recommended, though some people prefer night. MedlinePlus, a US source, says thyroid medicine works best on an empty stomach and suggests asking a provider whether bedtime suits. A systematic review of studies, published in a journal and held on PubMed Central, reported that morning and bedtime dosing were equally effective. The NHS says that for a forgotten tablet, take it when remembered unless the next one is nearly due, and do not take two together to make up.

body.heading: How can food, coffee and other medicines affect it?
body.body: The NHS says other medicines, supplements and foods can affect how well levothyroxine is absorbed, which is why it is taken before food, caffeinated drinks and other medicines. A systematic review on PubMed Central, Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements, found that coffee, soy products, fibre, calcium or iron supplements and enteral nutrition all decreased absorption, although the evidence was limited. It reported that keeping a gap between levothyroxine and these products is one way to avoid the problem. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists fibre supplements, calcium, iron, multivitamins, aluminium hydroxide antacids and bile-acid binding medicines as products to space apart from thyroid hormone. NHS trust leaflets also advise against taking calcium or iron at the same time. Sources differ on the gap needed, so a pharmacist or the prescriber can advise for one person, using the leaflet in the pack.

body.heading: Why are regular blood tests needed?
body.body: The NHS says a person starts on a low amount that is adjusted over time, with regular blood tests until the right amount of levothyroxine has been reached. It says that once the amount is right, a blood test is usually done once a year to monitor hormone levels. MedlinePlus, a US source, also says hormone levels are checked at the start and then at least once a year. The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or planning to be, because further tests are needed and the amount of levothyroxine is likely to need changing.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping?
body.body: The NHS says to keep taking the medicine unless advised to stop. It says an underactive thyroid is a lifelong condition, so people usually need levothyroxine for the rest of their lives. MedlinePlus, a US source, says to keep taking it even when feeling well and not to stop without talking to a doctor. A pharmacist or GP is the usual route for questions about changes to treatment.

body.heading: What side effects can happen, and who can advise?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine does not usually have side effects, because the tablets replace a missing hormone. It says most side effects happen when the amount is too high, and they often improve once the amount is changed. Effects listed include trouble sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating and hair loss, and too much can also bring chest pain, diarrhoea and being sick. The NHS says serious side effects are rare and names an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), with a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing, and thyroid crisis, with a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or faintness, or jaundice. The NHS page says to call NHS 111 when someone taking levothyroxine thinks they might be having serious side effects. For other side effects, the NHS says to speak to a doctor or pharmacist. If more than the prescribed amount has been taken, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible, and to call NHS 111 if one cannot be reached or it was done on purpose.

liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.name: Liver blood tests: what the results mean
liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.summary: Liver blood tests can point towards a possible problem but do not name the cause, and results that are not normal are very common.
keyPoints: Liver blood tests, once called liver function tests, are a group of tests that can include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.
A result outside the reference range does not always mean liver disease, and a normal result does not always rule it out.
The pattern of results helps point towards liver cell injury or a problem with bile flow.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes needs an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What are liver blood tests?
body.body: Liver blood tests are a group of blood tests, once known as liver function tests or LFTs. They can include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.

body.heading: What do ALT and AST show?
body.body: ALT and AST are enzymes that leak into the blood when liver cells are injured. ALT is more specific to the liver, while AST can also be high when muscle is damaged elsewhere in the body. Common causes of this pattern include viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis and drug-induced liver injury. In alcohol-related liver injury AST is often higher than ALT, whereas in fatty liver disease ALT is often the higher of the two.

body.heading: What do ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin show?
body.body: Raised ALP and GGT point towards a problem with the flow of bile. Causes include blocked bile ducts, for example by stones, and some long-term diseases of the bile ducts. ALP also comes from bone, so GGT helps to show whether the liver is the source. Raised bilirubin causes jaundice, a yellowing of the eyes and skin. Bilirubin can also be raised without liver disease, as in Gilbert's syndrome, where the other liver tests are normal. Albumin is affected only when liver disease is at a severe stage, and other factors can also change albumin results. A normal GGT alongside a raised ALP points towards a source other than the liver, such as bone. Bilirubin is a pigment made when red blood cells break down, and the liver normally clears it. Albumin is a protein made by the liver.

body.heading: Does an abnormal result mean liver disease?
body.body: Abnormal results can occur in conditions that do not involve the liver, and normal results can be found in people with serious liver disease. The British Liver Trust says it is very common to have some liver blood test results that are not normal. It also says it is possible to have a normal liver blood test result and still have a serious liver condition. Medicines and herbal supplements can raise liver enzymes, as can some non-liver problems such as muscle injury. Guidelines usually start by repeating the tests, and move to further checks if results stay abnormal.

body.heading: What happens after an abnormal result?
body.body: Laboratories compare each result with their own range, so results are compared only with the range of the laboratory that did the test. If the results suggest a liver problem, a GP may calculate a FIB-4 index, which gives an indication of the amount of scarring in the liver. Depending on the results, age and possible causes, a GP may arrange more tests or regular repeat tests. Further tests can look for the cause, such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease or an effect of alcohol or medicines.

body.heading: When is yellowing of the skin urgent?
body.body: The NHS says jaundice can be a sign of something serious such as liver disease. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 when the skin or whites of the eyes look yellow. On brown or black skin the yellow colour is easier to see in the whites of the eyes. Itchy skin, darker urine and paler stools can come with it.

body.heading: What are fatty liver and alcohol-related liver disease?
body.body: NHS guidance names non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, in some pathways now called MASLD, as a common cause of abnormal liver tests. NHS hospital guidance says fatty liver disease (MASLD) is treated mainly by reversing its underlying cause, with weight loss a key part. Where alcohol is the cause, one pathway advises cutting out alcohol and repeating the test after a month. Local guidance suggests repeating the tests, including after stopping a medicine that may be affecting the liver. If results stay abnormal, guidance supports an ultrasound scan of the liver and bile ducts and blood tests for viral and autoimmune causes. Local pathways use a FibroScan result, as well as FIB-4, to decide who is referred to a liver clinic. Jaundice can have causes outside the liver, including gallstone disease and the breakdown of red blood cells (haemolysis).

loneliness-and-health.name: Loneliness and health: effects and what helps
loneliness-and-health.summary: Severe or long-lasting loneliness can affect mental and physical health, according to the NHS. Staying in touch, joining groups and asking a GP about social prescribing can help.
keyPoints: The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia, and of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression.
Regular contact with friends and family, joining a group or club, and volunteering are NHS suggestions for easing loneliness.
A GP can talk about social prescribing, which links people with a link worker for local support.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is loneliness, and is it a health issue?
body.body: Loneliness is the distress of feeling alone or disconnected, and it is not the same as spending time by yourself. The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia. It also says it might increase the risk of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression. Common triggers include bereavement, a break-up, moving away, becoming a parent or carer, and long-term illness.

body.heading: What helps with loneliness?
body.body: NHS suggestions include keeping in touch with friends and family. The NHS also suggests joining a group, for example around something you enjoy. Volunteering is another NHS suggestion. The NHS also suggests doing activities you enjoy. The NHS also suggests talking openly about how loneliness feels, and notes that comparing yourself with others, especially on social media, can make you feel lonelier. For older people, the NHS suggests keeping in touch by phone or video chat, and volunteering.

body.heading: What can a GP or the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS suggests speaking to a GP about social prescribing, which connects people with a link worker who can point to local support. NHS talking therapies can help with common problems such as stress, anxiety and depression. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with loneliness, because they can contribute to poor mental health. The NHS says a GP can help if low mood lasts or if things tried at home are not helping.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If loneliness feels overwhelming, free support lines are open at any time of day or night. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS advice is to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), open at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.name: Looking after your teeth and gums
looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.headline: Looking after your teeth and gums: brushing, cleaning between teeth and dental check-ups
looking-after-your-teeth-and-gums.summary: The NHS describes brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day, cleaning between the teeth and cutting down on sugary food and drink.
keyPoints: The NHS recommends brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day for about two minutes.
The NHS advises spitting after brushing rather than rinsing, because rinsing washes away fluoride left on the teeth.
Gum disease is driven by plaque; the early stage, gingivitis, can often be reversed with effective cleaning.
NICE says the interval between dental check-ups for adults should be no longer than 24 months and no shorter than 3 months for routine recall.

body.heading: How do brushing and fluoride help?
body.body: The NHS recommends brushing with fluoride toothpaste twice a day for about two minutes. It says electric and manual toothbrushes are both effective when every surface is cleaned. The NHS advises spitting out after brushing rather than rinsing, because rinsing washes away the fluoride still on the teeth. A fluoride mouthwash can help if it is used at a different time from brushing.

body.heading: What about cleaning between teeth and sugar?
body.body: The NHS describes cleaning between the teeth with floss or interdental brushes to remove plaque along the gum line. It says wooden toothpicks can damage the gums. The NHS advises cutting down on sugary food and drink, especially between meals. Its effect depends on how often the teeth are exposed to sugar as well as how much is eaten. Acidic drinks such as fruit juice and squash can also wear teeth.

body.heading: What is gum disease?
body.body: Bacteria in dental plaque build up on the teeth and along the gum line, and plaque is the main driver of gum disease. Gingivitis, the early stage, makes the gums swollen and red, and they can bleed. It can often be reversed with effective cleaning. Untreated, gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, which damages the bone and tissue that support the teeth and cannot be reversed, though treatment can control it. Gum disease is often painless, so it may not be noticed until a dental check. A Leeds Teaching Hospitals leaflet says smoking significantly increases the risk of gum disease, and the NHS lists stopping smoking among the advice for early-stage gum disease.

body.heading: How often are dental check-ups needed?
body.body: NICE guideline CG19 says the longest interval between oral health reviews for adults should be 24 months, and the shortest for routine recall should be 3 months. It says longer intervals suit people who have shown they can maintain good oral health and are not at risk of oral disease. NHS inform says people in Scotland are seen according to their oral health needs, which may mean more frequent visits or fewer if their oral health is good.

body.heading: Who gets free NHS dental care, and when is a dentist needed?
body.body: NHS dental treatment in England is free for some groups, including children under 18 (or under 19 in full-time education), pregnant women and women who had a baby in the past 12 months, and people on certain benefits. The NHS advises having red, swollen, sore or bleeding gums checked by a dentist. NHS pages say people not registered with a dentist can search for one on the NHS website, and that NHS 111 can put them in touch with an urgent dental service in England.

low-ferritin-what-it-means.name: Low ferritin: what it means and what next
low-ferritin-what-it-means.summary: A low ferritin level means the body's iron stores are low, and doctors then look for the cause, which is often blood loss.
keyPoints: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, so a low level means there is not much iron in store.
Ferritin can fall before blood iron levels fall, which makes it the most useful indicator of iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency is often caused by blood loss or pregnancy, so doctors look for the source.
Inflammation, infection and liver disease can raise ferritin, so it is often read alongside CRP.
The report shows the reference range used by the laboratory, which differs between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a ferritin test measure?
body.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in the body. The test estimates how much iron is held in store. Ferritin levels are low in long-term iron deficiency and high in long-term iron overload. Lab Tests Online UK describes it as the most useful indicator of iron deficiency.

body.heading: What does a low ferritin level mean?
body.body: A low ferritin points to iron deficiency. Ferritin tracks the body's iron stores, so a low result reflects low stores. Stores can drop well below normal before the iron level in the blood itself falls, so ferritin can show the problem early. Low iron can exist without anaemia, and symptoms such as tiredness can still be present. Ferritin can also fall when protein levels are very low, as in some cases of malnutrition.

body.heading: Why do iron stores run low?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is caused by a lack of iron, often because of blood loss or pregnancy. NHS formulary guidance lists heavy periods, bleeding in the digestive tract, coeliac disease and a poor diet among the causes. It also lists ulcers, medicines such as aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers, and bowel cancer as possible digestive causes, which is why the cause is looked for. UK guidance recommends checking for coeliac disease in people with iron deficiency anaemia. An NHS leaflet says blood loss from the gut is the most common cause of iron deficiency anaemia in adult men and postmenopausal women. A UK NHS guideline calls oral iron tablets the first-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy. A UK NHS guideline lists intravenous iron for anaemia that has not improved despite oral iron, or when oral iron is not tolerated.

body.heading: What symptoms go with low iron?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness, shortness of breath, noticeable heartbeats and pale skin as common symptoms. Less common symptoms include hair loss, ringing in the ears, a sore tongue and a craving for non-food items. That craving, called pica, can be for items such as ice, paper or clay. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms like these appear, and a GP appointment is the usual route for a ferritin test.

body.heading: Why can a ferritin result be misleading?
body.body: Ferritin is not only a store of iron. Lab Tests Online UK says levels can be high in inflammatory conditions, infection and liver disease. Because inflammation can push ferritin up and hide a shortage of iron, CRP is often checked alongside it. A high ferritin can signal long-term iron overload, especially haemochromatosis, but further investigation is needed before that diagnosis is made. NHS laboratory guidance for GPs notes that when inflammation is also present, ferritin may be normal or raised even when iron stores are absent.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A GP usually takes a blood test, and ferritin is the key marker of how much iron is stored. If the cause is not clear, the GP may arrange further tests to find the source. A GP may refer to a specialist if no cause can be found. Iron tablets are the usual first treatment, and the NHS says they are taken for about six months. Side effects of iron tablets, mainly in the digestive system, are common. Iron can also be given by infusion into a vein, which is used less often. Guidance says patients are monitored in the first weeks for a haemoglobin response to iron tablets.

body.heading: What helps iron stores recover?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is treated with iron tablets and with iron-rich foods. NHS guidance points to dark green leafy vegetables and dried fruit as food sources. NHS guidance says drinking orange juice after an iron tablet may help the body absorb the iron. Tea, coffee, milk and dairy foods, and wholegrain cereals can stop the body absorbing iron from other foods and tablets. One NHS page suggests taking iron tablets with or soon after food to reduce the chance of side effects. Formulary guidance says treatment continues for a period after the haemoglobin level returns to normal. Iron tablets can cause constipation, diarrhoea, tummy pain, nausea and darker stools. A Scottish guideline notes that pregnant women lose iron during and after delivery. It recommends that women who start oral iron continue it through pregnancy and for some months after the birth.

lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.name: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.headline: Lowering blood pressure with lifestyle changes: what the NHS and UK charities list
lower-blood-pressure-with-lifestyle-chan.summary: The NHS advises everyone with high blood pressure to make lifestyle changes, such as eating less salt, being more active and cutting back on alcohol.
keyPoints: The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes, with or without medicine.
The NHS gives a limit of no more than 6g of salt a day for adults, and much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods.
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day, partly because they contain potassium.
The NHS also lists regular activity, losing weight if overweight, keeping alcohol low and stopping smoking.

body.heading: Do lifestyle changes matter if medicine is offered?
body.body:
The NHS says everyone with high blood pressure is advised to make healthy lifestyle changes. Whether medicine is needed as well depends on the blood pressure readings and on the person's risk of heart attack or stroke. NICE publishes a patient decision aid for adults, titled How do I control my blood pressure? Lifestyle options and choice of medicines.

The NHS lists the main changes as eating less salt, eating a healthy balanced diet, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, being more active, losing weight if overweight and stopping smoking.

body.heading: What do the sources say about salt?
body.body:
The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day. The NHS says much of the salt people eat is already in everyday foods such as bread, breakfast cereal and ready meals. Blood Pressure UK says most people eat almost twice the recommended six grams a day.

The NHS salt page lists foods that are high in salt, such as bacon, cheese, stock cubes, soy sauce and salted nuts. When a label lists only sodium, multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. NICE recommends that clinicians encourage people to keep their dietary sodium intake low. Blood Pressure UK says salt substitutes made from potassium chloride can be high in potassium, so people with kidney problems or diabetes are advised to check with a doctor or nurse first.

body.heading: What about fruit, vegetables and potassium?
body.body:
Blood Pressure UK advises at least five portions of fruit and vegetables every day. It says they also contain potassium, which can help to balance the effects of salt. Canned, frozen and dried fruit and vegetables also count, and the charity advises choosing canned products without added salt or sugar. The British Heart Foundation explains that potassium helps the kidneys remove sodium from the blood and pass it out in urine.

The British Heart Foundation describes the DASH diet as a plan that trims sodium while raising potassium, calcium and fibre. It contains plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy products, and is low in salt, saturated fat, sugary foods and alcohol. The British Heart Foundation advises getting potassium through food rather than supplements, as too much can be harmful.

body.heading: How do alcohol, weight and activity fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises against regularly drinking more than 14 units of alcohol a week, and says to spread drinking over three days or more. The NHS lists losing weight, if overweight, among the changes that can help lower blood pressure. The NHS advice is to be active regularly, with at least 150 minutes of exercise a week, and says moderate activity is enough.

body.heading: What else do the NHS pages mention?
body.body: The NHS also lists cutting back on caffeine and stopping smoking among the changes that can help. NHS dietitian fact sheets say supplements of calcium, magnesium or potassium are not recommended as a way to lower blood pressure. Sources do not all give the same figures, so the NHS pages are the ones used here for limits on salt and alcohol.

lumbar-puncture-what-happens-and-what-to.name: Lumbar puncture: what happens and what to expect
lumbar-puncture-what-happens-and-what-to.summary: A lumbar puncture uses a needle in the lower back to collect the fluid around the spinal cord, and the pressure of the fluid may also be measured.
keyPoints: A lumbar puncture is usually done in hospital under local anaesthetic, and leaflets give different times, from about 15 minutes to 40 minutes.
Fluid from around the spinal cord is collected for testing.
A headache is the most common side effect, and serious complications are described as extremely rare.
Some results come back within a day and others take weeks, so the team can say when to expect them.

body.heading: What is a lumbar puncture?
body.body:
A lumbar puncture is a procedure in which a needle is placed between the bones of the lower spine to reach the fluid that surrounds the spinal cord and brain. This fluid is called cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF.

The NHS says it is usually done in hospital. A local anaesthetic numbs the lower back, the needle goes in between the spinal bones and fluid is collected for testing.

Doctors use it to collect spinal fluid for testing and to measure the pressure of the fluid.

body.heading: What happens during the procedure?
body.body:
One leaflet says it typically takes around 15 to 20 minutes but can take longer, and another says 20 to 40 minutes. The lower back is cleaned and numbed with a local anaesthetic injection before the needle is placed.

Leaflets say to expect to rest flat for a short period afterwards, and the team caring for you gives the details.

body.heading: What are the side effects and risks?
body.body:
Headache, back pain and bruising are common side effects. The headache is the most frequent. It can start from a few hours to two days after the procedure and last for a few days.

Leaflets say lying flat usually helps the headache.

Serious complications are described as extremely rare. Very rare complications include infection, bleeding, nerve injury, hearing loss and double vision. One hospital trust leaflet says serious harm from complications like these occurs in fewer than one in 10,000 lumbar punctures.

body.heading: When should I get help after a lumbar puncture?
body.body: Leaflets list a severe headache that does not ease on lying flat, a fever, neck stiffness or leg weakness as reasons to get urgent advice from the hospital team or NHS 111. The hospital team who did the test, NHS 111 or the GP the same day can advise, and 999 is for emergencies.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body: It depends on the test. Some results can come back within a day. Other tests take longer, sometimes up to 10 weeks. The team caring for you can say when to expect them.
