pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.name: Pelvic pain in women: causes and when to act
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.headline: Pelvic pain in women: common causes, red flags and which NHS route to use
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.summary: Pelvic pain in women often comes from period pain, ovarian cysts or endometriosis, but a few causes are serious. The NHS says to call 999 for severe or worsening pain.
keyPoints: The NHS lists period pain, ovarian cysts, endometriosis and pregnancy-related pain among the common causes of pelvic pain in women.
Rarer causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease and womb or ovarian cancer.
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area.
Pain that comes and goes or does not go away is a reason for a routine GP appointment.

body.heading: What causes pelvic pain?
body.body: The NHS says pelvic pain is more common in women. Common causes include period pain, an ovarian cyst, endometriosis and pain related to pregnancy. Rarer but more serious causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, womb cancer and ovarian cancer.

body.heading: What is pelvic inflammatory disease?
body.body: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the female reproductive organs. PID is often caused by a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea. Bacteria that normally live in the vagina cause some cases.

body.heading: When is a routine GP appointment appropriate?
body.body: The NHS suggests booking a GP appointment if pelvic pain comes and goes or does not go away. Bloating that does not go away, weight loss or changes in bowel habit are further reasons. Pain during sex is also a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: When should you call NHS 111 or an urgent GP?
body.body: The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 for pelvic pain with difficulty peeing or pooing, blood in urine or stool, unusual vaginal discharge, or a very high temperature. The same advice applies if the person is or may be pregnant. For an ovarian cyst, sudden severe pelvic pain is a reason for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area. Fainting or feeling dizzy, pain at the tip of the shoulder, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding and sudden confusion are also on the 999 list. For PID, the NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E for severe pelvic pain or heavy vaginal bleeding, and not to drive yourself.

body.heading: Which tests might follow?
body.body: If PID is suspected, a GP may take a sample of vaginal discharge to test, and an ultrasound scan may be used. Some people with PID have a negative swab result, so a negative swab does not rule it out.

periods-whats-normal-and-when-to-see-a-g.name: Periods: what is normal and when to see a GP
periods-whats-normal-and-when-to-see-a-g.summary: The NHS gives an average cycle of about 28 days. A GP can help if periods change, become painful or stop.
keyPoints: The NHS says the average cycle is about 28 days, and regular cycles of 21 to 35 days are also normal.
NI Direct says a period usually lasts 2 to 7 days.
The NHS lists periods lasting longer than 7 days and bleeding between periods as reasons to see a GP.
Period pain that affects daily life is a reason to see a GP, according to NI Direct.
Not being pregnant and having missed more than 3 periods in a row is a reason to see a GP, according to the NHS and NI Direct.

body.heading: What does a normal period look like?
body.body:
A period is the time in the menstrual cycle when the womb lining is shed and leaves the body as blood. If an egg is not fertilised, the levels of the hormones oestrogen and progesterone fall.

The NHS says the average menstrual cycle is about 28 days. It also describes regular cycles of 21 to 35 days as normal. NI Direct, the Northern Ireland government health service, says a period usually lasts 2 to 7 days. Sources vary a little on the exact ranges, so the numbers are a guide and not a strict rule.

body.heading: What counts as an irregular period?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales says periods are usually called irregular when the gap between them is under 21 days or over 35 days. The NHS says irregular can also mean a change in how much blood is lost or in how long bleeding lasts.

The NHS names several common causes. These include puberty, the years around the menopause, pregnancy and changing hormonal contraception. NI Direct also lists stress, sudden weight loss or gain and over-exercising as common reasons for missed or changed periods. The NHS also names polycystic ovary syndrome and thyroid problems as possible causes.

body.heading: When do periods or bleeding between periods need a GP?
body.body:
The NHS lists periods lasting longer than 7 days and bleeding between periods as reasons to see a GP. It also lists periods that have become irregular, and difficulty getting pregnant. NHS Inform advises contacting a GP about bleeding between periods or after sex, and about periods that come closer together or further apart than usual. It adds that cancers of the womb or cervix can, in rare cases, cause bleeding between periods, which is one reason it is worth having checked.

The NHS describes signs of heavy bleeding, such as passing blood clots larger than about 2.5 centimetres and needing two types of period product at the same time. Heavy periods are covered on their own page on this site.

body.heading: When is period pain a reason to see a GP?
body.body:
NI Direct says period cramps are usually caused by the womb muscle tightening, and that the womb wall contracts more strongly during a period to help the lining shed. It lists hormonal contraception, exercise and over-the-counter painkillers such as ibuprofen or paracetamol among the things that can ease the pain. It advises seeing a GP if the pain is so severe that it affects daily life.

Period pain that disrupts daily activities is also one of the symptoms NICE lists as a reason to suspect endometriosis. The NHS advises seeing a GP about possible endometriosis symptoms, especially if they have a big impact on life, and says it may help to write the symptoms down first. A GP may refer someone to gynaecology if initial treatment does not work or is not tolerated. A normal ultrasound scan does not rule endometriosis out.

body.heading: Which pelvic pain needs urgent help?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales advises asking for an urgent GP appointment, or getting help from NHS 111, if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when moving or touching the area. The same page lists difficulty passing urine or opening the bowels, a very high temperature and pregnancy as other reasons for urgent help.

NHS 111 Wales says a few conditions that cause pelvic pain need emergency treatment, such as appendicitis and peritonitis. It describes NHS 111 as the service for when medical help is needed fast but it is not a 999 emergency. Emergencies are for 999.

body.heading: What if periods stop, or have not started?
body.body:
NI Direct and the NHS advise seeing a GP when someone is not pregnant, has had a negative pregnancy test and has missed more than 3 periods in a row. NI Direct lists pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss and over-exercising among the common reasons for missed periods.

For periods that have not started, the NHS says to see a GP if they have not begun by the age of 15. NHS 111 Wales gives 15, or 13 if there are no other signs of puberty. NHS Inform puts it at around 16. Reasons for a delayed start include being underweight, intense exercise, severe stress, an eating disorder, hormone problems and medical conditions. NHS Inform notes that some people start their periods later than others, and that this can be normal. A GP will typically ask about health and may arrange blood tests to find the cause.

body.heading: What helps before a GP appointment, and what about premenstrual symptoms?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales suggests that before seeing a GP about period problems, it can be useful to keep a diary of symptoms through the menstrual cycle. This gives the doctor a detailed picture of what happens, and when. Using an app or a diary to track periods can also show whether cycles are irregular.

NI Direct links premenstrual syndrome to shifting hormone levels across the cycle. Symptoms such as mood changes, irritability, headaches, tiredness, bloating and breast tenderness usually start in the two weeks before a period and ease once it starts. Not everyone has them. A more severe form, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, can disrupt daily life.

persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.name: A cough that will not go: causes and tests
persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.summary: The NHS advises a GP visit for a cough lasting over 3 weeks, and an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell.

The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak.
The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines.

body.heading: What causes a cough that lasts?
body.body: The NHS cough page lists smoking, heartburn (acid reflux), allergies and infections such as bronchitis as causes. NHS guidance describes asthma, bronchiectasis, acid reflux and postnasal drip as causes of a long-lasting cough. Some NHS hospital trust leaflets list ACE inhibitors, a type of blood pressure medicine, as a cause of a long-lasting cough. NHS inform says a persistent cough is often of unknown cause. The NHS says bronchitis often gets better without treatment in around 3 weeks. A chest infection usually gets better on its own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough and mucus can last up to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are generally not used for viral chest infections such as flu or viral bronchitis.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines. A local NHS self-care leaflet says there is little evidence on whether over-the-counter cough medicines relieve symptoms.

body.heading: When should a cough be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened. A South East London Cancer Alliance page urges people with a persistent cough to contact their GP. The NHS lung cancer symptoms page lists symptoms including chest or shoulder pain, weight loss without trying, and tiredness.

body.heading: When is a cough urgent?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell. The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak. For people with bronchiectasis, the NHS says to call 999 if more than a few streaks of blood are coughed up.

body.heading: What does the GP do?
body.body: A GP may listen to the chest. NHS inform says a GP may arrange tests such as a chest X-ray, breathing or lung function tests, and a sample of phlegm. NHS pages say antibiotics are not usually prescribed for coughs, and a GP may refer people to a specialist if the cause is unclear.

pet-and-bone-scans-what-to-expect.name: PET and bone scans: what to expect
pet-and-bone-scans-what-to-expect.summary: PET and bone scans both use a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection. Both scans involve a waiting period after the injection.
keyPoints: A PET scan uses a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection to scan inside the body.
PET scans help diagnose or plan treatment for conditions such as cancer, dementia and epilepsy.
A bone scan uses a tracer that collects in bone and shows areas where bone is breaking down and being repaired.
Both involve a small amount of radiation, and hospitals give their own instructions on preparation and waiting times.

body.heading: What is a PET scan?
body.body:
The NHS describes a PET scan as a test that uses a small amount of radiation to scan inside the body. A small amount of radioactive tracer is given by injection.

A PET-CT scan combines the PET scan with a CT scan.

body.heading: Why would I need one?
body.body: The NHS says PET scans are used to diagnose or plan treatment for certain conditions, such as cancer, dementia or epilepsy.

body.heading: What is a bone scan?
body.body:
A bone scan is a nuclear medicine test that looks at the activity of cells in the bones. A tracer is injected, collects in the bones, and a special camera takes pictures of it.

Areas where more tracer collects show up as hot spots. A bone scan can show areas where bone is breaking down and being repaired.

body.heading: How do I prepare, and what is the day like?
body.body:
Hospitals usually give fasting instructions for a PET scan, which vary, and ask people to remove metal items such as jewellery.

After the injection, people usually rest for around an hour while the tracer spreads through the body. The scan itself usually takes around 30 to 60 minutes, and longer at some hospitals, and people need to stay still.

For a bone scan, leaflets describe a wait of a few hours after the injection, and some suggest drinking plenty of fluids and emptying the bladder often. A camera then takes pictures of the bones.

Each hospital's own leaflet has the exact instructions.

body.heading: Is the radiation a concern?
body.body:
Both scans involve a small amount of radiation. The NHS describes the radiation risk from the tracer injection as very small. Hospital leaflets describe the radiation dose from a bone scan as small.

Some hospitals advise limiting close, prolonged contact with pregnant women and young children for a period afterwards, and staff say for how long. Departments ask anyone who is or might be pregnant to contact them before the scan.

body.heading: When do results come back?
body.body:
After a PET scan people can usually go home soon afterwards. A radiologist reviews the images and the report goes to the doctor who referred the person. The NHS says it usually takes 1 or 2 weeks to get PET scan results.

Bone scan results vary by hospital, from days to a few weeks, so the hospital that arranged the scan can say.

pet-and-bone-scans-what-to-expect.metaDescription: PET and bone scans both use a small amount of radioactive tracer given by injection. Both scans involve a waiting period after the injection.

physical-activity-guidelines-adults.name: How much exercise adults need each week
physical-activity-guidelines-adults.summary: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus strength work.
keyPoints: The NHS lists at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults aged 19 to 64.
Strengthening activities for the major muscle groups on at least two days a week are in addition to the aerobic minutes.
The NHS talk test separates moderate activity, where a person can talk but not sing, from vigorous activity, where only a few words fit between breaths.
The guidance also advises reducing long periods of sitting, and the 2019 update dropped the older rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes.

body.heading: How much activity do adults aged 19 to 64 need?
body.body: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week, or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity activity a week. It also describes a mix of moderate and vigorous activity as a way of reaching the target. The NHS adds that 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week can give similar health benefits to 150 minutes of moderate activity. The guidance says activity should be spread across the week, and that all adults should aim to be active every day.

body.heading: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
body.body: The NHS uses a talk test: at moderate intensity a person can still talk but not sing. Brisk walking, cycling, dancing, water aerobics and pushing a lawn mower are listed as moderate activities. At vigorous intensity breathing becomes hard and fast, and a person cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. Running, swimming, fast or uphill cycling, skipping and team sports are listed as vigorous activities. The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines say very vigorous activity, such as sprinting or stair climbing, can count too, in shorter periods or mixed with other intensities.

body.heading: What are strengthening activities?
body.body: The NHS says adults should do strengthening activities on at least two days a week, working all the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. Lifting weights, push-ups, sit-ups, heavy gardening such as digging and carrying heavy shopping are given as examples, along with yoga, pilates and tai chi. The NHS says these sessions are needed in addition to the aerobic minutes, because they do not count toward the 150 minutes. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance adds that any strengthening activity is better than none.

body.heading: Does sitting still matter?
body.body: The NHS guidance advises reducing the time spent sitting or lying down, and breaking up long periods of not moving with some activity. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says adults should aim to minimise time spent sitting and, where possible, break up long inactive periods with at least light activity.

body.heading: What do the guidelines say about benefits and short bouts?
body.body: The NHS says exercising even once or twice a week can reduce the risk of heart disease or stroke. The 2019 revision of the UK guidelines removed the earlier rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes. The guidance says there is no minimum amount of physical activity needed for some health benefit.

body.heading: What does regular activity do for health?
body.body: The NHS says regular activity lowers the risk of conditions including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and dementia. It also says activity can improve self-esteem, mood, sleep quality and energy.

body.heading: What changes for adults aged 65 and over?
body.body: NHS guidance for older adults advises being active every day, even lightly. It recommends activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week. The NHS advises speaking to a GP first for anyone who has not exercised for some time or who has medical conditions or concerns.

pregnancy-scans-and-tests-on-the-nhs.name: Pregnancy scans and tests on the NHS
pregnancy-scans-and-tests-on-the-nhs.summary: NHS pregnancy care includes booking blood tests, a dating scan and a mid-pregnancy anomaly scan, plus optional screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes.
keyPoints: The booking appointment with a midwife is usually between 8 and 12 weeks and includes blood tests and checks of blood pressure and urine.
The dating scan, usually at 11 to 14 weeks, estimates the due date from the baby's measurements.
Screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes is a choice, and taking part is up to the pregnant person.
The mid-pregnancy anomaly scan usually takes place between 18 and 21 weeks and checks for 11 physical conditions in the baby.

body.heading: What happens at the booking appointment?
body.body:
The booking appointment is the first main antenatal visit, and the NHS gives the usual timing as between 8 and 12 weeks. The midwife checks blood pressure and urine and offers a blood group test.

Blood is also taken at or around this time. NHS trusts describe booking-stage blood tests for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, sickle cell and thalassaemia, and the exact list can vary between trusts.

body.heading: What is the dating scan?
body.body: The dating scan is an ultrasound scan, usually offered at 11 to 14 weeks. It estimates when the baby is due from the baby's measurements.

body.heading: Is screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes compulsory?
body.body:
Taking part in this screening is a choice. If a person chooses it, the combined test pairs a blood test taken between 10 and 14 weeks with a measurement of the fluid at the back of the baby's neck, taken during the dating scan.

Edwards' and Patau's syndromes are also looked for at the mid-pregnancy scan if the person chooses screening. A blood test called the quad test, taken between 14 and 20 weeks, can be used for Down's syndrome when the combined test was not possible. It is less accurate than the combined test.

body.heading: What does the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan look at?
body.body:
The anomaly scan is an ultrasound that checks for 11 physical conditions in the baby and the position of the placenta, though not every condition can be found. The NHS lists it as usually between 18 and 21 weeks, and some trusts describe it as taking place between 20 and 22 weeks.

Screening for Edwards' and Patau's syndromes forms part of this scan for those who choose it.

body.heading: What if a screening result says there is a higher chance?
body.body:
A higher-chance result is not a diagnosis. The options described are a more accurate screening blood test, called the non-invasive prenatal test or NIPT, a diagnostic test such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, or no further tests.

The NHS summary says there are no known risks to the pregnant person or the baby from the blood tests or scans used for this screening. Diagnostic tests, such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, are different from screening and can give a definite answer. If the screening finds something, the person is contacted sooner.

For urgent concerns in pregnancy, the midwife, maternity unit or NHS 111 can advise, and 999 is for emergencies.

preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.name: Preventing food poisoning at home: the 4 Cs
preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.headline: Preventing food poisoning at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and cross-contamination
preventing-food-poisoning-at-home-the-fo.summary: NHS inform and the Food Standards Agency describe four steps for food safety at home: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination.
keyPoints: NHS inform describes four basic steps to food safety at home, known as the four Cs: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination.
The Food Standards Agency advises against washing raw meat, because washing can splash bacteria onto hands, utensils and worktops.
Cooked food is chilled promptly, and leftovers are reheated only once until steaming hot all the way through.
NHS pages advise people at higher risk of infection, such as pregnant women and people with a weakened immune system, to take extra care with some foods.

body.heading: What are the four Cs?
body.body: NHS inform describes four basic steps to food safety at home, known as the four Cs: cleaning, cooking, chilling and avoiding cross-contamination. The Food Standards Agency also lists cleaning, cooking, chilling and cross-contamination as the four core areas of good hygiene. Food Standards Scotland promotes the four Cs as a way to avoid campylobacter food poisoning.

body.heading: How do hands and surfaces fit in?
body.body: The Food Standards Agency advises washing hands after handling raw meat, fish and poultry. NHS inform says hands, surfaces and equipment should be cleaned before, during and after cooking, and the Food Standards Agency says cloths and tea towels should be washed on a hot cycle and left to dry before they are used again. A Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust sheet advises washing fruit and vegetables before they are eaten. The Food Standards Agency says raw meat should not be washed, because water can splash bacteria onto hands, clothes, utensils and worktops. NHS inform gives the same advice about raw chicken: cooking it thoroughly kills germs, and rinsing risks spreading them.

body.heading: What does cooking food thoroughly mean?
body.body: NHS inform says food should be cooked through so that harmful bacteria are killed. NHS inform says poultry, pork and offal should not be eaten pink. Food Standards Agency consumer messaging stresses reheating leftover food only once, and making sure it is steaming hot all the way through.

body.heading: How do chilling and cross-contamination work?
body.body:
NHS inform advises cooling cooked food and putting it in the fridge within two hours. Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust says leftovers should be eaten within two days. The Food Standards Agency says pre-packed food can be frozen up to midnight on its use-by date.

NHS inform describes cross-contamination as bacteria spreading from raw food to cooked food, utensils or surfaces. NHS inform advises separate boards and utensils for raw and ready-to-eat foods, and a Buckinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust sheet advises storing raw meat in a sealed container on the bottom shelf of the fridge. The Food Standards Agency advises using separate chopping boards and utensils for raw meat and other foods where possible.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk from some foods?
body.body: NHS pages on pregnancy and listeriosis list raw or runny eggs without the Lion stamp, pâté and ready-to-eat cold-smoked fish among the foods to take care with. The NHS says cold-smoked fish is safer if it is cooked until steaming hot.

references.title: NHS inform: Preparing and cooking food safely

prostate-problems-symptoms-and-when-to-s.name: Prostate problems: symptoms and seeing a GP
prostate-problems-symptoms-and-when-to-s.summary: Prostate symptoms are mostly urinary, such as a weak flow or going more often. Causes include enlargement, infection and cancer.
keyPoints: The NHS describes urinary changes, such as a weak flow, dribbling and needing to pee more often, as the main signs of an enlarged prostate.
Prostate Cancer UK says urinary changes are more often linked to a common non-cancerous enlargement than to cancer.
Early prostate cancer can cause no symptoms, according to NHS inform.
The NHS says to see a GP if there are any symptoms of an enlarged prostate.
The NHS enlarged prostate page says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if a man cannot pee at all.

body.heading: What are the common prostate symptoms?
body.body:
The prostate is a small gland below the bladder in men. For an enlarged prostate, the NHS describes urinary problems as the main sign. These include a weak flow, dribbling and needing to pee more often, including at night.

Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate. It can cause pain or stinging when passing urine, straining to pass urine and needing to go more often. The NHS also lists pain in the penis, scrotum, testicles or bottom, pain on ejaculation and fever.

Early prostate cancer can cause no symptoms, according to NHS inform, and Prostate Cancer UK says most men with early disease have no signs at all. NHS inform adds that symptoms tend to appear once a tumour presses on the urethra.

body.heading: What can cause prostate symptoms?
body.body:
The NHS says the cause of benign prostate enlargement is not clear, but it is thought to be linked to hormone changes as a man gets older. University Hospitals Sussex describes testosterone being converted into a hormone called dihydrotestosterone in prostate cells, with high levels of this hormone driving the enlargement. Why those levels rise is still being studied.

The NHS says prostatitis is often caused by infection. It is not always known what causes long-term prostatitis. Prostate cancer is another possible cause of urinary symptoms, and NHS inform notes that the symptoms of an enlarged prostate overlap with those of other conditions, including prostate cancer.

body.heading: Does an enlarged prostate mean cancer?
body.body:
Prostate Cancer UK says urinary changes are more often linked to a common non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate than to cancer. Because the symptoms overlap, NHS inform says the GP needs to be sure they are not caused by cancer.

Blood in the urine also needs checking. One NHS source says any blood in the urine must be investigated by a GP to rule out more serious conditions. NHS 111 Wales says urine with blood in it may look pink, red or brown.

body.heading: When should a man see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS says to see a GP if there are any symptoms of an enlarged prostate. NHS inform advises seeing a GP about any problems with, or changes to, the usual pattern of urinating.

NHS 111 Wales says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 Wales if there is blood in the pee or pain when peeing. The NHS enlarged prostate page says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if a man cannot pee at all. For prostatitis, the NHS gives the same urgent route if a man cannot pee, or if symptoms have not improved or have got worse after 48 hours of antibiotics.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body:
The NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and how they affect quality of life. The GP may feel the prostate through the wall of the back passage, which is called a rectal examination. A urine sample is usually tested, and a blood test may check how well the kidneys are working. A PSA blood test may also be offered, but the NHS says it cannot give a definite diagnosis of prostate cancer.

Men are usually asked to keep a record of what they drink and how often they pee, for at least three days. NHS inform says a symptom score called the International Prostate Symptom Score may be worked out. A referral to a specialist is typically made if the prostate feels abnormal or cancer is a concern. A specialist may arrange urodynamic tests of the urinary system, and NHS 111 Wales says a hospital may arrange an ultrasound scan of the bladder.

body.heading: What treatments are there for an enlarged prostate?
body.body:
NHS 111 Wales says that if symptoms are not causing many problems, doctors will usually recommend trying lifestyle changes first. MedlinePlus, a US source, suggests reducing evening fluids and limiting caffeine and alcohol.

Alpha-blockers relax the bladder neck and prostate muscle, and University Hospitals Sussex says they increase urine flow and improve symptoms. Another group of medicines, the 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, shrink the gland and may slow progression. NHS 111 Wales says they are recommended mainly for men at high risk of the condition getting worse. Surgery is generally reserved for moderate to severe symptoms that medicines do not control, and MedlinePlus describes transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) as the most common and most proven surgery for an enlarged prostate.

For sudden bacterial prostatitis, the NHS says treatment is with antibiotics. Long-term prostatitis is generally defined as symptoms lasting three months or more. A GP may refer a man to a urologist, and treatment can include medicines, counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy, and physiotherapy. The NHS says recovery is usually gradual and can take several months or years.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body:
NHS inform defines acute urinary retention as the sudden inability to pass any urine. It lists it as a possible complication of benign prostate enlargement, alongside urinary tract infections and, in later stages, bladder stones, bladder infections and kidney damage.

For a man who cannot pee at all, the NHS enlarged prostate page says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111. For prostatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden confusion, blue or pale skin or lips, a non-fading rash or severe difficulty breathing. NHS 111 Wales says that no improvement after 48 hours of antibiotics may signal a serious infection or sepsis.

protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.name: Protecting your hearing from loud noise
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.headline: Protecting your hearing from loud noise: headphones, earplugs and warning signs
protecting-your-hearing-from-loud-noise.summary: The WHO and NHS sources say noise-related hearing loss is permanent but can be prevented, mainly by lowering volume, taking breaks and using ear protection.
keyPoints: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented through safe listening, although the damage is permanent.
NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume.
Reusable musicians' earplugs reduce the volume of music without muffling it, according to an NHS trust leaflet.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears.

body.heading: Can loud noise cause permanent hearing loss?
body.body: The WHO says noise-induced hearing loss can be prevented by following safe listening, although the damage itself is permanent. Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust says that once the cochlea has been damaged no treatment or surgery can undo it. The WHO estimates that 1.1 billion young people worldwide could be at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening practices. NHS inform says hearing loss often develops with age or is caused by repeated exposure to loud noise, and that it is possible to reduce the risk of noise-induced hearing loss.

body.heading: What do the sources say about headphones?
body.body: NHS inform advises choosing headphones that block out more outside noise rather than turning up the volume. The Royal Free London leaflet says noise-cancelling headphones can help because they remove the urge to turn the volume up to drown out outside noise. The WHO advises keeping the volume low, taking short listening breaks and, where possible, using carefully fitted noise-cancelling earphones. The WHO's recommendations for young people include limiting daily use of personal audio devices to less than one hour. The Royal Free leaflet advises keeping the volume modest and taking a short break from headphones each hour. The WHO notes that smartphone apps can help monitor listening levels.

body.heading: How do earplugs and earmuffs differ?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe earplugs and earmuffs as working by reducing the level of sound that reaches the ears. Earplugs are described as probably best for long-term use, while very high noise levels may call for high-attenuation earmuffs. The Royal Free leaflet says reusable musicians' earplugs lower the volume of music without muffling it. Torbay and South Devon audiology says ordinary pharmacy earplugs are often designed for swimming or background noise and may not protect against damaging noise. The WHO recommends wearing earplugs in noisy venues.

body.heading: What are the warning signs of too much noise?
body.body: It suggests moving away from loudspeakers at loud events and taking a break from the noise every 15 minutes. RNID warns of a risk of hearing damage after just 15 minutes in a nightclub playing music at an average of 100 decibels without earplugs. The WHO advises watching for signs of hearing loss, such as ringing in the ears or trouble hearing some sounds or conversations.

body.heading: When does a change in hearing need medical advice?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears, hearing that has worsened over days or weeks, or hearing loss with earache or discharge from the ear. It advises a routine GP appointment when hearing is getting gradually worse. Arrangements for hearing assessments vary by area, and some NHS audiology services ask for a referral from a GP.

psa-test-what-it-shows-and-what-the-nhs-.name: PSA test: what it shows and what the NHS says
psa-test-what-it-shows-and-what-the-nhs-.summary: A PSA test measures prostate-specific antigen in the blood. The NHS says it is not a routine screening test, and results can be wrong in both directions.
keyPoints: A PSA test is a blood test that measures prostate-specific antigen, and a high level may be a sign of a prostate condition.
The NHS does not offer routine PSA screening, though testing is offered to some people, including men with a faulty BRCA2 gene and those with symptoms that suggest prostate cancer.
Men aged 50 or over without symptoms can ask their GP about a PSA test, after discussing the benefits and risks.
PSA results can be falsely reassuring or falsely alarming, and the test can find slow-growing cancers that might never have caused harm.

body.heading: What is a PSA test?
body.body:
A PSA test is a blood test that measures the amount of prostate-specific antigen. Prostate Cancer UK says a raised PSA may suggest a prostate problem, but not necessarily cancer.

A raised PSA can have several causes, so it is not a diagnosis on its own.

body.heading: Is PSA testing part of NHS screening?
body.body:
No. The NHS says routine PSA testing is not currently offered. The exception it describes is for men whose genetic tests have shown a faulty version of a gene called BRCA2.

A PSA test may also be recommended when someone has symptoms that could point to prostate cancer.

body.heading: Can I ask my GP for a PSA test?
body.body:
Outside the groups above, the NHS describes an informed-choice route in which a person can ask a GP about PSA testing. Men aged 50 or over can ask their GP about PSA testing even without symptoms.

The aim is to give clear information on the advantages and disadvantages of the test first. Asking a GP is the route to start that conversation.

body.heading: What are the benefits of a PSA test?
body.body: A GOV.UK programme page, now withdrawn, said a large European trial showed PSA testing can reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer.

body.heading: What are the limits and risks?
body.body:
The NHS says PSA tests are unreliable. A result can suggest cancer when there is none, which is called a false positive. A normal result does not rule cancer out either: the NHS says around 1 in 7 men with a normal PSA may have prostate cancer.

The test can also find cancers that are unlikely to cause harm, known as overdiagnosis. Overtreatment of such cancers is a recognised concern. This is why the NHS presents the decision as an informed choice.

Anyone worried about symptoms can contact a GP; NHS 111 can advise if the surgery is closed, and 999 is for emergencies.

puberty-what-happens-and-when-to-get-adv.name: Puberty: what happens and when to get advice
puberty-what-happens-and-when-to-get-adv.summary: Puberty brings body and mood changes at different ages, and NHS pages advise a GP appointment if it starts early or seems late.
keyPoints: MedlinePlus says puberty usually starts between ages 8 and 13 for girls and between ages 9 and 14 for boys.
Girls typically notice breast development first, boys usually begin with growth of the testicles and penis, and both have a growth spurt and may notice mood changes.
The NHS says signs of puberty before age 8 could be early puberty, and parents who notice early signs are advised to book a GP appointment.
NHS sources give different ages for delayed puberty, and delayed puberty often runs in families.
In a crisis, 999 is for immediate danger, NHS 111 has a mental health option, and Samaritans is on 116 123 at any time.

body.heading: What is puberty, and when does it start?
body.body:
Puberty is the time when a child's body changes as it grows towards adulthood. MedlinePlus says it usually starts between ages 8 and 13 for girls and between ages 9 and 14 for boys. One NHS trust gives an average of 11 for girls and 12 for boys, and describes any start within those ranges as normal. Girls are often the earlier of the two, and the timing varies a lot from child to child.

Both girls and boys have a growth spurt, and both may notice changes in mood. MedlinePlus says growth spurts typically last about 2 to 3 years. Sources differ on some age thresholds, so the figures in this guide are attributed to the page that gave them.

body.heading: What changes happen in girls?
body.body:
Girls typically notice breast development first. Pubic and underarm hair growth often comes with puberty in both sexes, and increased sweating is common too. Girls also have a growth spurt, and one source says a rapid increase in height usually occurs around 10 to 14 years.

One source says periods usually start between 8 and 14, and that most girls get them around 12 to 13.

body.heading: What changes happen in boys?
body.body: Boys usually begin with growth of the testicles and penis. Pubic and underarm hair growth and increased sweating are also common. One source says boys usually start their growth spurt about 2 years after puberty begins.

body.heading: How can puberty affect feelings and skin?
body.body:
One NHS leaflet says a child may become more emotional during this time. Hormonal shifts can cause mood swings, including intense emotions such as love, happiness, sadness and rage. A Healthier Together page notes that the part of the brain which regulates mood, memory and planning is still developing. Another local NHS page explains that changing hormone levels during puberty can affect mood.

Rising hormones increase sweat and skin oil, which can cause body odour, greasy hair and spots. Body odour and acne are common in both boys and girls.

body.heading: What happens with the first periods?
body.body:
A Healthier Together page says lots of young people have irregular periods when they first start, and it can take 2 to 3 years before a period settles into a normal rhythm. A Chelsea and Westminster hospital page says that in the first few years periods can be heavier and more irregular, and that over time they often become lighter and more regular.

The same page suggests that medical advice is sensible if periods cause very distressing symptoms or significantly affect daily life, for example by making it hard to attend school or usual activities. One source notes that medical advice is also sensible if periods start before age 8, or have not started by 15 (or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty).

body.heading: What counts as early or late puberty, and who can help?
body.body:
The NHS says that signs of puberty before age 8 could be early puberty. Other NHS guidance uses the term precocious puberty when a girl starts before age 8 and a boy starts before age 9. Parents who notice these early signs are advised to book an appointment with their GP practice. Early puberty can sometimes cause a child to stop growing sooner than expected, and Scottish referral guidance says it may reduce final adult height.

A Kingston and Richmond NHS leaflet says that in most cases of early puberty there is no underlying cause, particularly in girls, though sometimes it runs in the family. A GP may refer a child to a hospital paediatric outpatient clinic to rule out underlying health problems. Medicine is usually only recommended if early puberty is thought likely to cause emotional or physical problems, which might include short stature or early periods in girls.

NHS sources give different ages for delayed puberty. The main NHS page says that if puberty has not started by age 15, this could be delayed puberty. The Kingston and Richmond leaflet uses no signs of puberty by 13 in girls and by 14 in boys, and a Healthier Together page suggests seeing a GP if there are no changes by age 14. Delayed puberty often runs in families.

Another source lists puberty that starts but does not progress, or signs that appear in an unusual order, as reasons to contact the GP. If a GP suspects a problem, they may order blood tests, an X-ray of the wrist to estimate likely adult height, or an ultrasound or MRI scan. The GP may refer a child to a specialist, usually a general paediatrician or an endocrinologist (a doctor who knows about hormone problems), if there may be an underlying cause that needs investigation. If delayed puberty is caused by a disease or an eating disorder, treating the cause may help puberty develop normally.

body.heading: Where can young people get support?
body.body:
A Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS trust page says that anyone under 19 can call Childline on 0800 1111, and an Aneurin Bevan Healthier Together page describes Childline as a free, private and confidential service. For a routine question about puberty starting early or late, the NHS pages above point to a GP appointment.

For a mental health crisis, the NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance or go straight to A&E if someone has seriously harmed themselves or feels they may be about to harm themselves. For urgent help that is not an emergency, the NHS Every Mind Matters page points to NHS 111 online or calling 111 and choosing the mental health option, where a trained mental health professional answers. Samaritans is a free 24-hour helpline on 116 123, and callers do not need to be suicidal.

reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.name: Reliever and preventer inhalers explained
reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.headline: Reliever and preventer inhalers: what is the difference?
reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.summary: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen, while a preventer is taken every day to reduce airway inflammation.
keyPoints: A reliever is used when symptoms appear, and a preventer is taken every day, even when a person feels well, to reduce airway inflammation, according to Asthma + Lung UK.
NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler.
The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a steroid inhaler to help prevent thrush; Asthma + Lung UK says a spacer can also reduce steroid side effects.
The NHS and Asthma + Lung UK both link needing a reliever more often than usual with asthma that is not well controlled; Asthma + Lung UK advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.
Asthma + Lung UK says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping in an asthma attack, and to ask for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment after managing an attack alone.

body.heading: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
body.body: A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms appear. Blue reliever inhalers contain salbutamol, a short-acting bronchodilator, which is a medicine that quickly opens the airways. A preventer inhaler is taken every day, even when a person feels well, and works over time to reduce airway inflammation. The two do different jobs. NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler. Asthma + Lung UK adds that relying only on a reliever makes symptoms and asthma attacks more likely.

body.heading: How are they used, and what else is there?
body.body: Salbutamol is the usual blue reliever. A preventer such as beclometasone is an inhaled steroid. Asthma + Lung UK says a GP or nurse should discuss switching from a blue-only reliever to an anti-inflammatory reliever, known as an AIR inhaler, which combines a reliever with a low-dose steroid. The NHS says steroid inhalers should not be stopped without medical advice. In COPD, the NHS says short-acting bronchodilator inhalers are usually the first treatment. A steroid inhaler may be suggested if breathlessness continues on a long-acting inhaler or flare-ups stay frequent, and it is usually combined with a long-acting medicine in one inhaler.

body.heading: What does a spacer do?
body.body: A spacer is a chamber used with a pressurised metered-dose inhaler, the kind that sprays out a puff of medicine. Asthma + Lung UK says using a spacer can also prevent side effects from steroid medicines in preventer or combination inhalers. It also says a tight seal around the mouthpiece helps make sure the full dose is received, and that a whistling sound from the spacer means the person is breathing in too fast.

body.heading: Should the mouth be rinsed after a steroid inhaler?
body.body: The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a beclometasone inhaler, to help prevent thrush. Asthma + Lung UK gives similar advice, saying to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out after using an inhaler that contains steroid, to reduce the chance of side effects. The NHS steroid inhaler page also advises using a spacer. The rinsing advice applies to inhalers that contain steroid.

body.heading: What are the side effects?
body.body: The NHS lists shakiness, a faster heartbeat and headaches as the typical side effects of salbutamol. It says serious side effects are rare. Muscle pain or weakness, muscle cramps, or an irregular or more noticeable heartbeat can be a sign of low potassium levels, and the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if these happen. For beclometasone, the NHS lists oral thrush and a dry or sore throat as common side effects, and its steroid inhaler page also lists a hoarse or croaky voice. If thrush develops, the NHS says a pharmacist can recommend an antifungal mouth gel, and the beclometasone inhaler is kept up while the gel is used. The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or struggling breathing, or skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, and for chest pain after using more than the recommended dose. If more than the recommended dose has been used and the heartbeat is fast or noticeable, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.

body.heading: What can needing a reliever more often mean?
body.body: The NHS says needing a salbutamol inhaler more often than usual could be a sign that the condition is not well controlled. Asthma + Lung UK says regularly needing a reliever inhaler points to asthma that is not under control, and advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: Asthma + Lung UK says an asthma attack is an emergency, and that 999 should be called for an ambulance if the reliever is not helping. It says to call 999 if a person feels worse at any point, and to call 999 straight away if there is no reliever inhaler to hand. It adds that even a person who feels able to get to A&E should call 999 for an ambulance, so they can be treated on the way to hospital, and that the call handler should be told it is an asthma attack. After an attack treated with the reliever alone, Asthma + Lung UK advises asking for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment.

sedating-and-non-sedating-antihistamines.name: Sedating and non-sedating antihistamines
sedating-and-non-sedating-antihistamines.summary: The NHS lists chlorphenamine as sleep-inducing and cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine as non-drowsy, though cetirizine can still cause sleepiness.
keyPoints: Antihistamines block the effects of histamine, which the body releases when it meets something it is allergic to.
The NHS lists chlorphenamine (Piriton) among sleep-inducing antihistamines, and cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine among non-drowsy ones.
Non-drowsy does not mean never drowsy: the NHS says some people find cetirizine quite sleepy, and not to drive or ride a bike if it makes them sleepy.
The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy, and that loratadine is usually the antihistamine recommended if one is needed.
A pharmacist or doctor can advise on choosing an antihistamine; the NHS names NHS 111 for some side effects and 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction.

body.heading: What do antihistamines do?
body.body:
Antihistamines are medicines that block the effects of histamine. The body releases histamine when it meets something it is allergic to, and histamine sets off allergy symptoms such as itching, sneezing and watery eyes.

The NHS lists cetirizine as an antihistamine used for hay fever, conjunctivitis (red, itchy eyes), eczema, hives and reactions to insect bites and stings. Cetirizine and loratadine can be bought without a prescription from supermarkets, convenience stores and pharmacies.

body.heading: Which antihistamines are sedating and which are not?
body.body:
Antihistamines are often sorted into two groups, called sedating and non-sedating. The NHS lists chlorphenamine (Piriton), cinnarizine, diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine and promethazine as sleep-inducing antihistamines, and acrivastine, cetirizine, fexofenadine and loratadine as non-drowsy ones. The NHS says non-drowsy antihistamines are less likely to make a person sleepy.

A leaflet from Cambridge University Hospitals names cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine as non-sedating tablets that usually do not cause drowsiness, so they can be taken during the day, unlike sedating chlorphenamine (Piriton).

Even within the non-drowsy group there are differences. The NHS says cetirizine is more likely to cause sleepiness than loratadine, desloratadine or fexofenadine.

body.heading: What side effects can they cause?
body.body:
For cetirizine, the NHS lists feeling sleepy and tired as the most common side effect. Headaches, dry mouth, feeling sick, dizziness and diarrhoea are also listed. The NHS adds that although cetirizine is classed as non-drowsy, some people find it makes them quite sleepy.

For chlorphenamine, the NHS lists drowsiness and blurred vision among the common side effects. It says children and people aged over 65 have more chance of getting some side effects, such as feeling restless or excited.

The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if the eyes or skin turn yellow, if someone bruises or bleeds more easily than normal, or if they have difficulty peeing.

body.heading: What do the NHS and hospital leaflets say about driving and alcohol?
body.body:
For cetirizine, the NHS says not to drive or ride a bike if it makes a person sleepy, and not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery when feeling dizzy or shaky. The NHS also recommends avoiding alcohol with cetirizine because it can increase sleepiness. MedlinePlus, a US source, similarly advises avoiding alcoholic drinks with it. The Cambridge leaflet says cetirizine can enhance the effects of alcohol.

For chlorphenamine, the NHS says not to drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery if it leaves a person sleepy, with blurred vision, dizzy or unable to concentrate. It adds that it is an offence to drive if your ability to drive safely is affected, and that a doctor or pharmacist can advise anyone unsure whether it is safe to drive. The NHS also notes that some liquid products contain a little alcohol.

body.heading: What about pregnancy, breastfeeding and children?
body.body:
The NHS says chlorphenamine can be taken in pregnancy and that there is no good evidence it harms the baby. It can cause drowsiness, so a doctor or pharmacist may recommend a non-drowsy antihistamine such as loratadine. The NHS also says loratadine is usually the antihistamine recommended in pregnancy.

For breastfeeding, the NHS says loratadine or cetirizine are usually OK. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service names chlorphenamine as the preferred sedating antihistamine and cetirizine or loratadine as preferred non-sedating ones, and suggests monitoring the baby for drowsiness, irritability, poor feeding and inadequate weight gain. The NHS chlorphenamine page says side effects in breastfed babies are very rare, and to contact NHS 111 or a healthcare professional if a baby feeds less well than usual or seems unusually sleepy or irritable.

The NHS says most adults and children aged 1 year or over can take chlorphenamine. It lists people who may not be able to take it, including those with primary angle closure glaucoma, epilepsy, an enlarged prostate, bladder or urination problems, asthma or other lung conditions, heart disease, or liver or kidney problems.

body.heading: When should someone get advice, and when is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS points people who are unsure about taking an antihistamine, for example in pregnancy or when driving, to a pharmacist or doctor. NHS 111 is named for some side effects, such as yellow eyes or skin, and for a breastfed baby who feeds poorly or seems unusually sleepy.

The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction. These include swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, and blue, grey or pale skin. They also include sudden confusion, drowsiness or dizziness, and fainting without waking.

The NHS says taking too much chlorphenamine can be dangerous and that medical advice should be sought. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for signs such as a very fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat, breathing problems, a seizure, uncontrolled movements, confusion or agitation, or hallucinations.

sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.name: Sepsis: warning signs and when to act
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.headline: Sepsis: the warning signs in adults and children and when to call 999
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.
keyPoints: Sepsis can be life-threatening and needs urgent hospital treatment; it can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
Signs in adults include confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing and blue, pale or blotchy skin.
Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness, poor feeding, and a rash that does not fade under a glass.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone may have sepsis, and not to drive there.
Treatment is in hospital and usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids into a vein.

body.heading: What is sepsis?
body.body:
Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection. The NHS says it can develop very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

It can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis. The exact cause is not always clear.

body.heading: What are the signs in adults?
body.body:
The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale or blotchy skin. Passing no urine all day, or very little, is another sign.

Not everyone with sepsis has every sign.

A rash that does not fade under a glass is rare in sepsis, but it can be a sign of meningitis, so call 999 or go to A&E.

In adults, a very high or very low temperature can also be a sign.

body.heading: What are the signs in babies and children?
body.body:
For babies and young children, the NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, blue, pale or blotchy skin, being unusually sleepy, and a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

In babies and young children, poor feeding can also be a sign.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk?
body.body:
Anyone can get sepsis, but the chance is higher in babies under 12 months and people over 75. It can sometimes occur in people who are otherwise fit and healthy.

People with a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or from taking corticosteroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.

People with diabetes and people who have recently had surgery are also more likely to develop sepsis.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child shows signs of sepsis, or if there is a worry that it could be sepsis. It advises asking someone to drive, or calling for an ambulance, rather than driving oneself.

For a worry about an infection when sepsis is not suspected, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact the GP. When it is unclear whether it could be sepsis, the NHS says it is still better to call 999.

body.heading: How is sepsis treated, and what happens afterwards?
body.body:
Sepsis is treated in hospital. Treatment usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids given into a vein. Some people need intensive care.

Recovery can take a long time, and some people take months or longer to feel back to normal. Some people have longer-lasting problems after sepsis, such as tiredness and changes in mood, which is sometimes called post-sepsis syndrome.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Sometimes surgery is needed to remove the source of infection. Post-sepsis syndrome can also cause problems with memory or concentration, and support such as physiotherapy or counselling may help.

shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.name: Shortness of breath: causes and next steps
shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.summary: Breathlessness has many causes, from asthma and infections to heart and lung disease, and severe difficulty breathing needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness.
Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath.
The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg.

body.heading: Why do people get short of breath?
body.body:
NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness. NHS inform also lists a severe allergic reaction, a collapsed lung and a blood clot in the lung as possible causes of sudden breathlessness. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, is a partial collapse of the lung caused by a small tear in the lung surface.

The NHS lists several possible causes of breathlessness, including COPD, scarring of the lungs, heart failure, asthma, chest infections and being overweight. In heart failure, fluid builds up in the lungs and makes breathing harder.

body.heading: What do asthma, COPD, heart failure and a lung clot look like?
body.body: Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways. The NHS lists breathlessness as the most common symptom of heart failure; it may happen after activity or at rest, may be worse when lying down, and may wake a person at night. It lists tiredness, swollen ankles and legs, and feeling lightheaded or fainting as other heart failure symptoms. An NHS trust leaflet says the most common symptom of a pulmonary embolism is breathlessness, with chest pain that is worse on breathing or coughing, and it also lists cough and fever.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath. The NHS says chest tightness or heaviness, or pain that spreads to the arms, back, neck or jaw, is also a reason to call 999 or go to A&E. The NHS adds sudden confusion, or lips or skin turning pale, blue or grey, to the signs for calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to take them or call an ambulance.

body.heading: When should breathlessness be seen urgently or soon?
body.body: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg. NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if breathlessness is new or unexplained. The NHS advises seeing a GP if breathlessness has lasted longer than a month, gets worse with normal activity or when lying down, or comes with swollen ankles.

body.heading: What does the GP ask about and test?
body.body: NHS inform's guidance asks whether breathlessness came on suddenly or slowly and whether anything triggered it, such as exercise. An NHS England pathway for persistent breathlessness lists an ECG, a chest X-ray and spirometry among the first-line tests. Spirometry is a breathing test that measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast. The same pathway says an ECG showing atrial fibrillation with breathlessness should prompt a heart specialist assessment, including an echocardiogram.

body.heading: How is breathlessness treated?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For COPD, treatment usually involves relieving symptoms with medicines such as inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help. Heart failure is managed with lifestyle changes and medicines or surgery. A blood clot in the lung can be treated with anticoagulants, which are drugs that thin the blood. NHS leaflets describe pursed-lip breathing as a technique that can help keep the airways open for longer and reduce the work of breathing, for example in COPD.

sleep-problems-what-helps.name: Sleep problems: what helps and when to get help
sleep-problems-what-helps.summary: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and that a GP can arrange CBT when habits alone do not help.
keyPoints: The NHS describes insomnia as regular difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early.
A steady bedtime and wake time, a dark, quiet room and winding down without screens are habits the NHS Every Mind Matters pages describe for better sleep.
The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing habits has not helped, or if sleep trouble has lasted for months.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the main treatment described by NHS sources; sleeping pills are rarely prescribed.

body.heading: What counts as insomnia?
body.body:
The NHS says a person who regularly finds it hard to fall asleep, stay asleep or wake up too early may have insomnia. It also says insomnia usually gets better by changing sleeping habits.

A primary care pathway from NHS South Yorkshire advises considering life events and physical or mental health problems as possible triggers of insomnia. Primary care guidance for GPs in the NHS lists physical conditions such as sleep apnoea among the possible causes of insomnia. It also suggests that a clinician asks whether a medicine could be a cause, and considers anxiety or depression as possible underlying factors.

body.heading: Which sleep habits do NHS pages describe?
body.body:
The NHS Every Mind Matters pages say a regular sleep routine can make it easier to fall asleep, because going to bed and getting up at similar times each day helps the body know when it is time to sleep. They suggest keeping the same routine on days off. They also suggest keeping phones, tablets and computers away for an hour before bed, because the light can delay sleep. Reading, meditation or breathing exercises are given as alternatives.

A dark, quiet and cool bedroom is a recurring recommendation across NHS pages. NHS pages also advise against caffeine, smoking and alcohol in the hours before bed, although the exact timing differs from page to page. Some pages advise against napping during the day and describe regular daytime exercise as helpful. For someone who worries in bed, the NHS suggests writing a list of tasks for the next day before going to sleep.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest when sleep will not come?
body.body: If a person is still awake after about 20 minutes, the NHS suggests getting up, doing something relaxing in another room, and going back to bed when sleepy.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped insomnia, or if there has been trouble sleeping for months. A GP may refer a person for cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, which helps change the thoughts and behaviours that get in the way of sleep. The NHS says GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia, because they can have serious side effects and a person can become dependent on them.

body.heading: What does CBT for insomnia involve?
body.body: The NHS recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, as the first treatment for insomnia. CBT-I can be delivered in person, in groups or online, for example through the Sleepio programme, which is designed to be completed over six weeks; availability and cost to the patient vary by area. A primary care guideline from Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West advises that medicines are best avoided in the long-term management of insomnia.

body.heading: How much sleep do adults need, and why does it matter?
body.body: NHS sources put the amount most adults need at about 7 to 9 hours a night. One NHS page says age, health and daily routine can all affect how much sleep a person needs. NHS Every Mind Matters says getting enough sleep can support mood, energy, the immune system and overall health. A United States guide from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute adds that regularly getting too little or very poor quality sleep increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and other health problems. NHS pages list feeling very tired, irritable or sleepy during the day among the signs of not sleeping enough.

body.heading: Could another sleep disorder be involved?
body.body: The NHS says a person may be referred to a sleep clinic if they have symptoms of another sleep disorder, such as sleep apnoea.

sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.name: Sore throat: causes, treatment, when to act
sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.summary: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic.
A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week.
NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling.

body.heading: What causes a sore throat?
body.body: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic. A University Hospitals Sussex NHS leaflet lists tonsillitis, laryngitis, strep throat and glandular fever as other common causes of a sore throat. NICE suggests scoring tools (FeverPAIN or Centor) to spot people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic, and these include fever, pus on the tonsils, tender neck glands and no cough.

body.heading: How long does it last, and what helps?
body.body: A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week. NHS 111 Wales says a pharmacist can advise about paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain, and a hospital trust leaflet notes that not everyone can take ibuprofen safely.

body.heading: Are antibiotics needed?
body.body: NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic. NICE says a scoring tool (FeverPAIN or Centor) should be used to identify people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.

body.heading: What are tonsillitis, glandular fever and quinsy?
body.body: A GP can often diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, a swab can show whether bacteria are the cause, and a blood test for glandular fever is recommended if symptoms are severe or will not go away. The NHS says glandular fever is most common in people aged 15 to 24. Antibiotics do not work for glandular fever because it is caused by a virus. Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a complication of tonsillitis.

body.heading: When should a GP be seen?
body.body: The NHS says to contact a GP practice if a sore throat has not started to improve after a week, and to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, or a weakened immune system. A sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days, or that gets worse rather than better, may suggest glandular fever.

body.heading: When is a sore throat an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling. Other reasons are a high-pitched noise when breathing in, a sore throat that is severe and getting worse quickly, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or trouble speaking. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to drive them or call 999.

spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.name: Spirometry: the lung function test explained
spirometry-lung-function-test-explained.summary: Spirometry measures how much air can be blown out and how fast. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.
keyPoints: In spirometry the person breathes through a mouthpiece, with a nose clip, into a machine that measures airflow.
Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between.
Results are compared with values predicted for someone of the same height, age and sex.
The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.

body.heading: What is spirometry?
body.body: Spirometry is the most common lung function test. It measures how much air a person can blow out and how quickly. Spirometry is the main test for detecting airflow obstruction, while other lung function tests measure lung volumes and gas exchange.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: The person wears a nose clip so air goes through the mouth, and breathes through a mouthpiece into the lung function machine. They breathe normally, take a deep breath in, and then blow out as hard and fast as possible. Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between. One NHS trust says the test normally takes around 15 minutes.

body.heading: Why is spirometry done?
body.body: The NHS says spirometry measures how much air a person can breathe out in one breath, and it is also called a lung function test. It is used to find out whether symptoms come from a lung condition such as asthma, COPD or pulmonary fibrosis (scarring of the lungs), to monitor an existing condition, or to check fitness before surgery. NHS England guidance says NICE recommends quality-assured spirometry as one of several objective tests for diagnosing asthma and COPD. The same guidance says normal spirometry does not rule out asthma.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: One NHS practice suggests avoiding vigorous exercise for 30 minutes before the test. The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing. It also notes that a recent chest infection, or recent antibiotics or steroids, can affect the results. Preparation varies, and patients are told whether they need to stop any inhalers or medicines beforehand.

body.heading: How is the test done, according to the NHS?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets say staff record the person's height and weight, which are entered into the machine for the calculations. The person uses a nose clip, breathes in deeply, seals their lips around the tube and breathes out as hard and fast as possible. The NHS says this is repeated two more times, and that staff may ask the person to use an inhaler and repeat the test. The NHS says the appointment should take no more than an hour, and that dizziness during or just after the test is possible but should be brief. The NHS says the test should not be done during a chest infection or soon after a heart attack or stroke. Trust and practice pages say the results are reviewed and then sent to the doctor who requested the test, who discusses them with the person.

body.heading: What is the reliever step?
body.body: The test is sometimes repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways. The person takes the test, uses the inhaler, waits a short time and repeats the test. The comparison shows how much the airways respond to the medicine, and the test is sometimes used when asthma is being investigated.

body.heading: What do the results show?
body.body: Results are compared with predicted values for someone of the same height, age and sex. A typical report shows the measured values alongside the predicted values. In obstructive conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways narrow, making it harder for air to flow out of the lungs. Restrictive conditions are different, because they decrease the amount of air the lungs can hold. One NHS leaflet says results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP.

body.heading: Are there any risks?
body.body: NHS leaflets describe the test as painless and non-invasive, with dizziness or fainting the most common side effects and more serious complications very rare. The test needs a good effort, which can make some people feel dizzy or faint. Some people feel dizzy or faint, and coughing is common.
