sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.name: Sprains and strains: treatment and recovery
sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.headline: Sprains and strains: how they are treated and when it is more than a sprain
sprains-and-strains-treatment-and-recove.summary: The NHS describes PRICE care for the first 2 to 3 days, and most sprains and strains feel better after about 2 weeks.
keyPoints: A sprain is a torn or twisted ligament, while a strain is an overstretched or torn muscle, often called a pulled muscle.
The NHS describes PRICE for the first 2 to 3 days: protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation.
The NHS suggests paracetamol for pain, ibuprofen gel for swelling, and speaking to a pharmacist about the best option.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E after a crack, if the body part has changed shape, or if it is numb, tingling, cold, blue or grey.
NHS 111 is the route the NHS gives for severe or worsening pain, large or growing swelling, not being able to put weight on the injury, or self-care not helping.
Strenuous exercise such as running may need to be avoided for up to 8 weeks because of the risk of further damage.

body.heading: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
body.body:
A sprain is an injury to a ligament, one of the tough bands that connect the bones at a joint. The NHS says sprains most often happen in the wrists, ankles, thumbs and knees. A strain is an overstretched or torn muscle, which people also call a pulled muscle. The NHS says strains most often affect the feet, legs and back.

The NHS lists pain, tenderness or weakness, swelling or bruising, difficulty putting weight on the area, and sometimes muscle spasms. A broken bone can cause similar signs, which is why the warning signs later in this guide matter.

body.heading: What does the NHS describe for the first few days?
body.body:
For the first 2 to 3 days the NHS describes five steps known as PRICE. The letters stand for protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation. Rest means stopping exercise or activities and trying not to put weight on the injury.

For ice, NHS trust leaflets describe an ice pack, or a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a towel, held on for 15 to 20 minutes at a time every 2 to 3 hours. Several leaflets warn against putting ice directly on the skin. Compression means a bandage that is firm but not too tight, and elevation means keeping the injury raised. The timings vary between sources.

Several NHS trusts also use the word HARM for the first 48 to 72 hours: avoid heat, alcohol, running and massage.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pain relief and moving the injury?
body.body:
The NHS suggests paracetamol to ease pain and ibuprofen gel to help with swelling. It also says a pharmacist can advise on the best option. The Northern Ireland government site nidirect says ibuprofen should not be taken for the first 48 hours after an injury because it may slow healing, so advice differs between UK sources.

NHS guidance also says to keep the joint or muscle moving once pain allows, so that it does not become stiff. Some trust leaflets describe starting gentle movement early for sprains, while strained muscles are usually rested for at least a few days.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to call 999 or go to A&E?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if there was a crack at the time of the injury. The same applies if the injured body part has changed shape, or if it is numb or tingling. Skin that has turned blue or grey, or feels cold, is also on the list. The NHS says not to drive there; someone else can drive, or 999 can be called for an ambulance.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to get help from NHS 111 or a GP?
body.body:
The NHS lists reasons to get help from NHS 111. These are pain that is very bad or getting worse, and swelling or bruising that is large or growing. Others are being unable to put weight on the injury, an area that is very stiff or hard to move, and self-care that has not helped. A very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery, can point to infection and leads to the same advice.

NHS 111 Wales says to see a GP if the injury is getting worse or is not feeling better after treating it yourself.

body.heading: How long does recovery take, and when can normal activity restart?
body.body: The NHS says most sprains and strains feel better after about 2 weeks. It adds that strenuous exercise, such as running, may need to be avoided for up to 8 weeks because of the risk of further damage. NHS 111 Wales says severe sprains and strains can take longer than 2 weeks. These timings are general, and recovery that is slower than usual is one reason the NHS gives for seeking advice.

body.heading: Is physiotherapy needed?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales says a GP may refer a person to a physiotherapist if recovery is slower than usual. The main NHS page adds that NHS physiotherapy is not available everywhere and waiting times can be long. A physiotherapist can assess the injury and guide exercises to restore movement and strength.

statins-common-questions-answered.name: Statins: common questions answered
statins-common-questions-answered.headline: Statins: what they do and the common concerns, as the NHS describes them
statins-common-questions-answered.summary: The NHS says statins lower the cholesterol the body makes, to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, and they are usually taken long term.
keyPoints: Statins work by lowering the amount of cholesterol the body makes, which helps stop cholesterol building up in blood vessels.
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease and to people who already have it.
Statins are usually taken long term, and the NHS says stopping can let cholesterol rise again.
Muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause is something the NHS says to get medical advice about.
Grapefruit juice affects some statins more than others, so the NHS says to ask a pharmacist or GP about the one prescribed.
The NHS says that stopping a statin can let cholesterol rise again, so it advises talking to a doctor first.

body.heading: What do statins do?
body.body:
Statins are medicines that lower cholesterol.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance made by the liver and carried in the blood.

According to the NHS, statins reduce how much cholesterol the body makes. This helps prevent a build-up of cholesterol in the blood vessels. High cholesterol can lead to cardiovascular disease, which includes heart attacks, strokes and peripheral arterial disease.

Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are two of the statins the NHS describes, along with others such as simvastatin and pravastatin.

body.heading: Who are statins for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They may also be offered to people who already have cardiovascular disease, to lower the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

NICE has published a patient decision aid, "Are statins the best choice for me?", for people weighing up whether statins are right for them.

The NHS says most adults can take atorvastatin, and that it is sometimes prescribed for children aged 10 and over. Caution is needed for people with liver or kidney problems or a past allergic reaction to a statin. The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy.

body.heading: How long are statins taken for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins are usually taken long term.

For atorvastatin, the NHS says it can be taken for many years and works best when taken for a long time. It says cholesterol should fall within about four weeks if the medicine is taken as prescribed.

The NHS advises continuing atorvastatin even when a person feels well.

body.heading: What side effects can statins cause?
body.body:
For atorvastatin, the NHS lists headaches, dizziness, nausea, muscle aches and digestive upset such as diarrhoea or indigestion as common side effects.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says side effects often ease as the body gets used to the medicine, and that serious ones are rare.

The NHS lists rare serious effects including liver inflammation, pancreatitis, muscle damage and allergic reactions. It says yellowing of the skin or eyes can be a sign of liver problems, and that prompt medical attention is needed. For rosuvastatin, severe breathing or swallowing problems, or sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, are emergencies for which the NHS says to call 999.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says to contact a doctor if side effects last more than a few days or get worse.

body.heading: What about muscle pain?
body.body:
The NHS lists muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause as possible signs of muscle damage. For rosuvastatin it says to get medical advice promptly if these happen.

For atorvastatin, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for these symptoms. The NHS says that if side effects are the reason someone wants to stop, the doctor may be able to change the dose or switch medicine.

body.heading: Do grapefruit juice and other things affect statins?
body.body:
The NHS says grapefruit and grapefruit juice can affect some medicines by raising the level of the medicine in the blood, which makes side effects more likely.

The NHS treats statins differently: grapefruit juice is a particular concern with simvastatin, while atorvastatin is affected mainly by large amounts and some other statins are generally not a concern.

The NHS also says drinking a lot of alcohol regularly increases the chance of side effects and liver problems with atorvastatin.

It advises talking to a GP or pharmacist about grapefruit if it is a regular part of the diet and a medicine that is affected has been prescribed.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping a statin?
body.body:
The NHS says stopping atorvastatin may cause cholesterol to rise, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It says there are no withdrawal symptoms and no evidence that atorvastatin is addictive.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping because of side effects, since the problem may be unrelated to the medicine. The NHS also advises not stopping a medicine without advice.

stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.name: Stomach ache: causes by area and warning signs
stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.summary: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache.
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What usually causes a stomach ache?
body.body: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache. The NHS links intense pain around the time of a period, sometimes with pain during or after sex and when pooing, with endometriosis.

body.heading: Does the area of the pain point to a cause?
body.body:
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis. NHS 111 Wales links severe pain that lasts for hours in the upper centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones. It links ongoing cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain and cramping of IBS may be relieved by going to the toilet. Stomach ulcer pain is usually in the upper tummy, may feel burning and is often worse at night. Gastritis can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick. Gastritis is inflammation of the lining of the stomach. Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain around the top of the tummy that develops suddenly, and gallstones and alcohol are its most common causes.

body.heading: What do appendicitis, gallstones and diverticular disease look like?
body.body: Appendicitis is when the appendix becomes inflamed; it usually causes pain in the lower right side of the tummy and is sometimes accompanied by nausea and loss of appetite. An NHS 111 Wales page says appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital. Many people with gallstones have no symptoms, but a stone can cause pain, jaundice or pancreatitis. NHS inform says diverticulitis, the inflamed form of diverticular disease, tends to cause more severe tummy pain, especially on the left side, and a fever. NHS 111 Wales advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for blood or mucus in the stool, pain that gets worse or does not go away, or a high temperature or shivers.

body.heading: When is stomach pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe. Other reasons on the NHS page include struggling to breathe, confusion, and blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue. NHS inform adds chest pain and difficulty breathing to the reasons to call 999. For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden, severe tummy pain together with any of: pain spreading to the back, bloating that does not go away, a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.

body.heading: When should it be checked the same day or by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For gastritis, a GP might arrange a breath test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a stool test or a blood test. Stomach ulcers may be treated with antibiotics for a Helicobacter pylori infection or with medicines that reduce stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors.

stop-smoking-nhs-support.name: Stopping smoking: the support the NHS offers
stop-smoking-nhs-support.summary: NHS stop smoking services offer nicotine replacement, medicines and professional support, and people in England can self-refer through NHS Better Health.
keyPoints: NHS stop smoking services provide nicotine replacement therapy and prescription medicines, together with professional support in the first months after quitting.
Vapes are not available as medicines on the NHS, though some local services may offer a free starter pack.
The NHS says cravings are short-lived and that withdrawal symptoms are temporary.

body.heading: What help do NHS stop smoking services provide?
body.body: NHS stop smoking services offer information and advice and professional support during the first few months after someone stops smoking. They provide nicotine replacement therapy, such as patches and gum, and medicines such as varenicline and bupropion. In England people can refer themselves to a local service through the NHS Better Health website, and can also speak to a GP. What a local service offers, such as eligibility for a free e-cigarette starter pack, varies by area.

body.heading: How do nicotine replacement and medicines work?
body.body: Nicotine replacement therapy comes as patches, gum, lozenges, microtabs, and mouth and nasal sprays. The NHS says nicotine replacement therapy gives the body nicotine without the other harmful chemicals found in cigarettes and tobacco. Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine in the brain. NHS pages say that a nicotine-free medicine such as varenicline or cytisine can be combined with a nicotine product, and describe the combination as giving the best chance of success.

body.heading: Where do vapes fit in?
body.body: E-cigarettes are not currently available as medicines, so stop smoking services cannot supply them and they cannot be prescribed on the NHS. Some local stop smoking services may still offer a free starter pack.

body.heading: What happens in the body after stopping?
body.body: The NHS sets out a timeline: within about 20 minutes the pulse rate begins to return to normal. By 48 hours carbon monoxide levels in the blood have fallen to those of a non-smoker. After one year the risk of a heart attack is about half that of a person who smokes, and after ten years the risk of lung cancer is about half. NHS pages also report mental health benefits: once the withdrawal stage has passed, people report less anxiety, depression and stress.

body.heading: What are cravings and withdrawal like?
body.body: The NHS says withdrawal symptoms are temporary, usually strongest in the first week and lasting on average three to four weeks. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS site, says cravings should ease after the first two to three weeks. The NHS says an individual craving lasts only a short time. Walking, chewing sugar-free gum and deep breathing are among the coping ideas it lists.

body.heading: What other support is available?
body.body: In November 2024 NHS England announced a rollout of varenicline, a stop smoking pill, to help tens of thousands of people a year try to quit.

body.heading: Why does the NHS stress stopping?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site says the harm from smoking reaches beyond the lungs, including a higher risk of dementia and inflammation that can worsen joint pain. The relief a cigarette seems to give from stress is short-lived, and smoking can make anxiety and low mood worse over time, according to the NHS.

stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.name: Stress: how it shows up and where to get help
stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.summary: Stress is a reaction to mental or emotional pressure that can affect mood, body and behaviour, and the NHS says support is available when it affects daily life.
keyPoints: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often linked to feeling a loss of control.
Stress can show up as emotional changes, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and changes in behaviour.
The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.
Adults in England can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP.

body.heading: What is stress?
body.body: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often related to feeling a loss of control over something, though sometimes there is no obvious cause. Common triggers it lists include pressure at work, relationship or family difficulties, money worries, illness and bereavement. The NHS says most people feel stressed sometimes and some find stress helpful or even motivating, but that if it is affecting life there are things that may help. The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.

body.heading: How does stress show up in the body and behaviour?
body.body: The NHS says stress can affect emotions, causing feelings such as irritability, anger and tearfulness. Physical symptoms listed include headaches, stomach problems, muscle tension and dizziness. Behaviour can change too, for example with sleep problems, loss of appetite, or drinking or smoking more.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for managing stress?
body.body: NHS pages suggest identifying the cause as the first step, then breaking large tasks into small targets and focusing on what can be changed. Controlled breathing, deep muscle relaxation and mindful breathing are listed as ways to reduce tension and some of the physical signs of stress. Talking to trusted friends, family or colleagues, or contacting a helpline, is also suggested. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve stress, because these can contribute to poor mental health.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest getting help?
body.body: If urgent help is needed for mental health but it is not an emergency, the NHS says to use NHS 111 online or call 111 and choose the mental health option, or to ask for an urgent GP appointment. In England, adults aged 18 and over can refer themselves directly to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP, and in some areas the minimum age is 16. If stress has led to thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call 999 if there is immediate danger, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option for urgent help, or contact Samaritans free at any time on 116 123.

body.heading: What happens in the body during stress?
body.body: An NHS self-help guide describes stress as the body's reaction to feeling under threat, known as the fight or flight response, and says a certain amount of pressure can be helpful and motivating. The British Heart Foundation explains that the brain signals the body to release hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. It says that if this response keeps being switched on again and again, over time it can take its toll on the body.

stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.name: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.headline: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs and why 999 is the route
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.summary: A stroke and a TIA are both emergencies: the NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 even if the symptoms pass.
keyPoints: The FAST test checks for face drooping, arm weakness and speech problems, and the NHS says to call 999 if any sign is present.
A TIA, sometimes called a mini-stroke, is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to the brain, and its symptoms recover completely within 24 hours.
Symptoms of a TIA can pass, but the person still needs to be assessed in hospital, so call 999.
Treatment differs for strokes caused by a blood clot and strokes caused by bleeding, which is why a hospital scan comes first.
The Stroke Association runs a support helpline for people affected by stroke.

body.heading: What are the signs of a stroke?
body.body:
The FAST test is used across the UK to spot a stroke. It checks the face, the arms and the speech: has the mouth or eye drooped, can the person raise both arms fully and keep them there, and is their speech slurred or hard to understand.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say that any one of these signs is a reason to call 999. NHS England has found that many people wait too long to call 999, with an average of 88 minutes between the first symptom and the call.

If any one of these signs is seen, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to wait for more symptoms to appear.

A stroke is a medical emergency, so call 999 even if symptoms seem minor or go away.

body.heading: What is a TIA, and how does it differ from a stroke?
body.body:
A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, is often called a mini-stroke. A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

NHS hospital guidance says the symptoms of a TIA recover completely within 24 hours. If symptoms last longer than that, it is classed as a stroke.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 for a suspected stroke or TIA, even if the symptoms seem minor or go away.

A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

body.heading: Why does a TIA matter if the symptoms pass?
body.body:
After a suspected TIA there is a risk of a stroke, which is why aspirin is given straight away to help prevent one.

For this reason the NHS says a suspected TIA should be assessed urgently, even if the symptoms have gone by the time the ambulance arrives. A person whose symptoms have cleared still needs to be seen in hospital.

body.heading: What happens in hospital?
body.body:
A scan is used to find out whether a stroke is caused by a blood clot (ischaemic) or by bleeding in the brain (haemorrhagic), because the treatments differ.

For an ischaemic stroke, emergency options include clot-busting medicine, called thrombolysis, and removal of the clot with a catheter, called thrombectomy. A stroke caused by bleeding is treated differently, with treatment aimed at stopping the bleeding and relieving pressure on the brain, sometimes with surgery.

Hospital teams aim to scan the brain soon after symptoms begin, which is part of why calling 999 matters.

A brain scan is done soon after symptoms begin to show whether a stroke is caused by a clot or a bleed.

Clot-busting drugs carry a risk of bleeding, so doctors weigh the risk against the benefit for each person.

Thrombectomy is used for clots that are too large for clot-busting drugs to break down.

body.heading: How is a suspected TIA treated?
body.body:
For a suspected TIA, the NHS says aspirin is usually given to lower the risk of a stroke, unless there is a medical reason to avoid it. The NHS says the person should be referred to a specialist within 24 hours of the start of their symptoms.

Care after a TIA can include a blood thinner such as aspirin, a statin, and blood pressure tablets if needed. Medicines that thin the blood or reduce clotting may be used, and sometimes surgery is offered to clear a narrowed artery in the neck.

After a TIA, treatment can include a blood thinner, a statin and blood pressure tablets if needed, and some people have surgery to unblock a narrowed neck artery.

body.heading: Where can people find support?
body.body:
The Stroke Association runs a Stroke Helpline on 0303 3033 100 for stroke survivors, their families and carers.

A GP can explain what the diagnosis means and arrange follow-up care. In an emergency, the route is always 999.

The Stroke Association helpline is free to use and supports stroke survivors, families and carers.

sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.name: Sun safety and checking your skin
sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.headline: Sun safety and checking your skin: what the NHS and Cancer Research UK say
sun-safety-and-checking-your-skin.summary: The NHS advises sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and 4-star UVA protection alongside shade and clothing, and describes changing moles as a reason to see a GP.
keyPoints: The NHS says sunscreen should show an SPF of at least 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection, and should not be the only protection.
Cancer Research UK advises seeking shade, especially between 11am and 3pm in the UK.
The NHS says sunbeds and lamps can be more dangerous than natural sunlight, and Cancer Research UK says any level of sunbed use increases skin cancer risk.
The NHS says a new mole, or a change in an existing mole, may be a sign of melanoma and is a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about sunscreen?
body.body: The NHS says the label should show an SPF of at least 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection. SPF measures protection against UVB, and the star rating, up to five stars on UK sunscreens, shows UVA protection; the higher the star rating, the better. The NHS says sunscreen should not be relied on alone, and that suitable clothing and time in the shade when the sun is hottest also matter. Cancer Research UK recommends SPF 30 or higher with a 4 or 5 star UVA rating, used together with shade and clothing.

body.heading: What about shade, clothing and cloud?
body.body: Cancer Research UK advises seeking shade, especially between 11am and 3pm in the UK. It recommends covering up with clothes, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses with UV protection. It says tightly woven fabrics are generally better than thin or loosely woven ones. It also says that more than 90 per cent of UV rays can pass through cloud.

body.heading: Are sunbeds a safer way to tan?
body.body: The NHS says sunbeds and lamps can be more dangerous than natural sunlight because they use a concentrated source of UV radiation. Cancer Research UK says sunbed use increases the risk of skin cancer whatever the skin tone, and that any level of use adds to the risk. It names fake tan from a bottle and spray tans as alternatives. It says up to 9 in 10 cases of melanoma skin cancer in the UK could be prevented by staying safe in the sun and avoiding sunbeds.

body.heading: How can skin be checked for changes?
body.body: The NHS says a new mole, or a change in an existing one, may be a sign of melanoma. It lists changes in size, shape or colour as the key signs, along with a mole that is swollen, sore, bleeding, itchy or crusty. Normal moles are usually round with smooth edges, whereas melanomas are often an uneven shape and may be more than one colour. Cancer Research UK and the Royal Marsden describe an ABCDE checklist covering asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolving change; sources give different size thresholds, so none is given here. Some melanomas do not arise from an existing mole; nodular melanoma can appear as a raised dark lump. A mirror or a helper can be used to look at hard-to-see areas.

body.heading: When should a skin change be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a mole that has changed in size, shape or colour, that is painful or itchy, or that is inflamed, bleeding or crusty. It also advises seeing a GP about a new or unusual mark on the skin that has not gone away after a few weeks, including on the palms or soles. NHS 111 Wales also lists a dark area under a nail that was not caused by an injury. The route for a routine skin concern is a GP appointment.

supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.name: Supporting someone with a mental health problem
supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.summary: Listening, asking open questions and offering practical help are the NHS's main suggestions for supporting someone with a mental health problem, without forcing them to talk.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests telling the person you are worried, carrying on as usual, and offering to listen.
Open questions that start with how, what, where or when give the person room to answer in their own words.
The NHS advises against forcing someone to talk or to get help.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: How can you start the conversation and help?
body.body: The NHS suggests telling the person that you are worried about them. It also suggests carrying on as usual, so the person is not treated differently because of what they are going through. Open questions that start with how, what, where or when are recommended. The NHS says not to force someone to talk to you. The NHS gives going with the person to professional appointments as an example of practical help.

body.heading: How can you point someone towards professional help?
body.body: For people who need more support, the NHS lists contacting a GP, calling NHS 111, or self-referring to NHS talking therapies. The NHS directs anyone who cannot cope or keep themselves safe to urgent support.

body.heading: What if the person wants to start talking?
body.body: The NHS guidance for people talking about their own mental health suggests choosing someone they trust who can offer the kind of support they need, and planning what to say. It notes that some people find it easier to talk while walking, travelling in a car or cooking, and that a person does not have to say everything at once. If the person chosen does not feel able to help, the NHS says not to take it personally.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If someone is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.name: Swollen ankles and legs: causes and red flags
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.headline: Swollen ankles, feet and legs: common causes and when to get help
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.summary: Swollen ankles and legs often come from sitting or standing for long periods, but can signal a clot or a heart, kidney or liver problem. The NHS names the signs that need 111 or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS lists sitting or standing for long periods, a high-salt diet, being overweight, pregnancy and some medicines among the more common causes of swollen ankles and legs.
Less often, swelling comes from a blood clot, an infection, or a heart, kidney or liver problem.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs does not improve after a few days of home care, gets worse, or occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.
Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood or feeling faint with leg swelling may mean a clot in the lungs, which needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What commonly causes swollen ankles?
body.body: The NHS calls swollen ankles, feet and legs oedema, which is a build-up of fluid in the body’s tissues. The NHS lists sitting or standing still for long periods, a high-salt diet and being overweight as lifestyle factors. Pregnancy, varicose veins and thyroid problems can also cause swelling. Some medicines can also cause swelling.

body.heading: What are the less common causes?
body.body: Less commonly, swelling can follow an injury or an insect bite, or come from a blood clot or an infection. The NHS also lists problems with the heart, kidneys or liver as causes. The British Heart Foundation adds lymphoedema, a problem with the drainage of lymph fluid, as another cause.

body.heading: Why does one swollen leg matter more?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeking advice for swelling in only one leg when there is no known cause. The NHS describes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) as throbbing pain in one leg, usually in the calf or thigh, with swelling in that leg. The skin over a DVT can look red, blue or darker than usual.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs has not improved after a few days of home care, if it gets worse, or if it occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.

body.heading: What can ease the swelling?
body.body: The NHS says swelling in the ankles, feet or legs often goes away on its own. Its self-care advice includes raising the swollen area on a chair or pillows, gentle exercise such as walking, and avoiding long periods of standing or sitting. Wide, comfortable shoes with a low heel and washing and moisturising the feet to prevent infection are also mentioned. Treatment for swelling that does not settle depends on the cause. The British Heart Foundation says heart failure treatment includes medicines that help the heart pump more effectively and diuretics, which make you pass more urine and help relieve ankle swelling.

body.heading: Which signs mean urgent help?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for swelling that is severe, painful, sudden, red or hot, or that comes with a high temperature or shivering. The same page lists swelling in the feet, ankles or legs of a person with diabetes as a reason for urgent advice. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if leg swelling comes with shortness of breath or chest pain, because a clot can travel to the lungs. Coughing up blood or feeling faint are also described as symptoms of a clot in the lungs. In pregnancy, very swollen ankles, fingers, hands or face can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, and NHS inform says to contact a midwife or GP immediately.

teething-in-babies-signs-and-what-helps.name: Teething in babies: signs and what helps
teething-in-babies-signs-and-what-helps.summary: The NHS lists sore red gums, a flushed cheek and extra dribbling as signs of teething, and suggests gum massage or a cool teething ring.
keyPoints: The NHS says teething can cause few or no symptoms, and lists a sore red gum, one flushed cheek, dribbling, chewing and fretfulness as possible signs.
NHS sources say teething does not usually cause diarrhoea or a high temperature, so those signs may have another cause such as an infection.
A worried parent can contact a GP or call NHS 111, and NHS pages say to call 999 when a baby has a fit.
Suggested comfort measures include gum massage, a teething ring cooled in the fridge and chilled fruit or vegetables for older babies, with supervision.
The NHS says there is little evidence that teething gels work, and the MHRA says gels with a local anaesthetic are sold from pharmacies only.
Tooth cleaning with a smear of fluoride toothpaste starts when the first tooth comes through, and local NHS guides advise registering the baby with a dentist.

body.heading: What are the usual signs of teething?
body.body: Teething is the time when a baby's first teeth, called milk teeth, push through the gums. The NHS says a baby will probably get their first tooth some time in their first year, but the timing varies, and some babies start before 4 months or after 12 months. One NHS service says most babies start teething at around 6 months. Baby teeth sometimes come through with no pain or discomfort, or with only mild symptoms that last a few days. When there are signs, the NHS lists a sore, red gum where the tooth is coming through and one flushed cheek. Other signs it lists include dribbling more than usual, chewing on things and being more fretful than usual. A baby may also sleep badly, and one NHS page mentions a slightly raised temperature of less than 38C. Bottom teeth often come through before the matching upper teeth.

body.heading: Which symptoms are not caused by teething?
body.body: NHS leaflets say teething does not usually make a baby unwell, and that it does not usually cause diarrhoea or a high temperature. Those signs may have another cause, such as an infection. The NHS also says some people think teething causes diarrhoea, but there is no evidence for this. One NHS guide warns against explaining away signs of illness by assuming it is only teething. A baby with a raised temperature who is sleeping more than usual, is hard to feed or has fewer wet nappies than normal is described by one NHS family service as showing warning signs. A baby who seems unusually listless and unhappy may have something other than teething. A Welsh NHS patient leaflet says to contact a GP or call NHS 111 if a baby seems unwell or in distress.

body.heading: When should a parent get medical help?
body.body: The NHS says a GP can be contacted, or NHS 111 called, if a symptom is worrying. NHS guidance says a high temperature in a baby is a reason to contact a GP or NHS 111 rather than assume teething, and one NHS resource says a high fever may point to a condition unrelated to teething and should be checked by a GP. For most children with a high temperature, the NHS describes care at home, with a GP or NHS 111 contacted if a parent is worried. NHS pages say to call 999 when a baby has a fit, and they also list a rash that does not fade when pressed and a baby who is difficult to wake among the signs that need urgent help. Where a parent is unsure, the emergency route for a baby having a fit is 999, and the routes for a baby who seems unwell are a GP or NHS 111.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest to ease teething?
body.body: The NHS describes gently rubbing the baby's gums as a common way to help. A teething ring can also help, and some rings can be cooled first in the fridge. The NHS says freezing a ring could damage a baby's gums, and a teething ring should never be tied around a baby's neck. Some NHS pages also mention wiping away dribble to help prevent a rash. An NHS resource says that for babies of 6 months or older, chilled pieces of fruit or vegetables such as banana, cucumber or melon can help. These should be given with supervision, because of the risk of choking. A Nottinghamshire NHS leaflet adds that healthy foods such as raw fruit and vegetables can be helpful.

body.heading: What about teething gels and medicines?
body.body: The NHS says there is little evidence that teething gels work. The MHRA, the UK medicines regulator, reviewed gels containing the local anaesthetic lidocaine and found a lack of evidence of benefit. It advised that these products should be a second-line option, used after non-medicinal measures and after talking to a healthcare professional. GOV.UK reports that such gels have been sold from pharmacies only since 2019. NHS pages say adult oral gels can be harmful to babies. The MHRA also says oral gels containing choline salicylate are no longer suitable for people younger than 16 for teething pain. The reason is a theoretical risk of Reye's syndrome, which the NHS describes as a rare condition that can be fatal. NHS pages also mention paracetamol or ibuprofen for babies who are old enough and still in pain after other measures, and a pharmacist can advise if there is any doubt.

body.heading: When should tooth cleaning start, and when is the dentist involved?
body.body: The NHS says brushing starts as soon as the first milk tooth breaks through. It describes a baby toothbrush with a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste, used as soon as teeth start to come through. Local NHS guides describe brushing twice a day, including last thing at night. They say the toothpaste should be spat out and the mouth not rinsed with water afterwards, because rinsing washes away the fluoride. One local NHS guide says a baby should be registered with a dentist when the teeth start coming through. Local services differ on the timing of the first visit. Some recommend a first visit before the age of one, and one Yorkshire health service suggests going as soon as the first tooth appears.

testicle-lumps-and-swelling-what-to-chec.name: Testicle lumps and swelling: what to check
testicle-lumps-and-swelling-what-to-chec.summary: The NHS says to check your testicles monthly for changes; a lump or swelling needs a GP visit, and sudden severe pain needs A&E or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower.
A healthy testicle feels smooth and firm, and one being slightly bigger or lower than the other is common.
The NHS says to book a GP appointment for a lump, swelling, change in shape or feel, or an ache that does not go away.
Most lumps have causes other than cancer, such as hydroceles, cysts, varicoceles or epididymitis.
Sudden, severe testicle pain is an emergency: the NHS says to go to A&E or call 999.
Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump, and the NHS describes it as rare.

body.heading: How do men check their testicles?
body.body:
The NHS suggests checking your testicles about once a month, during or just after a warm bath or shower. Some sources explain that the skin over the testicles is most relaxed then, so lumps are easier to feel. The testicles sit inside the scrotum, the bag of skin below the penis.

The NHS also describes feeling the tube at the back of each testicle, called the epididymis. It carries sperm, and it is normal for it to feel a little tender when touched.

body.heading: What should normal testicles feel like?
body.body:
The NHS says a healthy testicle feels smooth and firm. It is common for one testicle to be slightly bigger than the other, or to hang lower.

The epididymis at the back of each testicle can feel tender, and this is normal. Mild differences in size or position between the two sides are also described as common.

body.heading: Which changes are worth noticing?
body.body: The NHS lists several changes to look out for. These include a lump in a testicle, a swollen testicle, or a change in the shape or feel of a testicle. One testicle becoming bigger than the other can also be a change worth noting. So can an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum that does not go away. A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard is on the same list. The main sign of testicular cancer is often a painless lump or swelling in a testicle.

body.heading: What else can cause a lump or swelling?
body.body:
The NHS says most lumps and swellings in the testicles turn out to have causes other than cancer. It names several common ones, including varicoceles, hydroceles, epididymal cysts and epididymitis. MedlinePlus, a US health encyclopaedia, also lists a hernia among the causes of scrotal swelling.

A hydrocele is a swelling of the scrotum caused by a build-up of fluid. A varicocele is a soft lump that develops slowly above the testicle, usually on the left side. An epididymal cyst is a small, smooth, fluid-filled swelling that develops slowly in the epididymis. A hospital urology service says benign swellings generally only need surgery if they cause significant symptoms.

Epididymitis happens when the epididymis becomes swollen and painful, often because of an infection. The NHS says it is usually treated with antibiotics. It adds that in men under 35 the cause is usually a sexually transmitted infection, while in men over 35 it is more often a urine infection. NHS inform also describes epididymo-orchitis, where the testicle is involved as well, and links it to bacterial infections such as urine infections and sexually transmitted infections, and to mumps.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS says to make a GP appointment if you notice a lump or swelling in a testicle. The same goes for a change in the shape or feel of a testicle, or one testicle becoming bigger than the other. An ache that does not go away is also a reason to book an appointment. The NHS still wants these changes checked, even though most turn out not to be cancer.

A GP will examine the testicles and may arrange an ultrasound scan. An ultrasound scan will usually tell benign swellings apart from cancerous ones, according to a UK hospital trust.

body.heading: Is sudden severe testicle pain an emergency?
body.body:
Yes, the NHS treats sudden, severe pain in a testicle as an emergency. It can be a sign of testicular torsion, where the testicle twists and the blood supply to it is cut off. Torsion needs surgery as soon as possible. The NHS route is to go to A&E or call 999, rather than waiting to see a GP.

NHS guidance also lists testicle pain together with feeling sick, being sick or tummy pain, or pain that has lasted more than an hour, as reasons to go to A&E or call 999. The NHS epididymitis page adds that a sudden swelling with severe pain should go straight to A&E, because it is important to make sure it is not torsion.

body.heading: Could it be testicular cancer?
body.body:
Testicular cancer is one possible cause of a lump or swelling, and NHS sources describe it as rare. Its main signs are the same ones described above, such as a lump, swelling, or a heavy, firm or hard scrotum. NHS inform says it tends to affect men between 15 and 49 years of age. Cancer Research UK estimates that fewer than four in every 100 testicular lumps are cancerous.

Cancer Research UK says that depending on the symptoms and other factors, a GP may make an urgent referral to a specialist. The NHS says a referral does not definitely mean you have cancer. Most lumps are not cancer, but a GP is the person to check any lump or swelling.

thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.name: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.summary: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together, because free T4 helps to interpret an abnormal TSH.
keyPoints: TSH is the main test for thyroid problems, and free T4 helps to interpret an abnormal TSH.
Free T4 is measured when the TSH is raised, to tell overt from subclinical hypothyroidism.
A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is followed over time.
Severe illness and some medicines can change thyroid results without a thyroid disease.

body.heading: What do TSH and T4 show?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes thyroid hormones. TSH is linked to the pituitary gland, and a pituitary problem can cause too much or too little of it. A medical review describes TSH as the main test for finding problems with the thyroid gland itself. Free T4 is measured to tell overt from subclinical hypothyroidism when the TSH is raised. Results are read as a pattern of TSH and free T4 together, not one number alone.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an underactive thyroid?
body.body: A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. The NHS says an underactive thyroid is diagnosed with blood tests for TSH and T4. The NHS says diagnosis of an underactive thyroid also usually involves a neck examination. Thyroid UK says some people continue to have symptoms while taking levothyroxine.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an overactive thyroid?
body.body: A British Thyroid Foundation leaflet says an overactive thyroid, or hyperthyroidism, is diagnosed with a blood test measuring thyroid hormones.

body.heading: What if the results are borderline?
body.body: A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism. The British Thyroid Foundation says blood TSH levels return to normal in around half of people with subclinical thyroid disease. A test for thyroid antibodies helps to judge that risk. The British Thyroid Foundation says there is little clinical evidence that treatment gives long-term benefit in subclinical thyroid disease. MedlinePlus says abnormal T4 levels can sometimes be a sign of a pituitary problem that causes too much or too little TSH.

body.heading: Can illness or medicines change the result?
body.body: Abnormal T4 levels do not always mean a condition that needs treatment. MedlinePlus says pregnancy, oestrogen levels, liver problems and severe body-wide illness can affect T4 results.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. The NHS says this treatment is long term to prevent symptoms. NHS inform says a mild case with no symptoms may not need treatment. Regular blood tests check the dose is right, and NHS inform says side effects usually only occur with too much levothyroxine. Thyroid UK says that if symptoms do not improve on levothyroxine, TSH is measured again and the dose may be adjusted. Pregnancy often means the levothyroxine dose needs to be changed, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What can cause an underactive or overactive thyroid?
body.body: In the UK the main cause of an underactive thyroid is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease. Symptoms of an underactive thyroid tend to appear gradually and can be mild, such as tiredness, weight gain, constipation and low mood. Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. Symptoms of an overactive thyroid include nervousness, poor sleep, a fast or irregular heartbeat, trembling and weight loss. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can include anti-thyroid medicines, beta-blockers for symptoms such as tremor, and radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid afterwards. TSH receptor antibodies are associated with Graves' disease, so antibody tests can help find the cause of an overactive thyroid. Some people with Graves' disease develop eye problems, known as thyroid eye disease. UCLH says radioactive iodine may worsen thyroid eye disease, so treatment may be postponed until the eye problems are stable or given with steroid or thyroid medication cover. Beta-blockers can relieve symptoms of an overactive thyroid such as tremor and a fast heartbeat, but they do not affect how much thyroid hormone is made.

tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.name: Tiredness and fatigue: causes and next steps
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.headline: Tiredness that will not go away: common causes and what a GP checks
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.summary: Tiredness is common and often has an ordinary cause such as poor sleep, stress or illness. The NHS advises a GP appointment when it lasts a few weeks without explanation.
keyPoints: The NHS lists poor sleep, an unhealthy lifestyle, hormonal changes, some illnesses and some medicines among the common causes of tiredness.
The NHS advises booking a GP appointment when tiredness has lasted a few weeks without a clear reason, affects daily life or comes with other symptoms such as weight loss.
A GP may arrange blood tests to look for conditions such as anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid.
Self-help advice from the NHS covers diet, exercise, relaxation and sleep habits.

body.heading: What counts as fatigue?
body.body: Everyone feels tired from time to time, and the NHS treats tiredness as a common symptom with many possible causes. Fatigue is described by the NHS as tiredness that is not relieved by rest and sleep. If there is no obvious reason for the tiredness and it goes on for a while without improving, the NHS says it may be a sign of a medical condition.

body.heading: What are the common causes?
body.body: The NHS names poor sleep or difficulty getting to sleep (insomnia) and an unhealthy lifestyle as common causes. Hormonal changes can also make people tired. Stress, depression and bereavement are also listed as triggers. Some medicines, including chemotherapy, can cause tiredness. Among medical conditions, the NHS mentions sleep apnoea, iron deficiency anaemia, diabetes and an overactive thyroid as possible reasons. Gasping, snorting or choking noises during sleep are one of the reasons the NHS gives for seeing a GP, because they can point to a sleep problem.

body.heading: When is it worth seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises a routine GP appointment if tiredness has lasted a few weeks and the cause is unclear. A GP appointment is also advised if the tiredness affects daily life. Other symptoms alongside the tiredness, such as weight loss or changes in mood, are further reasons to book one.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: A GP will usually ask about lifestyle and general health to look for an explanation. The NHS says tests may be needed, such as blood tests to check for anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid. If the cause is still unclear, a GP may refer the person to a specialist.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for self-care?
body.body: The NHS self-help advice covers eating a healthy diet, taking exercise, finding ways to relax and improving sleep. Caffeine can disrupt sleep, which is one reason it appears in the NHS tips. The NHS also says there is some evidence that talking therapies such as counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may help with fatigue, and a GP can arrange a referral. Eating regular meals and healthy snacks through the day is part of the NHS advice for keeping energy steady. The NHS self-help page says regular physical activity improves energy over time. It also links excess weight with tiredness, because carrying extra weight puts extra strain on the heart. Stress uses up a lot of energy, so the NHS suggests relaxing activities. Alcohol lowers the quality of sleep, which can leave a person tired the next day.

body.heading: Could it be ME/CFS?
body.body: Myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a long-term condition whose most common symptom is extreme tiredness. There is no specific test for ME/CFS, so a diagnosis is made from the symptoms and by ruling out other conditions that could explain them.

travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.name: Which travel vaccinations might be needed?
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.headline: Travel vaccinations: what the NHS says about which are needed and when to arrange them
travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS advises getting travel vaccine advice several weeks before departure, as needs depend on the destination, and some vaccines are free while others are paid for.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP practice, pharmacy or private travel clinic well ahead of a trip, because some vaccines need time to work or come as a course.
Which vaccines are advised depends on the countries visited, and TravelHealthPro lists the advice for each destination.
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through the GP, including diphtheria, tetanus and polio, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera, while others are usually paid for.
Yellow fever vaccination is given only at designated centres, is not free on the NHS, and leads to an international certificate.
Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine, and the NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel.
Pregnancy and health conditions can change which vaccines are suitable, so the NHS advises telling the person giving the vaccine.

body.heading: When should travel vaccinations be arranged?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP practice nurse or a private travel clinic well before a trip. Some vaccines need time to build protection, and some come as a course of several doses spread over weeks or months. The NHS travel vaccinations page gives around four to six weeks before departure.

Leaving it late is not a reason to skip the appointment. TravelHealthPro says some vaccines can still be given at the last minute, and malaria tablets can be started on the day of travel if needed. It adds that people who are pregnant or have a long-term condition may need to be seen earlier.

body.heading: Where can country-specific advice be found?
body.body:
Needs differ from one country to another. TravelHealthPro, run by the UK's National Travel Health Network and Centre, publishes country pages that list the vaccines and other health advice for each destination.

The NHS says a GP practice or travel clinic decides which vaccines are suitable and whether they can be given on the NHS.

body.heading: Which travel vaccines does the NHS list?
body.body:
The NHS lists several vaccines that may be advised for travel, depending on the destination. These include hepatitis A, typhoid, cholera, yellow fever, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis B, tick-borne encephalitis, meningitis and tuberculosis (TB).

The NHS also lists the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine among the vaccines relevant to travel.

body.heading: Which are free on the NHS and which are paid for?
body.body:
The NHS says some travel vaccines are free through a GP practice. These are the combined diphtheria, tetanus and polio vaccine, typhoid, hepatitis A and cholera.

Other travel vaccines are usually paid for. The NHS names hepatitis B, Japanese encephalitis, meningitis, rabies, tick-borne encephalitis, tuberculosis (TB) and yellow fever.

body.heading: What is the yellow fever certificate, and how is malaria prevented?
body.body:
The NHS says yellow fever vaccination is available only at designated centres and is not free on the NHS. It says the vaccine needs to be given at least 10 days before travel, and a checklist is used to confirm that a person can have it. A single dose is thought to give lifelong protection, and the certificate issued afterwards, the International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, is valid for life.

Malaria is prevented with tablets rather than a travel vaccine. The NHS advises getting advice from a GP, nurse, pharmacist or travel clinic before travel, ideally four to six weeks ahead, though advice can still be sought at the last minute.

body.heading: What about pregnancy and long-term conditions?
body.body:
The NHS advises telling the person giving a travel vaccine about any health conditions or pregnancy, and bringing a list of any medicines.

In pregnancy, the NHS says to avoid areas where yellow fever is common where possible. It lists yellow fever among the live vaccines not usually advised in pregnancy, but says it may be considered necessary when travelling to areas where yellow fever is common, because the risks of the illness are so high. The NHS advises anyone unsure to talk to a midwife or GP about the risks and benefits.

travel-vaccinations-what-the-nhs-says.metaDescription: The NHS advises getting travel vaccine advice several weeks before departure, as needs depend on the destination.

travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.name: Avoiding and managing travellers' diarrhoea
travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.headline: How travellers can avoid diarrhoea, and what the NHS says helps if it happens
travellers-diarrhoea-avoiding-and-managi.summary: Travellers can lower the risk of diarrhoea with careful food, drink and hand hygiene, and replacing lost fluid is the main way it is managed.
keyPoints: Travellers' diarrhoea is loose, frequent stools that start during or soon after a trip, usually from eating or drinking something contaminated.
Careful hand hygiene and food and water precautions are the main ways to lower the risk, though TravelHealthPro notes they do not give full protection.
The main aim in treatment is to replace lost fluid, and a pharmacist can suggest oral rehydration powder.
Loperamide can be bought without a prescription by people aged 12 and over, but TravelHealthPro advises against it when there is blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever or severe tummy pain.
Medical help is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever, signs of dehydration, or symptoms that do not improve within three days.

body.heading: What is travellers' diarrhoea and why does it happen?
body.body:
Travellers' diarrhoea is a bout of loose, watery stools that happens during a trip or shortly after it. It usually comes from swallowing germs in contaminated food or water. For most people it is unpleasant but mild and settles without specific treatment.

The NHS says diarrhoea in adults and children usually stops within 5 to 7 days, and any vomiting usually stops in 1 or 2 days. The NHS covers diarrhoea and vomiting together, since stomach bugs such as norovirus often cause both.

body.heading: What food and drink habits help avoid it?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro advises choosing food that is freshly prepared, fully cooked and served hot. NHS 111 Wales gives similar advice, suggesting salads and uncooked fruit and vegetables are best skipped unless the traveller has washed and peeled them.

Where tap water may not be safe, NHS 111 Wales recommends filtered or bottled water and advises against ice in drinks. Boiled water, hot drinks made with it, and bottled fizzy drinks with intact seals are described as generally safer choices.

body.heading: How does hand washing fit in?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro and Fit for Travel describe good hand hygiene, along with food and water precautions, as central to prevention. Washing hands with soap and water, for example before eating, is the usual method.

Even with careful hand washing and food and water preparation, travellers' diarrhoea remains a common travel-related illness. These precautions lower the risk but do not remove it, so TravelHealthPro advises travellers to be prepared to manage symptoms during a trip.

body.heading: What helps once diarrhoea has started?
body.body:
The NHS says the key step is to drink plenty of fluids, in small, frequent sips if feeling sick. A pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration powder, which replaces lost salts and sugars. TravelHealthPro notes that the water used to make it up should be safe.

The NHS says it is fine to eat when able to, and that fruit juice and fizzy drinks can make diarrhoea worse.

body.heading: Can loperamide or other medicines help?
body.body:
Loperamide is an anti-diarrhoeal medicine, and the NHS says a pharmacist can recommend it for short-term diarrhoea. The NHS says it can be bought without a prescription by anyone aged 12 or over, while younger children need a prescription.

The NHS lists blood in the stool and a high temperature as reasons not to take it. TravelHealthPro goes further, advising against loperamide when there is blood or mucus in the stool, a high fever or severe abdominal pain. It also advises against it for anyone with active inflammatory bowel disease.

body.heading: When should a traveller get medical advice?
body.body:
TravelHealthPro says medical care should be sought if symptoms have not improved within three days. It advises immediate medical care for a high fever, or for blood or mucus in the stool. Older people, children and other vulnerable travellers are advised to seek medical advice earlier if they cannot keep fluids down or show signs of dehydration.

The NHS lists feeling thirsty, headache, feeling light-headed, dark yellow strong-smelling urine and peeing less often among the signs of dehydration. It also lists a dry mouth and sunken eyes. The NHS says an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for signs of serious dehydration, such as unusual tiredness, dizziness that does not pass on standing, dark yellow urine or peeing less than usual, or fast breathing or heartbeat. For signs of shock, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E, and not to drive.

travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.name: Travelling with medicines: what the NHS says
travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.headline: Planning, packing and paperwork for medicines when travelling, as the NHS and TravelHealthPro describe
travelling-with-medicines-what-the-nhs-s.summary: The NHS and TravelHealthPro describe original packaging, hand luggage, a prescriber's letter and checking the rules of each destination country.
keyPoints: TravelHealthPro, whose medicines advice is also published on nhs.uk, describes keeping medicines in original pharmacy packaging, with a copy of the prescription and a prescriber's letter.
The same guidance describes carrying medicines in hand luggage, with some extra supply in the hold luggage.
TravelHealthPro says a prescriber's letter listing generic medicine names can help at border checks and if medicines need replacing or medical help is needed.
GOV.UK says that, when leaving the UK with medicine containing a controlled drug, a person should be able to show the medicine is theirs.
TravelHealthPro discourages obtaining insulin overseas, because names, brands, strengths and quality vary widely around the world.

body.heading: How should medicines be packed and carried?
body.body: TravelHealthPro describes keeping medicines in their original pharmacy packaging. It advises carrying a copy of the prescription and a letter from the prescriber. The same guidance describes carrying medicines in hand luggage, with some extra supply in the hold luggage. TravelHealthPro also says airline rules should be checked, particularly for liquids, because limits apply to the amount that can be carried in hand luggage. It adds that travellers should check that their medicines are permitted in the countries they will visit.

body.heading: What does a letter from the prescriber do?
body.body: TravelHealthPro suggests asking the prescriber for a letter that lists the medicines by their generic names. Generic names are the official names of the active ingredients, rather than the brand names on the box. TravelHealthPro says such a letter can be helpful during border control checks. It says the letter can also help if medicines need replacing or medical help is needed. Home Office advice on controlled drugs describes a letter that gives the traveller's name, the travel dates, the destination and the medicines with their quantities.

body.heading: Can liquid medicines go in hand luggage?
body.body: Airport limits on liquids in hand luggage can affect liquid medicines. NHS 111 Wales says essential medicines in amounts of more than 100ml can be taken in hand luggage with approval arranged in advance with the airline and airport. It says a letter from a doctor or a prescription should be carried as well. Because airline rules differ, TravelHealthPro advises checking them ahead of travel.

body.heading: What applies to controlled drugs and country rules?
body.body: Controlled drugs are medicines that are covered by drug laws, such as morphine, diazepam and codeine. GOV.UK has a page on travelling with medicine that contains a controlled drug. It also has a separate page on bringing such medicine into the UK. GOV.UK says that, for leaving the UK, a person should be able to prove the medicine is theirs, with a prescription or a letter from the clinician. GOV.UK describes personal licences for some controlled drugs, which are applied for through the Home Office. GOV.UK says the rules in other countries can differ, so the embassy of the country to be visited can be contacted. It warns that travelling with a medicine that is illegal in another country could lead to a fine or prison.

body.heading: What do the sources say about insulin?
body.body: TravelHealthPro advises carrying insulin in hand luggage, because it may freeze in the aircraft hold. It discourages obtaining insulin overseas. The reason given is that the names, brands, strengths and quality of insulin vary considerably around the world.

troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.name: Troponin blood test: what it shows
troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.summary: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.
keyPoints: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged.
The more damage, the more troponin reaches the blood, and levels rise over hours, so the test is often repeated.
A raised troponin may point to a heart attack, but other conditions can raise it too.
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that is tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw.

body.heading: What is troponin?
body.body: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins found in heart muscle. They are released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack. The more damage there is, the more troponin reaches the blood.

body.heading: Why is a troponin test done?
body.body: Clinicians mainly use the test to check whether a heart attack is happening or has recently happened. It is typically ordered when someone has chest pain or other signs of a heart attack. An NHS laboratory describes troponin as also helping to predict short-term and longer-term outcomes in acute coronary syndrome.

body.heading: How is it used in hospital?
body.body: The NHS treats an ECG as an important early test in a suspected heart attack, and says it should be done within 10 minutes of arrival at hospital. Blood tests look for troponin, which leaks slowly into the blood after damage to the heart. Levels usually rise over hours, so testing is often repeated over several hours. NICE describes taking a second troponin sample after the first, with timing that depends on the test and the first result. High-sensitivity tests can detect much smaller amounts of troponin than older tests.

body.heading: What does a normal or raised result mean?
body.body: MedlinePlus says normal levels hours after symptoms start make a heart attack unlikely, but doctors read results alongside symptoms and the ECG. Very high levels most often mean a heart attack has occurred. Raised levels do not always mean a heart attack, because other heart conditions can raise troponin. A UK study reported by University Hospital Southampton found raised troponin in some people with unrelated conditions, so results need careful interpretation. After a heart attack, levels may stay high for one to two weeks.

body.heading: How do the results fit with the ECG?
body.body: The ECG and troponin results together help to identify the type of heart attack. A STEMI shows particular changes on the ECG. An NSTEMI is found when the ECG does not show those changes but blood tests show heart damage.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS advises calling 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw. The NHS also advises calling 999 for someone who has passed out. The BHF advises calling an ambulance rather than travelling to hospital yourself, because paramedics can start care and tests on the way.

body.heading: What do NICE recommendations say about newer tests?
body.body: NICE recommends high-sensitivity troponin tests as options for ruling out a type of heart attack called NSTEMI in emergency departments. NICE describes strategies using a single sample on arrival or a second sample after the first, depending on the test and result. A review notes that troponin levels tend to be lower in women than in men because of smaller heart size. NICE material describes the ECG as the first-choice test for a suspected STEMI, with the diagnosis based on changes in the ST segment.

type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.name: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.headline: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared: causes, symptoms and treatment
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.
keyPoints: In type 1 diabetes the immune system attacks and destroys the cells that make insulin.
In type 2 diabetes the body makes too little insulin or the insulin it makes does not work well.
Type 1 often develops quickly, especially in young people, while type 2 develops slowly over years.
Type 1 is treated with insulin and blood glucose checks; type 2 is managed with lifestyle changes and sometimes medicines.
There is no cure for diabetes at the moment, although type 2 can sometimes go into remission.

body.heading: What do the two types have in common?
body.body:
Diabetes is a condition in which there is too much glucose, a type of sugar, in the blood. Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, a hormone made by cells in the pancreas.

The two types share several symptoms: increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss. The difference lies in why the problem arises and how it is managed.

body.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition. The immune system attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

In young people the symptoms usually develop very quickly, over a few days or weeks. In adults, the symptoms often take longer to develop, sometimes a few months.

body.heading: What causes type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Either the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work as well as it should.

Diabetes UK lists age, family history, ethnicity and weight among the risk factors.

Type 2 develops slowly over a period of years, so the signs may not be obvious.

body.heading: How are the two types treated?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin, which is needed for life, alongside monitoring of blood glucose.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with lifestyle changes such as eating healthily, exercising and trying to lose weight, and sometimes with medicines. Medicine may be added if needed, such as metformin, and some people also need insulin.

body.heading: Can diabetes be cured?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says there is no cure for diabetes at the moment. Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, and it can sometimes be prevented.

Remission does not mean the condition has gone for good, which is why regular checks are still part of care.

body.heading: How is diabetes checked, and who should be seen?
body.body:
Blood tests are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. The site's pages on blood glucose and on HbA1c explain what they show, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

The NHS says to get a GP appointment as soon as possible for the main symptoms of diabetes; for a child, to contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure what to do. The NHS website sets out the symptoms to look for.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: For a child with diabetes symptoms, contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure; call 999 if a child is very drowsy, confused, breathing fast or deeply, has severe tummy pain or keeps vomiting. In someone with diabetes, loss of appetite, feeling or being sick, a high temperature, stomach pain or fruity-smelling breath needs urgent medical attention, so call NHS 111 or 999 if severe. Remission means blood sugar stays below the diabetes level for at least six months without diabetes medicine.

references.title: Diabetes UK: Differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes
